ext-oblique.name: External oblique
ext-oblique.does: Rotates and side-bends the trunk; wraps the side of the abdomen.
ext-oblique.refers: Abdominal wall, the side of the belly and down into the groin; can feel like heartburn or a side stitch.

ant-delt.name: Anterior deltoid (front delt)
ant-delt.does: Lifts the arm forward and turns it inward; the main mover in pressing and front raises.
ant-delt.refers: Front of the shoulder and down the front of the upper arm, close to the muscle itself. Often blamed on the joint.

lat-delt.name: Lateral deltoid (middle delt)
lat-delt.does: Lifts the arm out to the side; holds the arm up when carrying or working at shoulder height.
lat-delt.refers: Outside of the shoulder cap and the side of the upper arm toward the deltoid's insertion.

post-delt.name: Posterior deltoid (rear delt)
post-delt.does: Pulls the arm back and turns it outward; works in rows and reaching behind.
post-delt.refers: Back of the shoulder and the back of the upper arm.

teres-major.name: Teres major
teres-major.does: The lat's little helper: pulls the arm down, back and inward.
teres-major.refers: Back of the shoulder and the back of the upper arm, sometimes the back of the forearm. Hurts reaching up and forward.

pec-major-clav.name: Pectoralis major, upper (clavicular) head
pec-major-clav.does: Raises the arm forward and across the body; the 'upper chest' in incline pressing.
pec-major-clav.refers: Front of the shoulder over the front delt, often mistaken for a front-shoulder joint problem.

pec-major-stern.name: Pectoralis major, lower (sternal) head
pec-major-stern.does: Pulls the arm down and across the chest; the main 'chest' in pressing and hugging.
pec-major-stern.refers: Front of the chest, down the inner arm to the inner elbow and the ring and little fingers. Chest pain must be checked by a doctor first.

subclavius.name: Subclavius
subclavius.does: Small muscle under the collarbone that steadies it against the breastbone.
subclavius.refers: Under the collarbone and down the front of the arm and forearm into the thumb, index and middle fingers.

coracobrachialis.name: Coracobrachialis
coracobrachialis.does: Deep upper-arm muscle that pulls the arm forward and toward the body.
coracobrachialis.refers: Front of the shoulder, the back of the upper arm and forearm, and the back of the hand toward the middle finger.

biceps-long.name: Biceps, long head
biceps-long.does: Bends the elbow, turns the palm up and helps hold the ball of the shoulder in its socket.
biceps-long.refers: Front of the shoulder over the biceps groove and down the front of the arm toward the elbow crease.

biceps-short.name: Biceps, short head
biceps-short.does: Bends the elbow and pulls the arm forward and across the body.
biceps-short.refers: Front of the shoulder near the collarbone tip, the inner front of the arm and the elbow crease.

triceps-long.name: Triceps, long head
triceps-long.does: Straightens the elbow and pulls the arm back; the only triceps head that crosses the shoulder.
triceps-long.refers: Back of the shoulder and arm, up toward the base of the neck, and down the back of the forearm.

triceps-lateral.name: Triceps, lateral head
triceps-lateral.does: Straightens the elbow; the outer 'horseshoe' of the back of the arm.
triceps-lateral.refers: Back of the upper arm and the outside of the elbow, a common tennis-elbow look-alike, and the back of the forearm.

triceps-medial.name: Triceps, medial head
triceps-medial.does: Deep head that straightens the elbow in every push.
triceps-medial.refers: The point of the elbow and the inner elbow, a golfer's-elbow look-alike, sometimes the ring and little fingers.

middle-trap.name: Middle trapezius
middle-trap.does: Pulls the shoulder blades together and holds them back.
middle-trap.refers: Burning ache between the shoulder blade and the spine, and the top of the shoulder.

lower-trap.name: Lower trapezius
lower-trap.does: Pulls the shoulder blades down and rotates them up so the arm can go overhead.
lower-trap.refers: Up the back of the neck to the base of the skull, the top of the shoulder, and along the inner shoulder blade. A hidden driver of neck tension.

rhomboid-minor.name: Rhomboid minor
rhomboid-minor.does: Upper rhomboid: pulls the top of the shoulder blade toward the spine.
rhomboid-minor.refers: Along the inner edge of the upper shoulder blade, next to the spine.

rhomboid-major.name: Rhomboid major
rhomboid-major.does: Pulls the shoulder blade toward the spine and down; steadies it when you pull.
rhomboid-major.refers: Between the shoulder blade and the spine. Often strained because tight chest muscles pull the blades apart.

wrist-ext.name: Wrist extensors (ECRL, ECRB)
wrist-ext.does: Lift the wrist; work hard to steady it when you grip or type.
wrist-ext.refers: Outside of the elbow (tennis elbow) and the back of the wrist and hand on the thumb side.

finger-ext.name: Finger extensors (extensor digitorum)
finger-ext.does: Straighten the fingers; work with every click, tap and grip release.
finger-ext.refers: Back of the forearm and back of the hand into the middle or ring finger; a 'stiff fingers' feeling.

wrist-flex.name: Wrist flexors (FCR, FCU)
wrist-flex.does: Bend the wrist and steady it in pulling and lifting.
wrist-flex.refers: Inside of the elbow (golfer's elbow) and the palm side of the wrist.

finger-flex.name: Finger flexors
finger-flex.does: Close the fingers and thumb into a grip.
finger-flex.refers: Palm and the front of the fingers, sometimes a 'trigger finger' catching feeling.

iliocostalis.name: Iliocostalis (outer back extensor)
iliocostalis.does: Outer column of the back extensors; keeps you upright and bends you sideways.
iliocostalis.refers: Low back and buttock from the lumbar part; the lower shoulder blade and even the belly from the thoracic part.

longissimus.name: Longissimus (middle back extensor)
longissimus.does: Long middle column of the back extensors; holds posture all day.
longissimus.refers: Low in the buttock and over the SI joint, often well below where the muscle actually is.

adductor-longus.name: Adductor longus & brevis
adductor-longus.does: Pull the thigh inward; steady the pelvis when you change direction.
adductor-longus.refers: Deep groin, the inner thigh and down to the inner knee and top of the shin.

adductor-magnus.name: Adductor magnus
adductor-magnus.does: The big inner-thigh muscle; pulls the leg in and helps extend the hip.
adductor-magnus.refers: Deep inside the pelvis and groin, and the inner thigh from the groin toward the knee.

biceps-femoris.name: Biceps femoris (outer hamstring)
biceps-femoris.does: Bends the knee, extends the hip and turns the lower leg out.
biceps-femoris.refers: Back of the knee on the outside and up the back of the thigh.

medial-hamstrings.name: Semitendinosus & semimembranosus (inner hamstrings)
medial-hamstrings.does: Bend the knee, extend the hip and turn the lower leg in.
medial-hamstrings.refers: The buttock crease, back of the thigh and the inner back of the knee, sometimes the inner calf.

vastus-intermedius.name: Vastus intermedius
vastus-intermedius.does: Deep quad under the rectus femoris; straightens the knee.
vastus-intermedius.refers: Front of the mid-thigh, worse climbing stairs or standing up from a chair.

suboccipitals.name: Suboccipitals
suboccipitals.does: Tiny muscles that tilt and steady the head at the base of the skull.
suboccipitals.refers: A band of headache from the base of the skull wrapping to behind the eye and the forehead. Often mistaken for migraine.

occipitalis.name: Occipitalis
occipitalis.does: Scalp muscle at the back of the head.
occipitalis.refers: Ache at the back of the head that can shoot through the skull to behind the eye, with scalp tenderness.

upper-trap.name: Upper trapezius
upper-trap.does: Shrugs and lifts the shoulders; holds up the arms all day.
upper-trap.refers: Up the side of the neck, behind the ear and into the temple (a question-mark shape). Very common tension headache source.

scm.name: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM)
scm.does: Turns and bends the head; runs from behind the ear to the collarbone.
scm.refers: Forehead, around and behind the eye, cheek, ear and top of the head. Can cause dizziness or ear fullness.

levator.name: Levator scapulae
levator.does: Lifts the shoulder blade and turns the neck.
levator.refers: The angle where the neck meets the shoulder, down the inner edge of the shoulder blade. Classic "stiff neck, can't turn my head".

scalenes.name: Scalenes
scalenes.does: Side-neck muscles that lift the top ribs when you breathe.
scalenes.refers: Chest, front and back of the upper arm, inner shoulder blade and down the forearm to the thumb and index finger. Can add tingling in the hand.

splenius.name: Splenius capitis & cervicis
splenius.does: Extend and rotate the head and neck.
splenius.refers: Pain on the top of the head, and deep ache inside the head behind the eye.

temporalis.name: Temporalis
temporalis.does: Closes the jaw; fan-shaped over the temple.
temporalis.refers: Temple headache, above the eyebrow and into the upper teeth.

masseter.name: Masseter
masseter.does: The main chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw.
masseter.refers: Jaw, cheek, in front of the ear and the back teeth. Can feel like an earache or toothache.

supraspinatus.name: Supraspinatus (rotator cuff)
supraspinatus.does: Starts lifting the arm out to the side; keeps the ball in the socket.
supraspinatus.refers: Deep ache at the top and side of the shoulder that can run down the outside of the arm to the elbow. Worse reaching overhead.

infraspinatus.name: Infraspinatus (rotator cuff)
infraspinatus.does: Rotates the arm outward; covers the back of the shoulder blade.
infraspinatus.refers: Deep in the front of the shoulder joint, down the front and outside of the arm. Hard to reach behind your back or sleep on that side.

teres-minor.name: Teres minor (rotator cuff)
teres-minor.does: Small outward rotator under the infraspinatus.
teres-minor.refers: A localized deep ache at the back of the shoulder.

subscapularis.name: Subscapularis (rotator cuff)
subscapularis.does: Rotates the arm inward; lines the underside of the shoulder blade.
subscapularis.refers: Back of the shoulder, down the back of the arm, sometimes a band around the wrist. Can feel like a frozen shoulder.

pec-minor.name: Pectoralis minor
pec-minor.does: Pulls the shoulder blade forward; tight with rounded shoulders.
pec-minor.refers: Front of the shoulder and chest, down the inner arm to the last three fingers. Can pinch nerves to the hand.

serratus.name: Serratus anterior
serratus.does: Wraps the ribs and holds the shoulder blade to the chest wall.
serratus.refers: Side of the rib cage and the bottom tip of the shoulder blade; a side "stitch" that hurts with deep breaths.

lats.name: Latissimus dorsi
lats.does: Pulls the arm down and back; the widest back muscle.
lats.refers: Bottom tip of the shoulder blade and down the back of the arm to the ring and little fingers.

intercostals.name: Intercostals
intercostals.does: Small muscles between the ribs that help you breathe.
intercostals.refers: Sharp or aching pain along the rib, worse with deep breaths, coughing or twisting.

brachioradialis.name: Brachioradialis
brachioradialis.does: Bends the elbow with the thumb up (hammer position).
brachioradialis.refers: Outside of the elbow and the web of the thumb.

supinator.name: Supinator
supinator.refers: Outer elbow and the thumb web; common in tennis elbow that won't settle.

ql.name: Quadratus lumborum (QL)
ql.does: Deep low-back muscle that hikes the hip and steadies the spine.
ql.refers: Low back and flank, over the SI joint and buttock, and the point of the hip. Hurts rolling in bed, standing up or coughing.

multifidus.name: Multifidus
multifidus.refers: Deep, pinpoint pain right next to the spine, the sacrum and sometimes the tailbone.

psoas.name: Psoas
psoas.does: Main hip flexor; runs from the lumbar spine to the thigh.
psoas.refers: Vertical band along the low back, plus the front of the thigh and groin. Hard to stand up straight after sitting.

iliacus.name: Iliacus
iliacus.does: Hip flexor lining the inside of the pelvis.
iliacus.refers: Groin, front of the thigh, and the back of the pelvis high in the glute. Often overlooked.

glute-med.name: Gluteus medius
glute-med.does: Holds the pelvis level when you stand on one leg.
glute-med.refers: Along the belt line, over the SI joint, the buttock and the top of the hip.

glute-min.name: Gluteus minimus
glute-min.does: Deep hip stabilizer under the glute medius.
glute-min.refers: Outer hip down the side of the thigh and leg to the ankle, or down the back of the thigh and calf. A common sciatica look-alike.

piriformis.name: Piriformis
piriformis.does: Rotates the hip outward; sits over the sciatic nerve.
piriformis.refers: Mid-buttock and back of the hip, down the back-outside of the thigh toward the calf.

glute-max.name: Gluteus maximus
glute-max.does: Extends the hip; powers stairs, hills and standing up.
glute-max.refers: Buttock and the tailbone; aches with long sitting and walking uphill.

tfl.name: Tensor fasciae latae (TFL)
tfl.does: Small front-outer hip muscle that pulls on the IT band.
tfl.refers: Front-outer hip down the outside of the thigh, usually stopping at the knee.

rectus-femoris.name: Rectus femoris (quads)
rectus-femoris.does: Front-thigh muscle that crosses both hip and knee.
rectus-femoris.refers: A deep ache around and behind the kneecap, and the front of the hip bone. Worse on stairs or after sitting.

vmo.name: Vastus medialis
vmo.does: Inner quad that guides the kneecap.
vmo.refers: Inner knee and inside of the kneecap; can make the knee feel like it buckles.

vastus-lateralis.name: Vastus lateralis
vastus-lateralis.does: Outer quad, the largest of the four.
vastus-lateralis.refers: Down the outer thigh to the outside of the knee; can make lying on that side painful.

popliteus.name: Popliteus
popliteus.does: Small muscle that unlocks the knee.
popliteus.refers: Back of the knee; worse crouching, walking downhill or running.

gastroc.name: Gastrocnemius
gastroc.does: Upper calf; pushes you off the ground and bends the knee.
gastroc.refers: Upper calf, back of the knee and the arch of the foot; deep cramp-like tightness.

soleus.name: Soleus
soleus.does: Deep lower calf; holds you upright when you stand and walk.
soleus.refers: Heel and Achilles tendon, lower calf; can contribute to plantar fasciitis.

tib-post.name: Tibialis posterior
tib-post.does: Deep calf muscle that holds up the arch.
tib-post.refers: Inner ankle and arch, along the inner shin; common with flat feet.

tib-ant.name: Tibialis anterior
tib-ant.refers: Front of the shin, front of the ankle and the big toe.

peroneals.name: Peroneals (fibularis)
peroneals.does: Outer-leg muscles that steady the ankle.
peroneals.refers: Outer ankle and outside of the foot; common after ankle sprains.

foot-intrinsics.name: Foot muscles (intrinsics)
foot-intrinsics.does: Small muscles in the sole that shape the arch.
foot-intrinsics.refers: Heel and sole of the foot; first-step-in-the-morning pain like plantar fasciitis.

suboccipitals.origin: Top two vertebrae in the neck (C1 and C2).
suboccipitals.insertion: Occipital bone at the base of the skull.
suboccipitals.action: Tilts the head back, turns the head side-to-side, and makes fine adjustments to head position. Key for head posture and balance.
symptoms: A headache that feels like a tight band starting at the base of your skull.
Pain that wraps forward to behind your eye or into your forehead.
The headache can feel deep, achy, and persistent, sometimes mistaken for a migraine.
Stiffness and reduced ability to nod or tuck your chin.
Pain is often worse when sitting at a desk or looking down at a phone.
May disrupt sleep if pillows don't support the neck properly.

questions.q: Does your headache feel like a tight band wrapping from the back of your head to behind your eye?
Is the pain worse when you spend a long time looking down at a screen or book?
Do you feel stiffness mostly when trying to tuck your chin to your chest?
Does pressing gently into the hollows at the very base of your skull reproduce the headache feeling?
Does your pain feel different from a typical 'stiff neck' on the side, and more like a deep headache?

tests.name: Chin Tuck Test
tests.how: Sit or stand tall. Gently tuck your chin towards your throat as if making a double chin, without looking down. Keep the back of your neck long.
tests.positive: Pain or a strong pulling sensation at the base of your skull, or an inability to perform the movement smoothly.

causes: Forward head posture from prolonged screen time ('tech neck').
Sleeping with too many pillows or on your stomach.
Whiplash injury from a car accident or fall.
Clenching your jaw or grinding your teeth (bruxism).
Eye strain causing you to jut your chin forward.
Stress and emotional tension.
redFlags: Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache.
Headache accompanied by fever, stiff neck (can't touch chin to chest), and confusion.
Headache after a head injury, especially with loss of consciousness or vomiting.
New headache over age 50, or a significant change in your usual headache pattern.

calm.name: Suboccipital Release
calm.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Place two lacrosse balls (or a peanut) under the base of your skull. Gently nod 'yes' and shake your head 'no' to massage the area.

calm.name: Chin Tucks
calm.dose: 2 x 10 slow reps, several times daily
calm.how: Gently nod your chin towards your throat as if making a double chin. This is a very small, subtle movement to activate the deep neck muscles.

calm.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back and focus on breathing into your belly, not your chest. This helps calm the nervous system and reduce overall muscle tension.

restore.name: Chin Glides
restore.how: Sit tall and gently glide your head backward over your shoulders, keeping your eyes level. This reverses the forward head posture that strains these muscles.

restore.name: Upper Cervical Mobility
restore.dose: 2 x 5 reps each way, once daily
restore.how: Tuck your chin slightly. Gently turn your head as far as you can to one side, then the other. The movement should feel like it's coming from the very top of your neck.

strengthen.name: Isometric Neck Holds
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10-second holds in each direction, daily
strengthen.how: Sit tall. Place your palm on your forehead and gently press your head forward into your hand without moving. Repeat pressing into your hand on the side and back of your head.

strengthen.name: Seated Posture Reset
strengthen.how: Use this video to actively correct your posture throughout the day, strengthening the muscles that support a neutral head position.

strengthen.name: Scapular Retraction
strengthen.how: Strengthening your mid-back muscles provides a stable base for your neck and head, reducing the strain on the suboccipitals.

habits: Adjust your monitor so the top third is at eye level to prevent looking down.
Take frequent micro-breaks from your desk to stand up and reset your posture.
Use a supportive pillow that keeps your neck in a neutral line with your spine.
Avoid cradling your phone between your ear and shoulder.
suboccipitals.expect: With consistent exercises and habit changes, most people feel a noticeable reduction in headache frequency and intensity within 2-4 weeks.
suboccipitals.seePro: If your headaches are severe, worsening, or accompanied by dizziness, numbness, or weakness, please book an appointment for a full evaluation.

occipitalis.insertion: Galea aponeurotica (a tough layer of fibrous tissue covering the top of the skull).
occipitalis.action: Pulls the scalp backward. Works with the frontalis muscle to raise the eyebrows and express surprise.
symptoms: Aching pain at the very back of the head.
Pain that feels like it shoots through the skull to behind one eye.
Tenderness of the scalp, making it uncomfortable to brush hair or wear a hat.
A feeling of pressure or a 'skull cap' of pain.
Pain is often triggered or worsened by stress and clenching.

questions.q: Is your scalp at the back of your head very tender to the touch?
Does the pain sometimes feel like it's shooting from the back of your head straight through to your eye?
Do you notice the pain more when you are stressed or clenching your jaw?
Does the pain feel superficial, like it's in the scalp itself, rather than deep in the neck joints?
Does wearing a tight hat, ponytail, or headband make the pain worse?

tests.name: Scalp Palpation
tests.how: Use your fingertips to gently but firmly press and move the skin over the bone at the back of your head. Explore the area for any exquisitely tender spots.
tests.positive: Finding a specific point of tenderness that, when pressed, reproduces your familiar head or eye pain.

causes: Chronic forward head posture, which puts tension on the entire back line of the body.
Emotional stress leading to unconscious scalp muscle tension.
Clenching the jaw or grinding teeth (bruxism).
Prolonged desk work or screen time.
Whiplash or other head/neck trauma.
redFlags: Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache.
Scalp tenderness with fever, weight loss, or vision changes (especially in older adults).
Headache that worsens with coughing or straining.
Pain that started after a significant head injury.

calm.name: Occipitalis Release
calm.how: Place a lacrosse ball or your fingertips on the tender spots at the back of your head. Apply gentle, sustained pressure or make small circles without sliding on the skin.

calm.name: Chin Glides
calm.how: Gently glide your head backward over your shoulders, keeping your eyes level. This reduces the tension on the back of the scalp.

calm.name: Box Breathing
calm.how: Inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4. This technique helps lower stress and reduce unconscious muscle clenching.

restore.name: Neck Neuroglide
restore.dose: 1 x 10 slow reps each side, daily
restore.how: This gentle nerve mobilization helps reduce tension patterns that can affect the scalp and neck.

restore.name: Seated Posture Reset
restore.how: Actively correcting your posture reduces the chronic strain on the muscles at the back of your head and neck.

strengthen.name: Deep Neck Flexor Activation
strengthen.how: Strengthening the muscles at the front of your neck helps to balance the tension at the back, improving head posture.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Building strength in your upper back creates a strong foundation for your neck and head, offloading the scalp muscles. Use a light weight.

habits: Be mindful of jaw clenching during the day; let your jaw hang loose with teeth slightly apart.
Avoid tight hairstyles, hats, or headbands that put pressure on the scalp.
Ensure your desk setup promotes a neutral head position.
Practice stress-reduction techniques like meditation or short walks.
occipitalis.expect: Scalp tenderness and referred pain often improve within 1-2 weeks with consistent release work and postural correction. Full resolution depends on managing underlying stress and habits.
occipitalis.seePro: If your headache is severe, doesn't respond to these measures, or is accompanied by vision changes, please book an appointment for a thorough evaluation.

upper-trap.origin: Base of the skull (occiput), nuchal ligament, and spinous process of C7.
upper-trap.insertion: Outer third of the clavicle (collarbone) and acromion process of the scapula (shoulder blade).
upper-trap.action: Shrugs the shoulders up, tilts and turns the head, and helps stabilize the shoulder blade.
upper-trap.nerve: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) and cervical nerves (C3, C4).
symptoms: Pain that wraps up the side of the neck to the temple, like a question mark.
A very common source of 'tension headaches'.
A heavy, aching, or burning feeling on top of the shoulder.
Stiffness in the neck, especially when tilting your head to the side.
Pain can be constant and is often worse at the end of a stressful workday.

questions.q: Does your pain start on top of your shoulder and travel up the side of your neck to your temple?
Do you feel a constant, heavy weight or ache on your shoulders, especially when stressed?
Does carrying a heavy bag or purse on your shoulder make the pain significantly worse?
Does tilting your head away from the painful side and gently pulling with your hand reproduce the pain?
Do you often find yourself shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears when you're concentrating or cold?

tests.name: Pincer Grip Palpation
tests.how: Use your opposite hand to grasp the thick muscle on top of your shoulder, between your neck and shoulder point. Squeeze gently and search for a tight, tender band of muscle.
tests.positive: Finding a very tender spot that, when squeezed, refers pain up the side of your neck or into your temple.

tests.name: Active Side Bend
tests.how: Sit tall and slowly tilt your ear toward your shoulder without shrugging. Compare the range of motion and sensation on both sides.
tests.positive: Significant tightness, pulling, or pain on the stretched side, or a noticeable difference in how far you can go compared to the other side.

causes: Chronic stress, which leads to unconscious shoulder shrugging.
Poor posture, especially slouching with a forward head.
Carrying heavy bags, backpacks, or children on one side.
Repetitive arm movements with poor shoulder stability (e.g., typing with a high keyboard).
Chilling of the muscle, like sitting in a draft.
Trauma such as whiplash.
mimics: Levator scapulae pain (more at the angle of the neck)
redFlags: Pain accompanied by numbness, tingling, or weakness that radiates down the entire arm.
Sudden, severe headache or neck pain after an injury.
Unexplained swelling or a lump in the neck/shoulder area.
Pain associated with fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss.

calm.name: Upper Trap Release
calm.dose: 2-3 minutes per side, once or twice daily
calm.how: Place a lacrosse ball between your upper trap muscle and a wall. Lean into the ball and gently roll up and down and side-to-side to find and release tender spots.

calm.name: Upper Trap Stretch
calm.dose: 2 x 30 seconds each side, twice daily
calm.how: Sit tall and gently tilt your ear toward your opposite shoulder. Use your hand for a light overpressure, but do not force it.

calm.name: Shoulder Shrugs & Drops
calm.how: Inhale and shrug your shoulders up to your ears, then exhale with a sigh and let them drop completely. This helps reset muscle tension.

restore.name: Eccentric Neck Stretch
restore.dose: 2 x 5 slow reps each side, daily
restore.how: Use a towel to gently resist as you slowly return your head from a side-bent position to neutral. This builds control and resilience in the muscle.

restore.name: Scapular CARs
restore.how: Controlled Articular Rotations help improve the movement and awareness of your shoulder blades, which can reduce the workload on the upper traps.

restore.name: Seated Posture Reset
restore.how: Regularly resetting your posture helps train your body to stop over-relying on the upper traps for support.

strengthen.name: Farmer Carry
strengthen.dose: 3 sets of 30-second walks, twice a week
strengthen.how: Carry a moderate weight in each hand. Keep your chest up and shoulders pulled down and back. This teaches the traps to stabilize the shoulder girdle correctly.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: This exercise strengthens the mid-back and external rotators, which helps to counterbalance the pull of tight upper traps and improve posture.

strengthen.name: Wall Slides
strengthen.how: This can also be done standing against a wall. It activates the lower trapezius and serratus anterior, muscles that help depress the shoulder blades and offload the upper traps.

habits: Adjust your chair and keyboard so your elbows are at a 90-degree angle and your shoulders are relaxed.
Use a backpack with two straps instead of a single-strap shoulder bag.
Be mindful of cradling your phone. Use a headset or speakerphone instead.
During stressful moments, take a deep breath and consciously drop your shoulders away from your ears.
upper-trap.expect: You can expect significant relief from pain and headaches within 1-2 weeks of consistent stretching and release work. Lasting relief comes from building strength and changing habits over 4-6 weeks.
upper-trap.seePro: If you have persistent numbness or tingling in your arm, or if the pain doesn't improve with conservative care, book an appointment for a more detailed assessment.

scm.origin: Top of the sternum (breastbone) and inner part of the clavicle (collarbone).
scm.insertion: Mastoid process of the temporal bone (the bony bump behind the ear).
scm.action: When one side acts, it turns the head to the opposite side and bends it to the same side. Acting together, they bend the neck forward.
scm.nerve: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) and cervical nerves (C2, C3).
symptoms: Pain in the forehead, often described as a 'headache over the eye'.
Pain around the eye, in the cheek, or in the jaw (TMJ) area.
Dizziness, vertigo, or a feeling of imbalance, especially with head turning.
Ear symptoms like ringing (tinnitus), fullness, or deep ear pain.
Pain at the top of the head or a sore throat feeling when swallowing.

questions.q: Do you experience pain or pressure in your forehead, above or around your eye?
Have you felt dizzy, off-balance, or had ringing in your ears that seems related to your neck pain?
Does the pain get worse when you turn your head to look over your shoulder, like when backing up a car?
Do you have pain in your cheek or jaw that has been mistaken for a sinus or dental problem?
Do you often sleep on your stomach or with your head turned sharply to one side?

tests.name: SCM Palpation
tests.how: Turn your head to one side and look slightly up; the SCM muscle will pop out. Gently pinch the muscle between your thumb and fingers and feel for tender, ropey spots from behind your ear down to your collarbone.
tests.positive: Finding a very tender spot that reproduces your specific headache, face pain, or dizziness.

causes: Whiplash injuries, even minor ones.
Forward head posture, which over-stretches and strains the SCM.
Sleeping on your stomach or with thick pillows.
Chronic coughing, or activities involving deep, forceful breathing (e.g., playing a wind instrument).
Turning your head to one side for long periods (e.g., watching TV, dual monitor setup).
mimics: Inner ear problems (e.g., BPPV, vestibular neuritis)
redFlags: Sudden onset of severe dizziness or vertigo, especially with difficulty speaking, walking, or seeing.
Pain or swelling of the lymph nodes along the muscle that doesn't resolve.
A pulsating sensation in the neck (do not press on this).
Headache accompanied by fever and a stiff neck that prevents you from touching your chin to your chest.

calm.name: SCM Release
calm.how: Gently pinch the muscle between your thumb and fingers as shown in the video. Hold tender spots with gentle pressure until they soften. Be careful not to press on the pulse in your neck (carotid artery).

calm.name: Gentle SCM Stretch
calm.how: Sit tall. Gently tilt your head back, then turn away from the side you want to stretch and tilt your ear to the opposite shoulder. You should feel a gentle pull along the front/side of your neck.

calm.name: Chin Glides
calm.how: This movement helps to reposition your head over your shoulders, taking the chronic strain off the SCM muscles.

restore.name: Neck Neuroglide
restore.dose: 1 x 10 slow reps each side, daily
restore.how: This nerve mobilization can help calm down the nerve pathways that contribute to SCM tension and its unusual symptoms like dizziness.

restore.name: Deep Neck Flexor Activation
restore.how: Strengthening the small muscles at the front of your neck provides stability and helps the SCM to relax and do its job of moving, not just holding.

strengthen.name: Isometric Neck Rotation
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10-second holds each side, every other day
strengthen.how: Place your hand on the side of your head. Gently try to turn your head into your hand, but don't let it move. This strengthens the SCM in a controlled way.

strengthen.name: Core Brace
strengthen.how: A stable core provides a foundation for your head and neck. Learning to brace your core reduces strain on neck muscles during daily activities.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: A strong upper back helps maintain good posture, which is the key to unloading the SCM long-term. Use a light weight and focus on form.

habits: Avoid sleeping on your stomach. Try sleeping on your back or side with a supportive pillow.
Position screens directly in front of you to avoid prolonged head turning.
When reading a book or on your phone, prop it up to eye level.
Practice diaphragmatic (belly) breathing to avoid using your neck muscles for respiration.
scm.expect: Symptoms like dizziness and ear fullness can improve quickly, within a week of starting release work. The headache and facial pain patterns may take 2-4 weeks to resolve as you improve your posture and strength.
scm.seePro: If you experience severe, persistent dizziness, hearing loss, or any of the red flag symptoms, please book an appointment immediately for a comprehensive neurological and vestibular screen.

levator.origin: Transverse processes of the top four cervical vertebrae (C1-C4).
levator.insertion: Superior angle and medial border of the scapula (top inner corner of the shoulder blade).
levator.action: Lifts the shoulder blade (scapula) and bends and turns the neck to the same side.
levator.nerve: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and cervical nerves (C3, C4).
symptoms: The classic 'stiff neck' pain, making it hard to turn your head to look over your shoulder.
A deep, nagging ache at the angle where your neck meets your shoulder.
Pain that refers down the inside edge of your shoulder blade.
A feeling that you constantly need to stretch your neck, but it provides little relief.
Waking up with a stiff neck after sleeping in an awkward position.

questions.q: Do you feel a sharp or aching pain right at the corner where your neck and shoulder meet?
Is your main problem an inability to turn your head to one side, as if your neck is 'locked'?
Does the pain also travel down along the inner border of your shoulder blade?
Do you often carry a bag on that shoulder or cradle a phone there?
Does the pain feel worse in the morning after sleeping?

tests.name: Head Turn Test
tests.how: Sit tall and try to turn your head to look over one shoulder, then the other. Keep your shoulders still.
tests.positive: Significant pain and/or a major restriction in movement on one side compared to the other. You may feel a sharp pull at the angle of your neck.

tests.name: Palpation at Insertion
tests.how: Reach over your opposite shoulder with your fingers and find the top, inner corner of your shoulder blade. Press firmly into the muscle at that corner.
tests.positive: Finding an exquisitely tender spot that reproduces your neck and shoulder blade pain.

causes: Sleeping with your head in an awkward position, especially on your stomach or with a poor pillow.
Holding a phone between your ear and shoulder.
Carrying a heavy backpack or purse on one shoulder.
Sitting in a draft or under an A/C vent, which can chill the muscle.
Forward head posture and rounded shoulders from desk work.
Emotional stress, leading to chronic shoulder shrugging.
mimics: Upper trapezius pain (often co-exists, but referral is different)
redFlags: Neck stiffness accompanied by high fever, headache, and sensitivity to light.
Pain, numbness, or weakness that radiates all the way down your arm to your hand.
A recent fall or trauma to the head or neck.
Difficulty swallowing or a change in your voice associated with the neck pain.

calm.name: Levator Scapulae Stretch
calm.dose: 2 x 30 seconds each side, twice daily
calm.how: Follow the video cues precisely: turn your head away from the painful side and look down towards your opposite armpit. Use gentle hand pressure.

calm.name: Levator Release
calm.how: Place a lacrosse ball between the top/inner edge of your shoulder blade and a wall. Lean in and roll gently to find and hold pressure on tender spots.

calm.name: Shoulder Blade Squeezes
calm.how: Sit or stand tall. Gently squeeze your shoulder blades together and down, as if tucking them into your back pockets. Hold for 2 seconds and release.

restore.name: Scapular CARs
restore.dose: 1 x 5 large, slow circles each direction, daily
restore.how: This exercise improves the mobility and control of your shoulder blade, which helps the levator scapulae to relax and function properly.

restore.name: Eccentric Neck Stretch
restore.dose: 2 x 5 slow reps in the levator stretch position, daily
restore.how: After stretching, use a towel to gently resist as you bring your head back to neutral. This builds strength and control in the muscle's lengthened range.

restore.name: Thoracic Rotation
restore.how: Improving mobility in your mid-back reduces the rotational stress on your neck, giving the levator a break.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: Pull a light band toward your face with elbows high, squeezing the shoulder blades back and down. Keep the neck long and relaxed.

strengthen.name: Farmer Carry
strengthen.dose: 3 sets of 30-second walks, twice a week
strengthen.how: Walking with weights teaches you to keep your shoulder blades 'down and back', strengthening the muscles that oppose the levator's shrugging action.

strengthen.name: Push Up
strengthen.dose: 3 sets to near failure, twice a week
strengthen.how: Proper push-ups (even on knees or a wall) strengthen the serratus anterior, a key muscle for scapular stability that helps offload the levator.

habits: Use a headset or speakerphone to avoid cradling the phone.
Evaluate your pillow: it should fill the space between your head and the mattress, keeping your neck neutral.
When sitting, ensure your armrests are at a height that allows your shoulders to relax down.
Alternate which shoulder you use to carry a bag, or switch to a backpack.
levator.expect: Acute 'stiff neck' pain and range of motion limitations often improve significantly within 3-7 days with consistent stretching and release. Chronic ache may take 3-6 weeks to fully resolve as you build strength and change habits.
levator.seePro: If you can't turn your head at all, or if the pain is severe and not improving after a week, please book an appointment. Also, seek care for any radiating arm symptoms.

scalenes.insertion: The top surfaces of your first and second ribs.
scalenes.action: Lifts the top two ribs to help you take a deep breath (accessory breathing). Also bends your neck to the side and helps with turning.
symptoms: Aching pain in the chest, sometimes mistaken for a heart issue.
Pain, numbness, or tingling that travels from the neck down the arm to the thumb and index finger.
A feeling of a 'dead arm' or waking up with a numb hand.
Aching pain between the shoulder blades.
Pain is often worse when taking a deep breath, coughing, or carrying heavy items.
Difficulty finding a comfortable sleeping position for your head and arm.

questions.q: Do you feel pain or tingling that runs from your neck down your arm to your thumb and index finger?
Does your pain get worse when you carry something heavy, like a bag of groceries?
Do you ever feel a strange, non-cardiac pain in your chest, especially after a lot of coughing?
Do you often wake up with a 'dead arm' or tingling in your hand?
Is your pain aggravated by looking at a phone or computer screen for long periods?

tests.name: Scalene Relief Test
tests.how: While sitting, gently lift the arm on the painful side and rest your forearm and hand on top of your head. Hold for 30 seconds.
tests.positive: A significant reduction or complete relief of your arm and hand symptoms while your arm is raised.

causes: Shallow, chest-breathing patterns, especially during stress or intense exercise.
Forward head posture from prolonged desk work or phone use ('tech neck').
Whiplash injury from a car accident or fall.
Chronic coughing from asthma, bronchitis, or allergies.
Carrying heavy backpacks or purses with a strap over one shoulder.
Sleeping with your arm overhead or under your head.
mimics: Cervical disc herniation (pinched nerve in the neck).
Angina or cardiac pain (always rule this out first with a physician).
redFlags: Chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea (call 911).
Sudden, severe weakness or loss of coordination in your arm or hand.
Pain that is constant, unrelenting, and not changed by position.
A cold, pale, or blue hand.

calm.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back with feet up on a chair. Focus on letting your belly rise as you inhale and fall as you exhale, keeping your chest and neck relaxed.

calm.name: Scalene Pressure Release
calm.how: Using the fingers of your opposite hand, gently press into the soft, ropy muscles in the groove on the side of your neck, above your collarbone. Hold gentle pressure on tender spots.

calm.name: Gentle Scalene Stretch
calm.how: Gently tilt your ear away from the shoulder you're stretching. To deepen, you can gently hold onto a chair or place your other hand over your head.

restore.name: Eccentric Scalene Control
restore.dose: 2 x 8 reps per side, every other day
restore.how: Use your hand to help lift your head from a side-tilted position, then slowly lower it back down over 3-5 seconds, controlling the movement.

restore.name: Neck & Arm Nerve Glide
restore.how: Gently move through the prescribed range of motion to mobilize the nerves that pass through the neck and arm. Move slowly and without pain.

restore.name: Postural Reset
restore.how: Follow the video cues to reset your head, neck, and shoulder position to a more neutral alignment.

strengthen.name: Deep Neck Flexor Activation
strengthen.how: Gently tuck your chin to create a 'double chin' and feel the deep muscles at the front of your neck engage. Don't use your large, outer neck muscles.

strengthen.name: Core Bracing
strengthen.how: Engage your abdominal muscles as if you're about to be punched in the stomach. Breathe normally while holding this tension.

strengthen.name: Loaded Carries
strengthen.how: Hold a moderate weight in each hand, stand tall with good posture, and walk. This builds postural endurance for the neck and shoulders.

habits: Set a timer to take a 'Walk Break' every 30-60 minutes to break up prolonged sitting.
Adjust your monitor height so the top of the screen is at or slightly below eye level.
Practice belly breathing throughout the day, especially when you feel stressed.
Avoid sleeping on your stomach or with your arm tucked under your head.
scalenes.expect: With consistent application of these steps, most people feel a noticeable improvement in 2-4 weeks. Full resolution may take 6-8 weeks.
scalenes.seePro: Book an evaluation if your symptoms include significant weakness, numbness that doesn't go away, or if the pain is not improving after 2 weeks of consistent self-care.

splenius.origin: The spine at the base of the neck and upper back (C7-T6).
splenius.insertion: The base of the skull (capitis) and the sides of the upper neck vertebrae (cervicis).
splenius.action: Working together, they tilt your head backward (extension). Working alone, one side turns and tilts your head to that same side.
splenius.nerve: Dorsal rami of the middle and lower cervical nerves.
symptoms: A headache that feels like it's on the very top of your head.
A strange, deep ache that feels like it's inside your skull, often behind one eye.
Neck stiffness, especially when trying to look down or turn your head.
Pain can sometimes feel like a 'cap' on your head.
Occasional blurry vision in the eye on the same side as the neck pain.

questions.q: Does your headache feel like it's on the very top of your skull?
Do you have a persistent, deep ache that feels like it's behind your eye?
Is your neck stiff and painful when you try to tuck your chin to your chest?
Does looking up for a long time (like painting a ceiling) trigger your neck pain or headache?
Do you spend many hours a day with your head tilted forward looking at a screen?

tests.name: Splenius Contraction Test
tests.how: Sit tall. Turn your head about 45 degrees to one side, then gently tilt your head backward to look up at the ceiling.
tests.positive: This movement reproduces the specific headache pain on the top of your head or behind your eye.

causes: Forward head posture from computer or phone use.
Whiplash injury, which overstretches these muscles.
Sleeping with too many pillows, forcing the neck into flexion.
Activities that require looking up for long periods (e.g., rock climbing, painting).
Emotional stress, leading to chronic neck tension.
mimics: Cervicogenic headache (headache originating from the neck joints).
redFlags: A 'thunderclap' headache that comes on suddenly and is the 'worst headache of your life' (call 911).
Headache accompanied by fever, stiff neck, confusion, or rash.
Headache that starts after a head injury.
New or worsening headache pattern, especially if over age 50.

calm.name: Gentle Chin Tucks
calm.how: Gently glide your chin straight back as if making a 'double chin'. Avoid tilting your head down; the motion is a straight glide.

calm.name: Splenius Pressure Release
calm.how: Place a lacrosse ball on the muscle at the back/side of your neck, just below the skull. Lean against a wall and apply gentle, sustained pressure to tender spots.

calm.name: Gentle Neck Flexion Stretch
calm.how: Sit tall and gently bring your chin toward your chest. Use your hand to apply very light overpressure on the back of your head. You should feel a stretch, not pain.

restore.name: Eccentric Neck Extension
restore.how: Use a towel to gently pull your head forward into flexion, then use your neck muscles to slowly resist the towel as you return to the start position over 3-5 seconds.

restore.name: Neck & Arm Nerve Glide
restore.how: This helps ensure the nerves in the area are moving freely. Follow the video cues and move gently without forcing into pain.

restore.name: Thoracic Spine Mobility
restore.how: Improving mobility in your upper back reduces the strain on your neck. Focus on rotating through your rib cage.

strengthen.name: Deep Neck Flexor Endurance
strengthen.how: Perform a gentle chin tuck and hold it, maintaining the contraction in the deep front-neck muscles. Breathe normally.

strengthen.name: Upper Back Strengthening
strengthen.how: Hinge at your hips with a flat back. Pull the weights up towards your chest, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top.

strengthen.name: Scapular Retraction
strengthen.how: Using a band or cable, pull the rope towards your face, aiming your hands towards your ears. Squeeze your shoulder blades together and back.

habits: Use a single, supportive pillow that keeps your neck in a neutral line with your spine.
Position your computer monitor so your eyes are level with the top third of the screen.
When reading on a phone, try to bring the phone up to your face rather than dropping your head down to the phone.
Take frequent micro-breaks from desk work to perform chin glides and look around.
splenius.expect: Headaches often decrease in frequency and intensity within the first 1-2 weeks. Neck stiffness may take 3-6 weeks to fully resolve with consistent exercises.
splenius.seePro: See a professional if your headache is severe, doesn't respond to self-care, or is accompanied by any of the red flag symptoms.

temporalis.origin: The temporal fossa, a large fan-shaped area on the side of your skull.
temporalis.insertion: A bony process on your lower jaw (coronoid process of the mandible).
temporalis.action: Closes your jaw (elevation) and pulls it backward (retraction). It's essential for chewing and clenching.
temporalis.nerve: Trigeminal Nerve (Cranial Nerve V, Mandibular Division).
symptoms: A headache felt in the temple and side of the head.
Pain that feels like it's above your eye or behind your eyebrow.
Sensitivity or aching in your upper teeth, which can be mistaken for a dental problem.
Pain when chewing hard or chewy foods.
Difficulty opening your mouth wide.
Pain is often worse during times of stress or concentration.

questions.q: Do you get headaches primarily in your temples?
Do your upper teeth ache, even though your dentist says they are healthy?
Is your headache worse after chewing gum, eating a tough steak, or clenching your jaw?
Do you wake up with a headache or a sore jaw?
Does the pain feel like a constant, dull ache above your eyebrow?

tests.name: Temporalis Palpation Test
tests.how: Place your fingertips on your temples. Clench your teeth firmly and feel the muscle bulge. Now relax and press firmly into the muscle, searching for specific, tender spots.
tests.positive: Pressing on a tender spot reproduces your temple headache or tooth sensitivity.

causes: Bruxism (clenching or grinding teeth), especially during sleep or concentration.
Excessive gum chewing or eating very hard/chewy foods.
Dental issues, such as a misaligned bite or recent dental work.
Emotional stress and anxiety.
Forward head posture, which can alter jaw mechanics.
mimics: Temporal arteritis (a serious condition in older adults).
redFlags: Sudden, severe, one-sided headache with vision changes, fever, or jaw pain when chewing (could be temporal arteritis).
Headache following a head injury.
Inability to close your jaw after it has been opened wide (jaw dislocation).
Numbness or weakness in the face.

calm.name: Temporalis Self-Massage
calm.how: With your jaw relaxed, use your fingertips to apply firm, slow, circular pressure to the tender areas in your temples. You can also try a 'pincer' grip on the muscle.

calm.name: Stress Reduction Breathing
calm.dose: 5 minutes, 1-2 times daily or when stressed
calm.how: Inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, hold for 4. This helps calm the nervous system and reduce clenching.

calm.name: Gentle Jaw Mobility
calm.how: With your tongue on the roof of your mouth, slowly open and close your jaw only to the point of mild tension, not pain. This encourages relaxed movement.

restore.name: Postural Correction
restore.how: Correcting forward head posture reduces strain on the jaw muscles. Gently glide your chin straight back without tilting your head.

restore.name: Tongue Posture Training
restore.how: Practice resting your tongue gently on the roof of your mouth, just behind your front teeth, with your teeth slightly apart and lips together. This is the jaw's natural resting position.

restore.name: Controlled Jaw Opening
restore.how: Place a finger on your chin. As you slowly open your mouth, provide gentle resistance with your finger. Then, as you close, gently resist the closing motion.

strengthen.name: Deep Neck Flexor Activation
strengthen.how: A stable neck provides a better foundation for the jaw. Gently tuck your chin and hold, feeling the deep muscles in the front of your neck work.

strengthen.name: Postural Endurance
strengthen.how: Regularly resetting your posture prevents the slow creep into a forward-head position that strains the jaw.

strengthen.name: Core Stability
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: A strong core helps stabilize the entire spine, reducing compensatory tension in the neck and jaw.

habits: Avoid chewing gum, ice, or very hard foods.
Cut food into smaller pieces to reduce the effort of chewing.
Place small sticky notes on your computer or mirror that say 'Relax Jaw' as a reminder.
If you clench at night, speak to your dentist about a night guard.
temporalis.expect: You can often feel relief from acute pain within a few days of starting massage and relaxation. Lasting improvement, especially if related to clenching, may take 4-6 weeks of consistent habit changes and exercises.
temporalis.seePro: Book an appointment if your pain is severe, you have clicking or locking in your jaw, or if self-care doesn't provide relief after 2-3 weeks. A dentist or TMJ specialist may be needed.

masseter.insertion: The outer surface of the angle and ramus of your mandible (your jawbone).
masseter.action: The primary muscle for closing your jaw. It is the strongest muscle in the body by weight, used for chewing and clenching.
masseter.nerve: Trigeminal Nerve (Cranial Nerve V, Mandibular Division).
symptoms: Deep ache or pain directly over the jaw joint, in front of the ear.
Pain in the cheek that can radiate up to the temple or down into the jaw.
A feeling of fullness or pain inside the ear, like an earache.
Aching in the lower back teeth (molars), often leading to unnecessary dental visits.
Limited ability to open your mouth, or pain when yawning.
A 'clicking' or 'popping' sound in the jaw joint (TMJ).

questions.q: Do you have pain right in front of your ear, especially when you chew?
Does it feel like you have an earache or toothache in your back molars, but the doctor/dentist can't find a cause?
Do you wake up with a sore, tired jaw?
Is your jaw pain accompanied by a clicking or popping sound when you open your mouth?
Do you find yourself clenching your teeth during the day when you are stressed or concentrating?

tests.name: Masseter Palpation Test
tests.how: Place your fingers on your cheek, just above the angle of your jaw. Clench your teeth to feel the muscle contract, then relax. Press deeply into the muscle belly to find tender, ropy bands.
tests.positive: Pressing on a tender spot reproduces your jaw, cheek, ear, or tooth pain.

causes: Bruxism (clenching or grinding teeth), often related to stress.
Habitual gum chewing, nail biting, or chewing on pens.
Malocclusion (a bad bite) or recent extensive dental work.
Direct trauma to the jaw.
Forward head posture, which changes the resting position of the jaw.
redFlags: Inability to open or close your jaw (a 'locked' jaw).
Sudden, severe swelling in the jaw or cheek area.
Pain accompanied by fever, which could indicate an infection.
Numbness in your jaw, chin, or lip.

calm.name: Masseter Self-Massage
calm.how: With your jaw relaxed, use your knuckles or fingertips to apply deep, slow stripping strokes from your cheekbone down to your jawline. You can also do this from inside your mouth (with a clean finger or glove) to release the deeper part of the muscle.

calm.name: Stress Reduction Breathing
calm.dose: 5 minutes, 1-2 times daily or when stressed
calm.how: Calming your nervous system is key to reducing clenching. Inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, and hold for 4.

calm.name: Gentle Jaw Mobility
calm.how: Place your tongue on the roof of your mouth. Slowly open and close your jaw without letting your tongue lose contact. This promotes a healthy hinge motion.

restore.name: Postural Correction
restore.how: A neutral head position is crucial for a relaxed jaw. Gently glide your chin straight back to stack your head over your shoulders.

restore.name: Tongue Posture Training
restore.how: Consciously rest your tongue on the roof of your mouth, with teeth slightly apart and lips closed. This is the 'freeway space' that allows the masseter to relax.

restore.name: Jaw Lateral Movement
restore.how: Look in a mirror. Slowly glide your lower jaw from side to side without pain. Keep the movement smooth and controlled.

strengthen.name: Deep Neck Flexor Activation
strengthen.how: Strengthening the supporting neck muscles helps unload the jaw. Perform a gentle chin tuck and hold.

strengthen.name: Postural Endurance
strengthen.how: Use this sequence to combat the forward head posture that contributes to jaw tension.

strengthen.name: Core Stability
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: A stable trunk provides a solid base for your head and neck, reducing the need for compensatory tension in the jaw.

habits: Adopt the 'lips together, teeth apart' mantra throughout the day.
Avoid chewing gum and tough foods like bagels or steak while the jaw is painful.
Try not to rest your chin in your hand.
If you grind your teeth at night, consult your dentist about a custom night guard.
masseter.expect: Pain can decrease significantly within 1-2 weeks with massage and habit changes. Full recovery and preventing recurrence depends on managing stress and postural habits, which can take 4-8 weeks to solidify.
masseter.seePro: Book an evaluation if you have significant clicking, locking, or deviation of your jaw, or if pain persists for more than 3 weeks despite your best efforts. A TMJ specialist or physical therapist can provide more specific care.

supraspinatus.origin: The top surface of your shoulder blade (supraspinous fossa).
supraspinatus.insertion: The top of your upper arm bone (greater tubercle of the humerus).
supraspinatus.action: Initiates lifting your arm out to the side (abduction) for the first 15-30 degrees. It also holds the 'ball' of your arm bone securely in the shoulder 'socket'.
symptoms: A deep, nagging ache felt on the top or outer part of your shoulder.
Pain that refers down the side of your arm, often stopping around the mid-arm or elbow.
A sharp pinch or pain when you try to lift your arm overhead, like reaching into a high cabinet.
Weakness when trying to lift your arm out to the side.
Pain at night, especially when you lie on the affected shoulder.
Difficulty with tasks like brushing your hair or putting on a coat.

questions.q: Do you feel a sharp pain in your shoulder when you start to lift your arm out to the side, especially between 60 and 120 degrees (a 'painful arc')?
Is the pain a deep ache on the outside of your shoulder that sometimes travels down your arm?
Does it hurt to lie on that shoulder at night?
Do you feel weakness when trying to hold a heavy object out to your side?
Is it difficult to reach behind your back, for example, to tuck in a shirt?

tests.name: Empty Can Test
tests.how: Lift your affected arm forward and out to the side about 45 degrees, keeping your elbow straight. Turn your thumb down as if emptying a can. Gently try to resist as you use your other hand to push down on your arm.
tests.positive: Significant pain or weakness in the shoulder compared to the other side.

tests.name: Drop Arm Test
tests.how: Use your good arm to help lift your painful arm straight out to the side, parallel to the floor. Now, try to slowly and smoothly lower it back down to your side.
tests.positive: You are unable to lower the arm slowly, or it suddenly drops. This can indicate a more significant tear and warrants a professional evaluation.

causes: Repetitive overhead activities (e.g., painting, swimming, throwing).
Lifting an object that is too heavy or with poor technique.
A fall onto an outstretched arm or directly onto the shoulder.
Poor posture (rounded shoulders) which narrows the space for the tendon.
Age-related degeneration or 'wear and tear' of the tendon.
mimics: Subacromial bursitis (often occurs alongside supraspinatus issues).
Cervical radiculopathy (a pinched nerve in the neck referring pain to the shoulder).
redFlags: Inability to lift your arm at all after an injury.
A visible deformity or 'lump' on your shoulder or collarbone after a fall.
Pain accompanied by fever, redness, or swelling, suggesting an infection.
Pain that is constant and severe, even at rest.

calm.name: Pendulum Swings
calm.dose: 2 x 30 sec in each direction, several times daily
calm.how: Lean over, supporting your good arm on a table. Let the painful arm hang down and use your body to create small, gentle circles. This provides gentle traction and movement without using the muscle.

calm.name: Supraspinatus Pressure Release
calm.how: Place a lacrosse ball between your shoulder blade and a wall. Find the muscle just above the 'spine' of your shoulder blade and apply sustained, gentle pressure to any tender spots.

calm.name: Scapular Wall Slides
calm.how: Perform this standing against a wall. Keep your forearms on the wall and slide them up and down, focusing on moving your shoulder blades without shrugging. Only go as high as you can without pain.

restore.name: Isometric External Rotation
restore.how: Stand in a doorway with your elbow bent to 90 degrees. Gently press the back of your hand into the door frame as if rotating outward. You should feel the muscle contract without any joint movement.

restore.name: Banded External Rotation
restore.how: Keep your elbow pinned to your side at a 90-degree angle. Rotate your forearm outward against light band resistance. The movement should come from your shoulder, not your wrist.

restore.name: Scapular Mobility
restore.how: Move your shoulder blade through its full range of motion—up, back, down, and forward—while keeping your arm relatively still. This improves shoulder blade control.

strengthen.name: Scaption Raises
strengthen.how: With a very light weight (or no weight), raise your arm with your thumb up at a 30-45 degree angle in front of your body. Only go to shoulder height. This is the natural plane of the shoulder blade.

strengthen.name: Rotator Cuff Endurance
strengthen.how: Hold your arm in the 'stop sign' position with a band providing tension. Perform small, quick vibrations to challenge the stability of the rotator cuff.

strengthen.name: Push-Up Plus
strengthen.how: In a push-up or quadruped position, keep your elbows straight and just move your shoulder blades. Push the floor away to spread them apart, then let them sink together. This strengthens the serratus anterior, a key shoulder stabilizer.

habits: Avoid sleeping directly on the painful shoulder. Try sleeping on your back or other side with a pillow to hug.
When lifting, keep your elbows close to your body to reduce strain on the shoulder.
Break up overhead tasks with frequent rest periods.
Strengthen your upper back muscles (rows, face pulls) to improve posture and shoulder mechanics.
supraspinatus.expect: Minor strains can feel better in 2-4 weeks. More significant tendinopathy or irritation can take 6-12 weeks of consistent, progressive rehabilitation to see significant improvement in strength and function.
supraspinatus.seePro: Book an evaluation if you have significant weakness (e.g., a positive Drop Arm Test), if the pain resulted from a specific trauma, or if there is no improvement after 3-4 weeks of dedicated rehab.

infraspinatus.origin: Infraspinous fossa of the scapula (the main flat part on the back of your shoulder blade).
infraspinatus.insertion: Greater tubercle of the humerus (the top, outer part of your upper arm bone).
infraspinatus.action: Primarily rotates your arm outward (external rotation), like when you're winding up to throw a ball. It also helps stabilize the shoulder joint.
symptoms: A deep, aching pain felt in the front of the shoulder.
Pain that travels down the front and outside of the arm, sometimes to the hand.
Difficulty reaching behind your back, like to fasten a bra or grab a wallet.
Inability to sleep on the affected shoulder due to pain.
A feeling of weakness when trying to lift or rotate your arm outward.

questions.q: Is it painful to sleep on your affected shoulder?
Do you feel a deep ache in the FRONT of your shoulder, even though the muscle is on the back?
Is it difficult to reach behind your back, like tucking in a shirt or fastening a bra?
Does the pain travel down the outside or front of your arm?
Do you have trouble combing your hair or reaching for something on a high shelf?

tests.name: External Rotation Resistance Test
tests.how: Bend your affected arm's elbow to 90 degrees, keeping it tucked into your side. Use your other hand to gently resist as you try to rotate your forearm outward.
tests.positive: Pain or noticeable weakness in the back of your shoulder compared to the other side.

tests.name: Hand-to-Back Reach
tests.how: Try to reach your affected arm behind your back and up toward your opposite shoulder blade. Compare how high you can reach with your good arm.
tests.positive: Significant pain or a major difference in how high you can reach.

causes: Repetitive overhead activities (e.g., throwing, swimming, painting).
Sudden trauma, like a fall onto an outstretched arm.
Poor posture, with rounded shoulders and a forward head position.
Sleeping on the same side every night, compressing the shoulder.
Weakness in the surrounding back and core muscles, which overloads the shoulder.
mimics: Cervical radiculopathy (pinched nerve in the neck)
redFlags: Sudden, severe pain with an inability to lift your arm at all (possible full-thickness tear).
Pain accompanied by fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss.
Visible deformity of the shoulder joint after an injury.
Numbness or tingling that is constant and doesn't change with position.

calm.name: Lacrosse Ball Release
calm.how: Lie on your back and place a lacrosse ball or tennis ball on the muscle belly on your shoulder blade. Gently roll to find a tender spot and hold pressure until the tenderness eases.

calm.name: Pendulum Swings
calm.dose: 2 x 10 circles each way, twice daily
calm.how: Lean over, supporting your good arm on a table. Let the affected arm hang down and gently swing it in small circles, using your body's momentum, not your shoulder muscles.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back with your feet on a chair or wall, knees and hips at 90 degrees. Focus on deep belly breaths to relax the nervous system and reduce muscle guarding.

restore.name: Sleeper Stretch
restore.how: Lie on your affected side with your arm bent at 90 degrees in front of you. Use your other hand to gently press your forearm down toward the floor until you feel a stretch in the back of the shoulder.

restore.name: Lying Open Book
restore.dose: 2 x 8 reps per side, once daily
restore.how: Lie on your side with knees bent and arms straight out in front. Keeping your hips still, rotate your top arm and upper body open toward the ceiling to improve thoracic mobility.

restore.name: Isometric External Rotation
restore.how: Stand in a doorway with your elbow bent to 90 degrees, tucked at your side. Press the back of your hand into the door frame as if trying to rotate outward, but don't let it move.

strengthen.name: Rotator Cuff External Rotation
strengthen.how: Use a light resistance band. Keep your elbow tucked into your side at a 90-degree angle and rotate your forearm outward against the band's resistance. Control the movement back.

strengthen.name: Abducted External Rotation
strengthen.how: Raise your arm to the side, parallel to the floor, with your elbow bent at 90 degrees. Rotate your hand upward toward the ceiling, keeping your shoulder blade stable.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Support one knee and hand on a bench. Pull a dumbbell up toward your chest, squeezing your shoulder blade. This strengthens the back muscles that support the rotator cuff.

habits: Avoid sleeping directly on the painful shoulder. Try sleeping on your back or other side with a pillow to hug.
When sitting, ensure your shoulders are relaxed and back, not rounded forward. Use our 'Seated Desk Posture Reset' video.
Take frequent micro-breaks from computer work to roll your shoulders back and down.
When lifting, keep your elbows close to your body to reduce strain on the shoulder joint.
infraspinatus.expect: With consistent adherence to the protocol, most people feel a significant reduction in pain within 2-4 weeks. Full strength and function may take 6-8 weeks to restore.
infraspinatus.seePro: If pain is severe, doesn't improve after 2 weeks of self-care, or if you suspect a tear from an injury, book an appointment for a full diagnostic evaluation.

teres-minor.origin: Upper two-thirds of the lateral border of the scapula (the outer edge of your shoulder blade).
teres-minor.insertion: Greater tubercle of the humerus (just below the infraspinatus insertion on your upper arm bone).
teres-minor.action: Rotates your arm outward (external rotation) and helps pull the head of the arm bone into the socket, stabilizing the shoulder.
symptoms: A distinct, localized, deep ache at the back of the shoulder.
Pain is often described as a 'silver dollar' sized spot of tenderness.
Pain is sharp when reaching overhead or across the body.
Unlike infraspinatus, the pain rarely travels far down the arm.
Tenderness to direct pressure on the muscle, just below the bony ridge of the shoulder blade.

questions.q: Do you feel a very specific, deep ache at the back of your shoulder, about the size of a coin?
Does pressing on the fleshy part just below the bony point of your shoulder reproduce your exact pain?
Is the pain mostly localized to the back of the shoulder, without traveling down your arm?
Does it hurt when you reach up and across your body, like putting on a seatbelt?
Is it painful to lie on that shoulder at night?

tests.name: Hornblower's Sign
tests.how: Lift your affected arm to the side to 90 degrees (parallel to the floor) and bend your elbow to 90 degrees. Try to hold this position; a positive test occurs if your arm drops into internal rotation.
tests.positive: Inability to hold the externally rotated position, indicating significant weakness.

tests.name: Palpation Test
tests.how: Reach across your body with your opposite hand to feel the back of your painful shoulder. Find the outer edge of your shoulder blade and press firmly into the muscle just below the bony spine.
tests.positive: Pressing on this spot reproduces your specific, deep ache.

causes: Overuse in throwing sports or racquet sports.
Working with arms overhead for long periods (e.g., electrician, painter).
A sudden forceful outward rotation of the arm.
Chronic poor posture with rounded shoulders.
Imbalance between the strong internal rotators (chest/lats) and weaker external rotators.
redFlags: Significant weakness or inability to rotate your arm outward after an injury.
A 'popping' or 'clicking' sensation deep within the joint during movement.
Pain associated with numbness or tingling in the hand, especially the pinky and ring finger.
Visible atrophy or wasting of the muscles on the back of the shoulder.

calm.name: Teres Minor Ball Release
calm.how: Place a lacrosse ball between your shoulder blade and the wall, targeting the tender spot on the outer edge. Lean into the ball and hold steady pressure or make small movements.

calm.name: Pendulum Swings
calm.dose: 2 x 10 circles each way, twice daily
calm.how: Lean over, supporting your good arm on a table. Let the affected arm hang down and gently swing it in small circles to decompress the joint.

calm.name: Scapular CARs
calm.dose: 2 x 5 circles each way, twice daily
calm.how: Keeping your arms straight, gently move your shoulder blades through their full range of motion: up, forward, down, and back. This promotes gentle movement and awareness.

restore.name: Doorway Chest Stretch
restore.how: Place your forearms on a door frame with elbows slightly below shoulder height. Step through gently to feel a stretch across your chest, which helps improve shoulder posture.

restore.name: Isometric External Rotation
restore.how: Stand in a doorway with your elbow bent to 90 degrees, tucked at your side. Press the back of your hand into the door frame to activate the muscle without movement.

restore.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
restore.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Press your forearms into the floor and slide them overhead, focusing on keeping your shoulder blades down and back.

strengthen.name: Rotator Cuff External Rotation
strengthen.how: With a light band and elbow at your side, rotate your forearm outward. Focus on the small muscles at the back of your shoulder doing the work.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: Using a cable or band at chest height, pull the handles toward your face, driving your elbows back and externally rotating your shoulders at the end of the movement.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Strengthen the supporting back muscles by rowing a dumbbell, focusing on squeezing the shoulder blade toward the spine.

habits: Strengthen your mid-back muscles (rhomboids, mid-traps) to create a stable base for your shoulder.
Be mindful of your posture when sitting or standing; avoid letting your shoulders slump forward.
When reaching overhead, engage your core and avoid arching your lower back.
Warm up properly before any sport or activity involving overhead arm movements.
teres-minor.expect: Because this is a small muscle, targeted exercises can bring relief within 1-3 weeks. Building robust strength to prevent recurrence typically takes 4-6 weeks.
teres-minor.seePro: If you have significant weakness (your arm drops in the Hornblower's test) or the localized pain doesn't improve with 2 weeks of care, schedule an evaluation to rule out a tear.

subscapularis.origin: Subscapular fossa (the entire front surface of your shoulder blade that faces your ribs).
subscapularis.insertion: Lesser tubercle of the humerus (a small bump on the front of your upper arm bone).
subscapularis.action: The primary internal rotator of the arm (rotates it inward). It's a powerful stabilizer that holds the head of the humerus in the socket.
subscapularis.nerve: Upper and Lower Subscapular nerves (C5, C6).
symptoms: Aching pain felt at the back of the shoulder and down the back of the upper arm.
A strange, band-like sensation or pain around the wrist, like a tight watchband.
Profound stiffness and inability to lift the arm, mimicking a 'frozen shoulder'.
Pain when reaching across the body or behind the back.
A 'catching' sensation in the shoulder with certain movements.

questions.q: Do you feel a strange band of pain or tightness around your wrist, even though the main problem is your shoulder?
Does your shoulder feel incredibly stiff, as if it's 'frozen', making it hard to lift your arm to the side?
Is the pain primarily at the back of your shoulder and down the back of your arm?
Is it painful to reach across your chest to touch your opposite shoulder?
Do you have difficulty reaching into your back pocket?

tests.name: Belly Press Test
tests.how: Place the palm of your hand on your stomach. Try to press into your belly while keeping your wrist straight. Compare the strength to your other side.
tests.positive: Pain in the shoulder, or you have to bend your wrist or let your elbow drift backward to generate pressure, indicating weakness.

tests.name: Lift-Off Test
tests.how: Place the back of your hand on your lower back. Try to lift your hand away from your back. If you can't, this is a positive test.
tests.positive: Inability to lift the hand off the back, or severe pain when attempting to do so.

causes: Repetitive forceful internal rotation (e.g., swimming, throwing).
Falling on an outstretched arm.
Immobilization of the shoulder, such as after a fracture or surgery.
Chronic poor posture, which shortens the muscle.
Over-training 'push' muscles (chest, front of shoulder) without balancing with 'pull' exercises.
mimics: Long head of biceps tendon pathology
Carpal tunnel syndrome (due to the wrist referral)
redFlags: Complete inability to lift your arm away from your side (abduction).
History of shoulder dislocation, as subscapularis tears are common with this injury.
Rapid onset of stiffness and pain without any known cause.
Pain accompanied by swelling, redness, or warmth over the shoulder joint.

calm.name: Subscapularis Release
calm.how: Lie on your side with your arm overhead. Use your opposite thumb to press gently into your armpit, searching for the tender muscle on the front of your shoulder blade. Hold gentle pressure.

calm.name: Pendulum Swings
calm.dose: 2 x 10 circles each way, twice daily
calm.how: Lean over a table, letting the arm hang loose. Use your body to create gentle momentum and swing the arm in small circles to decompress the joint.

calm.name: Shoulder Drop Hold
calm.how: Lie on your back and let your arm fall open to the side, supported by the floor. This provides a gentle, passive stretch to the front of the shoulder.

restore.name: Doorway Stretch (Internal Rotators)
restore.how: Stand in a doorway and place the back of your hand and wrist on the frame, with your elbow bent at 90 degrees. Gently turn your body away from the arm to feel a stretch.

restore.name: Isometric Internal Rotation
restore.how: Stand facing the outside edge of a door frame. With your elbow at 90 degrees, press your palm into the frame as if trying to rotate your arm inward.

restore.name: Rotator Cuff Internal Rotation
restore.how: Anchor a light band. With your elbow at your side, pull the band across your body, rotating your arm inward. Control the movement back to the start.

strengthen.name: Abducted Internal Rotation
strengthen.how: Lie on your back with your arm abducted to 90 degrees, elbow bent. Slowly lower a very light weight toward the floor, then rotate it back up. This strengthens the muscle in a functional position.

strengthen.name: Push Up
strengthen.dose: 3 x as many as possible with good form, every other day
strengthen.how: Perform push-ups (on knees or toes). This integrates the subscapularis with other pressing muscles like the chest and serratus anterior.

strengthen.name: Lat Pulldown
strengthen.how: This exercise strengthens the lats, which are partners in internal rotation, helping to balance the shoulder complex.

habits: Balance your workout routine. For every 'push' exercise (like bench press), do a 'pull' exercise (like rows).
Stretch your chest and lats regularly to prevent them from pulling your shoulder forward and shortening the subscapularis.
Avoid carrying heavy bags with a straight arm; keep your elbow slightly bent.
Practice proper posture, ensuring your shoulder blades are gently pulled back and down.
subscapularis.expect: Due to its tendency to cause significant stiffness, subscapularis issues can be stubborn. Expect gradual improvement in mobility over 3-4 weeks, with strength returning over 6-12 weeks. Consistency is key.
subscapularis.seePro: If you have symptoms of a 'frozen shoulder' (severe, progressive loss of motion) or if you fail the 'Lift-Off Test', it's crucial to get a professional diagnosis to rule out a full tear or adhesive capsulitis.

pec-minor.insertion: A small hook-like bone on the front of the shoulder blade (coracoid process).
pec-minor.action: Pulls the shoulder blade forward and down. It's a key muscle in creating 'rounded shoulder' posture and can pinch nerves and blood vessels going to the arm.
symptoms: Sharp pain at the very front of the shoulder, under the collarbone.
Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the arm and hand, especially the last three fingers.
Pain that worsens when reaching overhead or backward.
A feeling of the arm 'going to sleep' easily, especially when sleeping or carrying a backpack.
A rounded or forward-slumped shoulder posture on one side.
Difficulty taking a full, deep breath into the upper chest.

questions.q: Do you get numbness or tingling down your arm and into your hand when you carry a backpack or heavy purse?
Is your pain located in a specific spot at the very front of your shoulder, just below the collarbone?
Does reaching straight up, like to a high shelf, cause a sharp, pinching pain in the front of your shoulder?
Do you often wake up with a 'dead arm' or pins and needles in your hand?
When you look in the mirror, does one shoulder seem to sit lower and more forward than the other?

tests.name: Pec Minor Length Test
tests.how: Lie on your back on the floor with your knees bent. Let your arms rest at your sides, palms up. Check if the back of your shoulder is touching the floor.
