tests.positive: The back of your affected shoulder cannot rest comfortably on the floor without you arching your back. This suggests the pec minor is pulling it forward.

causes: Chronic slouching posture with rounded shoulders (desk work, phone use).
Repetitive overhead reaching, especially with poor mechanics.
Using a computer mouse that is too far away, causing a constant forward reach.
Heavy breathing from conditions like asthma or after intense cardio.
Sleeping in a curled-up fetal position.
mimics: Thoracic outlet syndrome (Pec Minor is a common cause of this)
redFlags: Persistent numbness, tingling, or weakness in the hand that doesn't go away with position changes.
A cool or pale hand compared to the other side, suggesting poor circulation.
A visible lump or deformity at the front of the shoulder.
Any chest pain that could be heart-related (see Pec Major red flags).

calm.name: Pec Minor Pressure Release
calm.how: Place a lacrosse ball between your upper chest (just below the collarbone) and a wall or door frame. Gently apply pressure and make small movements to release this small, deep muscle.

calm.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
calm.how: This gently opens the chest and reverses the slumped posture that shortens the pec minor. Focus on breathing into your upper chest.

restore.name: Corner Pec Stretch
restore.how: Stand in a corner, place forearms on each wall with elbows below shoulder height. Gently lean in until you feel a stretch in the front of your shoulders and chest. Avoid arching your back.

restore.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
restore.how: This activates the muscles that pull your shoulder blades back and down, directly opposing the pull of a tight pec minor.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: This is a key exercise to strengthen the upper back and external rotators of the shoulder, promoting better posture.

strengthen.name: Scap Push Ups
strengthen.how: This strengthens the serratus anterior muscle, which helps hold the shoulder blade against the rib cage and counteracts the pec minor's pull.

habits: Position your mouse close to your keyboard to avoid reaching.
Use a headset for phone calls instead of cradling the phone.
When sitting, imagine a string pulling the top of your head towards the ceiling.
Perform a 'Seated Desk Posture Reset' every 30 minutes.
pec-minor.expect: Relief from nerve-like symptoms can occur within a week of consistent release and stretching. Lasting postural changes and strength balance will likely take 6-8 weeks of dedicated effort.
pec-minor.seePro: Book an evaluation if you have persistent or worsening numbness, tingling, weakness, or color changes in your hand, or if your pain doesn't improve after 3 weeks.

serratus.name: Serratus anterior
serratus.origin: Outer surfaces of the upper 8 or 9 ribs.
serratus.insertion: The front side of the inner border of the scapula (shoulder blade).
serratus.action: Pulls the shoulder blade forward and around the rib cage (protraction), like when you punch or reach forward. It also holds the shoulder blade against the ribs and helps rotate it upward when you lift your arm overhead.
serratus.nerve: Long thoracic nerve (from cervical roots C5, C6, and C7).
symptoms: A sharp, nagging ache on the side of your chest or ribs, often described as a 'side stitch' that won't go away.
Pain that feels like it's under the bottom tip of your shoulder blade.
Difficulty taking a full, deep breath without a sharp pain or 'catch'.
A feeling of weakness or instability when pushing a door or performing a push-up.
Pain that is worse when lying on the affected side.
A sensation that your shoulder blade is 'winging' or not sitting flat on your back.

questions.q: Do you feel a sharp 'stitch' in your side when you try to take a deep breath or run?
Does the pain feel like it's located under the bottom tip of your shoulder blade?
Do you feel a 'catch' or sharp pain when you reach forward or push something, like a heavy door?
Is it uncomfortable to lie on the painful side at night?
Does the pain get worse with a persistent cough?

tests.name: Wall Push Test
tests.how: Stand facing a wall, about arm's length away. Place your hands on the wall at shoulder height and lean forward slightly. Slowly perform a push-up against the wall.
tests.positive: You feel pain on the side of your ribs, or you see the inside edge of your shoulder blade 'wing' out away from your back as you push.

causes: A sudden increase in strenuous exercise, especially running, swimming, or weightlifting.
Persistent, hard coughing from asthma, bronchitis, or allergies.
Repetitive pushing movements, like in push-ups or bench press with poor form.
Poor posture with shoulders rounded forward for long periods.
Sleeping in an awkward position on your side, compressing the muscle.
mimics: Gallbladder problems (if on the right side)
Heart-related pain (if on the left side)
redFlags: Pain accompanied by severe shortness of breath, dizziness, or sweating (could be a heart attack).
Pain that started after a significant fall or impact to your chest (could be a rib fracture).
Fever, chills, and a productive cough along with the chest pain (could be pneumonia).
Pain that doesn't change at all with movement or position (could be an organ issue).

calm.name: Side-Lying Rib Expansion
calm.how: Lie on your non-painful side with a small pillow under your waist. Focus on breathing into your painful side, feeling the ribs expand with each slow inhale.

calm.name: Gentle Torso Rotation
calm.dose: 2 x 8 reps per side, once daily
calm.how: Start on your hands and knees. Gently reach one arm under your body, rotating your torso slightly. Move slowly and only within a pain-free range.

calm.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back with your feet up on a chair. Focus on breathing deep into your belly, allowing your rib cage to expand gently without forcing it.

restore.name: Scapular Push-Ups
restore.how: In a plank or hands-and-knees position, keep your arms straight and pinch your shoulder blades together, then push them apart to round your upper back. The movement should only come from your shoulder blades.

restore.name: Wall Slides
restore.how: Stand with your back against a wall. Place your forearms on the wall in a 'goalpost' position. Slowly slide your arms up the wall, keeping your shoulder blades engaged, then return to the start.

strengthen.name: Wall Push Up
strengthen.how: Stand facing a wall and perform a push-up, focusing on feeling the muscles on the side of your ribs engage as you push away from the wall. Keep your core tight.

strengthen.name: Single Arm Dumbbell Press
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Lie on your back holding a light dumbbell in one hand, arm extended toward the ceiling. Punch the dumbbell straight up, lifting your shoulder blade off the floor. Control the movement back down.

habits: When sitting, use a chair with good back support to prevent slouching and rounding your shoulders.
Avoid sleeping on the painful side; try sleeping on your back with pillows for support.
Practice deep belly breathing throughout the day to avoid shallow chest breathing patterns.
When lifting, engage your core and push through your legs, not just your arms and shoulders.
serratus.expect: With consistent gentle movement and strengthening, you should notice a significant decrease in pain within 2-3 weeks. Full recovery and return to strenuous activity may take 4-6 weeks.
serratus.seePro: Book an appointment if the pain is severe, doesn't improve after 1-2 weeks of self-care, or if you have any of the 'Red Flag' symptoms.

lats.name: Latissimus dorsi
lats.origin: Spine (from mid-back to the sacrum), lower ribs, and top of the pelvis.
lats.insertion: The front of the upper arm bone (humerus).
lats.action: Pulls the arm down, toward the body, and rotates it inward. It's a powerful muscle for pulling movements like pull-ups, swimming, or rowing.
lats.nerve: Thoracodorsal nerve (from cervical roots C6, C7, and C8).
symptoms: A persistent, deep ache at the bottom angle of the shoulder blade.
Pain that travels down the back of the arm and forearm, sometimes reaching the ring and little fingers.
A feeling of stiffness or restriction when reaching overhead.
A dull ache in the mid-back, especially after pulling activities.
Difficulty sleeping on either side due to pressure on the muscle.
A 'pinching' sensation in the front of the shoulder when lifting the arm.

questions.q: Does the pain feel like a deep ache under your shoulder blade that refers down the back of your arm?
Do you feel a 'catch' or stiffness when you try to reach for something on a high shelf?
Have you noticed numbness or tingling in your ring and little finger along with this shoulder and back pain?
Does your mid-back ache after activities like swimming, rowing, or carrying a heavy backpack?
Is it difficult to bring your arm fully overhead without arching your lower back?

tests.name: Overhead Reach Test
tests.how: Stand with your back flat against a wall, feet slightly away from the wall. Try to raise both arms straight overhead to touch the wall with your thumbs, without arching your lower back or bending your elbows.
tests.positive: You feel a strong pull in your mid-back or the back of your armpit, or you are unable to touch the wall without your lower back arching away from it.

causes: Overuse from pulling exercises like pull-ups, rowing, or swimming.
Carrying heavy bags or backpacks consistently on one shoulder.
Prolonged sitting with poor posture, especially reaching forward for a computer mouse.
Vigorous activities like chopping wood or playing tennis.
Sleeping with an arm stretched far overhead.
mimics: Cervical radiculopathy (pinched nerve in the neck)
redFlags: Sudden, severe back pain that is not related to movement.
Pain accompanied by weakness in the legs or changes in bowel/bladder control (seek immediate emergency care).
Numbness or tingling that is constant, severe, and doesn't change with position.
Pain associated with fever, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.

calm.name: Child's Pose Lat Stretch
calm.how: From a kneeling position, fold forward and walk your hands out in front, then to one side to feel a stretch along the opposite side of your back. Breathe into the stretch.

calm.name: Foam Roller Release
calm.how: Lie on your side with a foam roller placed under the fleshy part of your back, just behind your armpit. Gently roll up and down, pausing on tender spots.

calm.name: Doorway Hang
calm.how: Grasp the top of a sturdy door frame. Let your knees bend and allow your body weight to gently stretch your lats and shoulders. Keep your core engaged.

restore.name: Quadruped Thoracic Rotation
restore.dose: 2 x 10 reps per side, once daily
restore.how: On hands and knees, reach one arm under your body, then open it up toward the ceiling. Follow your hand with your eyes to encourage rotation through your mid-back.

restore.name: Dynamic Childs Pose
restore.how: Sit back toward your heels with arms reaching forward, then walk the hands to one side to lengthen the opposite lat. Breathe into the side ribs.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8-12 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Hinge at your hips with a flat back. Pull the dumbbell up towards your hip, squeezing your shoulder blade towards your spine. Control the weight on the way down.

strengthen.name: Lat Pulldown
strengthen.how: Using a machine or band, pull the bar down to your upper chest. Focus on driving your elbows down and back, feeling the contraction in your back muscles.

habits: Adjust your desk setup so your mouse is close, preventing a constant forward reach.
When carrying bags, switch sides frequently or use a backpack with both straps.
Avoid sleeping with your arm stretched far overhead. Try hugging a pillow instead.
Warm up properly with dynamic stretches before swimming, climbing, or lifting weights.
lats.expect: You can expect relief from the sharpest pain within 1-2 weeks of stretching and release work. Building strength and resilience can take 4-8 weeks of consistent exercise.
lats.seePro: Schedule a visit if your overhead reach doesn't improve, if you have persistent numbness or tingling in your fingers, or if the pain significantly limits your daily activities after 2 weeks.

intercostals.name: Intercostals
intercostals.origin: The lower border of one rib.
intercostals.insertion: The upper border of the rib below.
intercostals.action: Elevate and depress the ribs to expand and contract the chest cavity, allowing you to breathe.
intercostals.nerve: Intercostal nerves (from thoracic spinal nerves T1-T11).
symptoms: A sharp, stabbing, or aching pain located directly between or along a single rib.
Pain that gets significantly worse with a deep breath, cough, sneeze, or laugh.
Tenderness to the touch in the space between two ribs.
A feeling of tightness or restriction around your chest.
Pain that is very localized to one specific spot, rather than being widespread.
Difficulty twisting or bending your torso without sharp pain.

questions.q: Is your pain sharp and located in a specific spot on your rib cage that you can point to with one finger?
Does taking a deep breath, coughing, or sneezing make the pain dramatically worse?
Can you press on a spot between your ribs and reproduce the exact pain?
Did the pain start after a bout of heavy coughing, a sudden twisting motion, or a direct impact?
Does twisting your upper body trigger the pain?

tests.name: Palpation Test
tests.how: Gently press with one or two fingers in the spaces between your ribs in the painful area. Compare the sensation to the same area on the opposite, non-painful side.
tests.positive: Pressing on a specific spot between the ribs reproduces your sharp pain.

causes: Forceful and repetitive coughing or sneezing.
A sudden, sharp twisting of the torso, such as in golf, tennis, or reaching into the back seat of a car.
A direct blow or impact to the chest or ribs.
Over-stretching the torso, such as reaching for something far to the side.
Lifting an object that is too heavy with poor technique.
mimics: Shingles (herpes zoster), which often follows a rib line
Costochondritis (inflammation of cartilage connecting ribs to the breastbone)
redFlags: Severe difficulty breathing or shortness of breath (call 911).
Pain accompanied by fever, chills, or a cough that produces colored phlegm.
Pain that occurred after a major trauma or fall, with risk of fracture or internal injury.
A visible deformity or a 'crunching' sound in the rib cage.

calm.name: Gentle Diaphragmatic Breathing
calm.how: Lie comfortably on your back. Breathe in gently through your nose, letting your belly rise, but only to the point before pain begins. Exhale slowly and fully.

calm.name: Supported Side Stretch
calm.how: Lie on your non-painful side with a pillow or rolled towel under your ribs. Let your body relax over the pillow to create a gentle opening stretch in the painful area as you breathe.

restore.name: Cat-Cow
restore.how: On your hands and knees (or seated), gently round your spine up towards the ceiling, then slowly arch it down. Move slowly and within a comfortable, pain-free range of motion.

restore.name: Lying Open Book
restore.dose: 2 x 8 reps per side, once daily
restore.how: Lie on your side with knees bent and arms extended in front of you. Keeping your hips still, rotate your top arm and torso open, as if opening a book. Only go as far as is comfortable.

strengthen.name: Core Brace
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 second holds, several times a day
strengthen.how: Gently tighten your abdominal muscles as if you are about to be poked in the stomach. Hold this gentle brace while breathing normally to help stabilize the rib cage.

strengthen.name: Dead Bug
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Lie on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees. Slowly lower one opposite arm and leg towards the floor while keeping your core braced and low back flat. Start with small movements.

habits: When you need to cough or sneeze, hug a pillow against your chest to brace the area and reduce painful movement.
Avoid sudden twisting motions. When turning, move your feet and let your whole body turn together.
Use proper lifting technique: bend at the knees and hips, and keep objects close to your body.
Sleep on your back or the unaffected side to avoid putting pressure on the strained area.
intercostals.expect: Intercostal strains can be very painful. Expect the sharpest pain to subside in 1-3 weeks, but a dull ache may linger for 4-6 weeks or more. It is important to avoid re-injury during this time.
intercostals.seePro: See a professional if the pain is severe and unmanageable, if you have any red flags, or if there is no improvement after 2 weeks of gentle care.

brachioradialis.origin: The lower, outer edge of the upper arm bone (humerus).
brachioradialis.insertion: The bony point on the thumb-side of the wrist (styloid process of the radius).
brachioradialis.action: Bends the elbow, especially with the forearm in a neutral, thumb-up position. Key movements include hammering, shaking hands, or lifting a grocery bag.
brachioradialis.nerve: Radial nerve (from neck roots C5, C6, C7).
symptoms: Aching pain on the top and outside of the forearm, near the elbow.
Pain that can travel down the forearm to the web of the thumb.
A feeling of weakness when gripping or lifting objects.
Sharp pain when turning a doorknob, using a screwdriver, or typing.
The 'meaty' part of the top of your forearm feels tender to the touch.
Difficulty holding a coffee mug or other heavy items.

questions.q: Does your pain feel worse when you lift something with your palm facing sideways, like carrying a grocery bag?
Do you feel an ache on the outside of your elbow that seems to travel down toward your thumb?
Is it painful to shake hands firmly or turn a key in a lock?
Does your grip feel weak, making it hard to hold a coffee mug or a hammer?
Is the pain located more on the muscular part of your forearm, rather than directly on the bony point of the elbow?

tests.name: Resisted Elbow Flexion Test
tests.how: Rest your forearm on a table, thumb pointing to the ceiling. Use your other hand to gently press down on your wrist while you try to bend your elbow.
tests.positive: Pain or a feeling of weakness in the muscle on top of your forearm near the elbow.

causes: Repetitive gripping activities like hammering, using tools, or extensive gardening.
Carrying heavy objects with straight arms, such as suitcases or shopping bags.
Sports involving forceful wrist and elbow movements like tennis, rock climbing, or rowing.
Typing for long hours with poor wrist posture.
A sudden, forceful pull on the arm, like catching a falling object.
mimics: C6 or C7 cervical radiculopathy (pinched nerve in the neck)
redFlags: Sudden, severe swelling and bruising after an injury.
Inability to move your wrist or elbow through their full range of motion.
Numbness or tingling that is constant and does not change with position.
A visible deformity in the arm or wrist after a fall.

calm.name: Brachioradialis Pressure Release
calm.how: Sit with your forearm resting on a table, palm down. Use the thumb of your other hand to apply firm, sustained pressure to tender spots in the muscle belly on top of your forearm.

calm.name: Gentle Wrist Circles
calm.dose: 2 x 10 circles each way, twice daily
calm.how: Without any weight, gently rotate your wrist in slow, controlled circles. Focus on a pain-free range of motion to improve joint mobility and blood flow.

calm.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back with feet up on a chair to relax the nervous system. Breathe in through your nose, letting your belly rise, and exhale slowly through your mouth.

restore.name: Brachioradialis Stretch
restore.how: Extend your arm straight out, palm down. Gently use your other hand to bend your wrist downward, then slightly turn your hand inward (like pouring a pitcher) to feel a stretch on top of the forearm.

restore.name: Eccentric Wrist Extension
restore.how: Rest your forearm on your thigh, palm down, holding a very light weight. Use your other hand to lift the weight up, then slowly lower it down over 3-5 seconds.

restore.name: Radial Nerve Glide
restore.how: Follow the video cues for the radial nerve portion: make a fist, bend your wrist, turn your arm in, and gently reach back while tilting your head away. Move slowly and without pain.

strengthen.name: Hammer Curls
strengthen.how: Hold a dumbbell in each hand with your palms facing each other (thumb up). Bend your elbows to lift the weights toward your shoulders, keeping your wrists straight. Lower slowly.

strengthen.name: Farmer Carry
strengthen.dose: 3 x 30 sec walks, every other day
strengthen.how: Hold a moderately heavy weight in each hand at your sides. Walk with tall posture, keeping your shoulders back and down, engaging your grip and core.

habits: Take frequent breaks from typing or manual work to stretch your wrists and forearms.
Use ergonomic tools with thicker handles to reduce grip force.
Lift heavy objects with palms facing up or towards each other, and keep them close to your body.
Adjust your desk and chair height to keep wrists in a neutral position. See our 'Desk Setup Tutorial'.
brachioradialis.expect: With consistent adherence to the protocol, most people feel a significant reduction in pain within 2-4 weeks. Full recovery and strength may take 6-8 weeks.
brachioradialis.seePro: Book an evaluation if your pain is severe, doesn't improve after 2 weeks of self-care, or if you experience significant numbness or weakness.

supinator.origin: The outer elbow bone (lateral epicondyle of the humerus) and nearby forearm bone (ulna).
supinator.insertion: The upper third of the other forearm bone (radius).
supinator.action: Turns the forearm so the palm faces up (supination). Key movements include turning a doorknob, using a screwdriver, or accepting change in your hand.
supinator.nerve: Radial nerve (from neck roots C6, C7).
symptoms: A deep, aching pain at the outer elbow, often mistaken for 'tennis elbow'.
Pain that may radiate down the back of the forearm to the web of the thumb.
Weakness or sharp pain when trying to turn your palm up against resistance.
Aching at rest, especially after a day of heavy hand use.
Tenderness when you press deeply into the muscles on the top of your forearm.
Pain that persists even when you are not actively gripping anything.

questions.q: Do you feel a deep ache on the outside of your elbow, even when you're not gripping anything?
Is it painful to turn a doorknob or use a screwdriver, specifically the motion of turning your palm upwards?
Have you been treated for 'tennis elbow' but the pain just won't go away?
Does pressing deeply into the muscle on the top of your forearm, a few inches below the elbow, reproduce your specific pain?
Is the pain a constant, deep ache rather than a sharp pain that only happens when you lift?

tests.name: Resisted Supination Test
tests.how: Rest your elbow on a table, bent to 90 degrees with your palm facing down. Use your other hand to resist as you try to turn your palm up towards the ceiling.
tests.positive: Pain deep in the outer elbow or forearm.

causes: Repetitive turning motions, such as using tools or playing racquet sports with a lot of spin.
Carrying heavy items with bent elbows and palms up, like a waiter's tray.
A fall onto an outstretched hand.
Prolonged typing on a non-ergonomic keyboard that forces forearm rotation.
Forcefully tightening screws or jar lids.
mimics: C6 or C7 cervical radiculopathy (pinched nerve in the neck)
redFlags: Inability to turn your palm up or down.
Constant, severe pins and needles or numbness in the hand.
Visible swelling or deformity around the elbow after an injury.
Pain that wakes you from sleep and is not relieved by changing position.

calm.name: Supinator Pressure Release
calm.how: Rest your forearm on a table. Use the fingers or thumb of your other hand to find and press on tender spots deep in the muscle on the top of your forearm, just below the elbow.

calm.name: Gentle Palm Up/Palm Down
calm.how: Sit with your elbow bent at 90 degrees and resting at your side. Slowly rotate your forearm to turn your palm up, then slowly turn it back down. Stay in a pain-free range.

calm.name: Box Breathing
calm.how: Follow the video cues to inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 4, exhale for 4, and hold for 4. This helps calm the nervous system to reduce muscle tension.

restore.name: Pronator Stretch
restore.how: Hold your arm out, palm up. Gently use your other hand to bend your wrist down, feeling a stretch on the top/inside of your forearm. Keep your elbow straight.

restore.name: Eccentric Wrist Pronation
restore.how: Rest your forearm on your thigh, palm up, holding a light weight. Use your other hand to help turn your palm down, then slowly control the motion as the weight turns your palm back up.

restore.name: Radial Nerve Glide
restore.how: Perform the radial nerve glide as shown in the video. This helps the nerve that passes through the supinator muscle to move more freely.

strengthen.name: Weighted Supination
strengthen.how: Hold a light dumbbell or hammer handle vertically. Rest your forearm on a table. Slowly rotate the weight so your palm turns up, then control it back to the start.

strengthen.name: Bicep Curl
strengthen.how: Perform standard bicep curls, focusing on the final part of the movement where you fully turn your palm up at the top. This strengthens the biceps, a primary supinator.

habits: Use power tools instead of manual screwdrivers for repetitive tasks.
Keep your wrists in a neutral (handshake) position when typing or using a mouse.
Open tight jars by using a gripper or tapping the lid to break the seal, rather than using maximum force.
Carry objects with palms facing in or down when possible.
supinator.expect: Pain relief often begins within 1-2 weeks of consistent release and stretching. Building strength to prevent recurrence can take 4-6 weeks.
supinator.seePro: If you have persistent pain despite 2-3 weeks of this program, or if you have significant weakness or numbness, schedule an appointment for a full evaluation.

ql.origin: The top, back border of the hip bone (posterior iliac crest).
ql.insertion: The lowest rib (12th rib) and the sides of the upper four lumbar vertebrae.
ql.action: Hikes the hip up on one side, side-bends the trunk, and stabilizes the pelvis and low back when walking or lifting.
symptoms: A deep, nagging ache in the low back, often worse on one side.
Sharp, stabbing pain when trying to stand up straight, roll over in bed, or cough.
Pain that refers over the top of the buttock (SI joint area) and sometimes to the front of the hip.
A feeling of being 'stuck' or unable to stand up straight after sitting for a while.
Pain that prevents you from finding a comfortable position in bed.
A feeling of intense vulnerability in the low back.

questions.q: Do you get a sharp, 'catching' pain in your low back when you try to roll over in bed or get out of a car?
Does coughing, sneezing, or taking a deep breath send a sharp pain into your low back or flank?
Is it difficult to stand up completely straight after you've been sitting for a while?
Does the pain feel very deep, like it's right next to your spine, but also spreads out over your buttock or hip?
Do you feel pain when you stand or walk, but find some relief by leaning on a shopping cart or countertop?

tests.name: Hip Hike Test
tests.how: Stand in front of a mirror. Try to lift one side of your pelvis straight up toward your ribs without bending your knee or leaning your torso.
tests.positive: Sharp pain in the low back on the side you are hiking, or an inability to perform the movement smoothly.

causes: Sitting for long periods, especially with poor posture or in a slumped position.
Lifting a heavy object, especially with a twisting motion.
A fall or direct blow to the low back, hip, or buttock.
Standing or walking on uneven surfaces for extended periods.
A true or functional leg length discrepancy.
Weak gluteal and core muscles, forcing the QL to overwork.
mimics: Kidney pain or kidney stone (check for fever, nausea, or changes in urination)
redFlags: Pain accompanied by fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss.
Loss of bowel or bladder control (this is a medical emergency).
Numbness or weakness in the legs that is severe or getting progressively worse.
Back pain that is constant, severe, and not relieved by any change in position.

calm.name: QL Pressure Release (Ball)
calm.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Place a lacrosse ball in the soft tissue of your low back, between your ribs and hip bone, just to the side of the spine. Gently rock your hips side to side.

calm.name: Pillow Squeeze Reset
calm.dose: 1 x 5 reps of 5 sec holds, as needed
calm.how: Follow the video instructions to gently reset the pelvis. This can provide immediate, temporary relief by relaxing deep muscles around the hips and low back.

calm.name: Dynamic Child's Pose
calm.how: From hands and knees, sit your hips back towards your heels. Gently rock side to side to feel a stretch in your low back and lats. Breathe deeply into your back.

restore.name: QL Side Bend Stretch
restore.how: Sit tall in a chair. Reach one arm overhead and gently lean to the opposite side, feeling a stretch in your flank and low back. Keep both sit bones on the chair.

restore.name: Core Brace Introduction
restore.dose: 2 x 10 reps of 10 sec holds, daily
restore.how: Learning to gently engage your deep core muscles provides stability for the lumbar spine, allowing the overworked QL to relax.

restore.name: Quadruped T-Spine Rotation
restore.how: This mobilizes the mid-back, which can reduce the strain on the low back and QL. Follow the video cues for smooth, controlled rotation.

strengthen.name: Side Plank
strengthen.dose: 3 x 30-60 sec hold per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Lie on your side, propped on your elbow. Lift your hips off the floor, creating a straight line from head to feet. Start from your knees if a full plank is too difficult.

strengthen.name: One-Sided Farmer Carry
strengthen.dose: 3 x 20-30 steps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Hold a single heavy weight in one hand. Walk with tall posture, fighting the urge to lean away from the weight. This directly challenges the opposite QL to stabilize the pelvis.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10-12 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Squeeze your glutes to lift your hips. Progressing to the single-leg version improves pelvic stability, reducing strain on the QL.

habits: Avoid sitting for more than 30 minutes at a time. Use the 'Walk Break Protocol Seated'.
When standing up from a chair, scoot to the edge, place feet wide, and hinge at your hips, keeping your back straight.
Sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees to keep your pelvis aligned.
When lifting, face the object, brace your core, and lift with your legs, not your back.
ql.expect: Acute QL pain can often be calmed within a few days. Consistent mobility and strengthening can lead to significant improvement in 2-4 weeks, with a focus on preventing recurrence over the next 2-3 months.
ql.seePro: If you have any red flag symptoms, or if the pain is severe and not improving with 1-2 weeks of care, book an appointment. Also see us if you suspect a leg length discrepancy.

multifidus.origin: Back of the sacrum and the transverse processes of vertebrae from the low back to the neck.
multifidus.insertion: The spinous processes (the bony bumps in the middle of your back) of the vertebrae 2-4 levels above the origin.
multifidus.action: These small, deep muscles provide fine-tuned stability to each individual joint of the spine, preventing small, painful movements.
multifidus.nerve: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves at each level.
symptoms: A deep, sharp, or burning pain felt right next to the spine.
Pain is often pinpoint and you can put a finger directly on it.
Can refer pain down to the sacrum, tailbone, or occasionally into the abdomen.
A feeling of instability or 'giving way' in the low back.
Pain is often worse when bending forward, twisting, or returning to upright from a bent position.
Often persists as a chronic low-grade ache after an acute back injury has healed.

questions.q: Can you point with one finger to a specific, deep spot of pain right next to your spine?
Do you feel a deep ache near your tailbone or sacrum that doesn't seem to be in the buttock muscles?
Does your back feel weak or like it might 'give out' with certain movements?
Is the pain worse when you bend forward to put on your socks and shoes?
Is the pain worse when sitting on a soft couch compared to a firm chair?

tests.name: Prone Leg Lift Test
tests.how: Lie face down. While keeping your pelvis flat on the floor, try to lift one leg straight up just an inch or two. Have a partner place their fingers on the muscles right next to your low back spine.
tests.positive: You feel a sharp, localized pain, or your partner feels the muscle on the lifting side contract late or not at all compared to the opposite side.

causes: A sudden twist or awkward lift that injures the deep spinal structures.
Prolonged sitting, which allows the multifidus muscles to weaken and atrophy.
Chronic poor posture, especially slouching.
Following a lumbar disc injury, as pain can inhibit these muscles from firing correctly.
Repetitive flexion activities like sit-ups or gardening.
mimics: Lumbar facet joint syndrome (very closely related and often co-existing)
redFlags: Saddle anesthesia (numbness in the groin/inner thigh area).
Loss of bowel or bladder control.
Unexplained, progressive weakness in the legs.
Pain that is severe, constant, and worse at night.

calm.name: Positional Release
calm.how: Lie on your back with several pillows under your knees to put your low back in a comfortable, neutral position. The goal is to find a position of maximum ease to let the deep muscles relax.

calm.name: Pillow Squeeze Pelvic Reset
calm.dose: 1 x 5 reps of 5 sec holds, 1-2 times daily
calm.how: This gentle isometric exercise can help reset the relationship between the pelvis and sacrum, calming the deep muscles that attach there, including the multifidus.

calm.name: Cat-Cow Gentle Mobilization
calm.how: Perform this movement very slowly and within a small, pain-free range. The goal is gentle movement to reduce stiffness, not a deep stretch.

restore.name: Dead Bug
restore.how: This is a key exercise for multifidus retraining. Focus on keeping your low back absolutely still as you move your limbs. Pressing your back gently into the floor helps activate the deep stabilizers.

restore.name: Quadruped Glute Kick
restore.dose: 3 x 15 per side, every other day
restore.how: From hands and knees, extend one leg back by squeezing your glute. The challenge is to keep your spine perfectly still, which requires the multifidus to work hard as a stabilizer.

restore.name: Core Brace Introduction
restore.dose: 2 x 10 reps of 10 sec holds, daily
restore.how: Practice co-contracting your deep abdominal and back muscles. Imagine gently tightening a corset around your midsection. This is the foundation of spinal stability.

strengthen.name: Bird-Dog
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: From hands and knees, extend the opposite arm and leg while keeping your torso completely level. This directly challenges the multifidus to prevent rotation.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10-12 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Lifting your hips requires the multifidus to stabilize the spine. The single-leg version increases the stability demand significantly.

strengthen.name: Rack Pull
strengthen.how: This is a limited range-of-motion deadlift. Set the bar on blocks so you only move it from just below the knees to standing. This strengthens the back in a safe, upright posture.

habits: Always sit with your feet flat on the floor and a small support in the curve of your low back.
When you bend, hinge at your hips, not your waist. Practice with the 'Dowel Hip Hinge'.
Engage your core brace ('Core Brace Intro Seated') before lifting anything, even if it's light.
Avoid sitting on couches or chairs that are too soft or deep, as this encourages slouching.
multifidus.expect: Because these are deep stabilizing muscles, retraining them takes time and focus. You may feel less 'instability' in 2-4 weeks, but building true endurance and automatic activation can take 3-6 months of consistent practice.
multifidus.seePro: Book an evaluation if you have any red flag symptoms, if the pain is the result of a specific injury, or if you are not making steady progress after 4 weeks. This type of pain often benefits from hands-on assessment.

psoas.origin: Sides of the lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae (T12-L5) and their discs.
psoas.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur (a small knob on the inside of the upper thigh bone).
psoas.action: A powerful hip flexor, it lifts your thigh toward your chest. It also helps stabilize your lower back.
psoas.nerve: Anterior rami of lumbar nerves L1, L2, and L3.
symptoms: A deep, vertical band of aching pain along one or both sides of your lower back.
Pain that refers to the front of your thigh and groin area.
Difficulty and pain when trying to stand up straight after sitting for a while.
A feeling of a 'catch' or 'click' deep in the front of the hip.
Pain that gets worse with prolonged sitting or walking.
Disrupted sleep, especially when trying to lie flat on your back.

questions.q: Do you feel a deep ache running vertically up your low back, right next to the spine?
Is it difficult or painful to stand up fully straight after sitting for more than 20-30 minutes?
Does your pain also show up in the front of your thigh or groin?
Does lying flat on your back feel uncomfortable or increase your back ache?
Do you feel better when you bring your knees toward your chest while lying down?

tests.name: Thomas Test (Modified)
tests.how: Sit on the edge of a sturdy bed or table. Lie back, pulling both knees to your chest. Hold one knee tightly and let the other leg hang down. Your low back must stay flat on the surface.
tests.positive: If the hanging thigh doesn't touch the surface or if the knee straightens out on its own, your psoas is likely tight.

causes: Prolonged sitting with hips flexed (e.g., desk work, driving).
Sleeping in a fetal position.
Repetitive hip flexion activities like running, cycling, or sit-ups.
A sudden fall or slip that forces the leg back.
Stress and shallow breathing patterns, as the psoas is connected to the diaphragm.
mimics: Hip joint arthritis or labral tear
redFlags: Pain accompanied by fever, nausea, or unexplained weight loss.
Loss of bowel or bladder control.
Numbness or tingling in the groin or 'saddle' area.
Severe, unrelenting abdominal or back pain that doesn't change with position.

calm.name: Psoas Release (Ball)
calm.how: Lie on your stomach. Place a soft ball (4-6 inches) just inside your hip bone. Gently sink your weight onto the ball, breathing deeply. Avoid pulsing or painful pressure.

calm.name: Constructive Rest Position
calm.how: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Rest your hands on your belly and focus on deep, diaphragmatic breathing.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back with your lower legs on a chair or box, so your hips and knees are at 90 degrees. Breathe deeply into your belly and low back.

restore.name: Couch Stretch
restore.how: Kneel in a lunge position with your back shin against a wall or couch. Keep your torso upright and gently squeeze your glute to feel a stretch in the front of the hip.

restore.name: Hip Neuroglide
restore.how: Follow the video to gently mobilize the nerves that run through the front of the hip, improving their ability to slide and glide.

restore.name: Quadruped Glute Kick
restore.dose: 2 x 15 reps per side, every other day
restore.how: On all fours, engage your core and lift one leg back, squeezing the glute at the top. This activates the opposing muscle to help the psoas relax.

strengthen.name: Dead Bug
strengthen.how: Lie on your back with arms and legs in the air. Lower the opposite arm and leg slowly while keeping your low back flat on the floor. This builds core stability.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.dose: 3 x 12 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Lie on your back with one foot flat on the floor and the other leg extended. Drive through your heel to lift your hips, squeezing the glute.

strengthen.name: Step Up
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Step onto a box or stair, driving through the heel of your front foot. Control the movement on the way down. This strengthens the glutes and quads.

habits: Use a standing desk or take frequent breaks from sitting every 30 minutes.
When sitting, ensure your hips are at or slightly higher than your knees.
Avoid sleeping curled up in a tight fetal position; try sleeping on your back with a pillow under your knees.
Practice deep belly breathing throughout the day to relax the diaphragm and psoas.
psoas.expect: With consistent adherence to the protocol, most people feel a significant reduction in pain and stiffness within 2-4 weeks. Full restoration of strength and function may take 6-8 weeks.
psoas.seePro: Book an appointment if your pain is severe, doesn't improve after 2 weeks of self-care, or is accompanied by any of the 'Red Flags'.

iliacus.origin: Iliac fossa (the inner surface of the pelvic bone).
iliacus.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur (shares a tendon with the psoas).
iliacus.action: Works with the psoas as a primary hip flexor, lifting the thigh toward the chest. Also helps stabilize the pelvis.
symptoms: A persistent ache deep in the groin or front pocket area.
Pain that refers to the front of the thigh.
A tender spot on the front of the hip, just inside the bony point (ASIS).
Pain that can also refer to the low back or upper buttock area.
Stiffness and pain when getting up from a chair, especially after a long car ride.

questions.q: Is your primary pain located deep in your groin, like in your front pocket?
Do you feel a very tender spot if you press your fingers just inside the bony point at the front of your hip?
Does the pain get worse when you are sitting for a long time, especially while driving?
Does your pain sometimes feel like it's in your low back or high in your glute, but the main spot is in the front?
Do you feel a 'catching' sensation in the front of your hip when you stand up?

tests.name: Iliacus Palpation
tests.how: Lie on your back with your knees bent. Find the bony point at the front of your hip (ASIS). Place your fingertips just inside this bone and gently curl them into your abdomen as you exhale. Slowly straighten your leg.
tests.positive: A sharp, localized tenderness or reproduction of your familiar groin pain indicates iliacus involvement.

causes: Prolonged sitting, which keeps the muscle in a shortened position.
Activities involving repetitive hip flexion, like running, cycling, or kicking.
Driving for long periods, especially with the gas pedal foot.
Wearing a heavy tool belt that presses on the front of the hips.
A history of falls or direct impact to the front of the pelvis.
mimics: Hip joint impingement (FAI) or labral tear
redFlags: A palpable lump or bulge in the groin area.
Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the front of the thigh.
Pain accompanied by fever, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
Inability to bear weight on the leg.

calm.name: Iliacus Release (Ball)
calm.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Place a small, soft ball just inside your hip bone. Let the ball sink in as you breathe deeply. Avoid any pulsing or sharp pain.

calm.name: Dynamic Childs Pose
calm.how: From a child's pose position, gently rock your hips side to side to create a mild stretch and movement in the deep hip flexors and low back.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back with your lower legs on a chair or box, so your hips and knees are at 90 degrees. This position helps the iliacus and psoas to relax.

restore.name: Couch Stretch
restore.how: This stretch targets the entire iliopsoas complex. Focus on keeping your torso upright and squeezing the glute of the back leg to deepen the stretch.

restore.name: Hip Neuroglide
restore.how: Gently mobilize the femoral nerve, which passes near the iliacus, to ensure it can move freely and reduce irritation.

restore.name: Glute Bridge
restore.how: Lie on your back with knees bent. Squeeze your glutes and lift your hips toward the ceiling. This activates the glutes, which helps the tight hip flexors to relax (reciprocal inhibition).

strengthen.name: Dead Bug
strengthen.how: This exercise strengthens the core muscles that stabilize the pelvis, reducing the strain on the iliacus.

strengthen.name: Bodyweight Squat
strengthen.how: Practice squatting with good form, focusing on using your glutes to power the movement up. This retrains proper hip mechanics.

strengthen.name: Lunges
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Lunges build single-leg stability and strength in the glutes and quads, which supports healthy hip function.

habits: Take frequent breaks from sitting. Use our 'Walk Break Protocol Seated' video.
Adjust your car seat to be more upright, reducing the sharp angle at your hips.
When standing, avoid locking your knees and letting your pelvis tilt forward.
Use a lumbar support roll when sitting to maintain a neutral spinal curve.
iliacus.expect: Most people experience noticeable relief within 1-2 weeks of consistent release work and stretching. Building strength to prevent recurrence typically takes 4-6 weeks.
iliacus.seePro: Schedule a consultation if the pain is sharp, doesn't improve with 2 weeks of this protocol, or if you suspect a hernia.

glute-med.origin: Outer surface of the ilium (pelvic bone), between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines.
glute-med.insertion: Greater trochanter of the femur (the bony point on the outside of your hip).
glute-med.action: Abducts the hip (moves leg out to the side) and stabilizes the pelvis. It's crucial for walking, running, and single-leg balance.
symptoms: A persistent, nagging ache along the belt line or top of the buttock.
Pain that can wrap around to the bony point on the side of the hip.
Pain that refers over the sacroiliac (SI) joint, often mistaken for an SI joint problem.
Difficulty and pain when lying on the affected side at night.
A feeling of weakness or instability in the hip, especially when climbing stairs or running.

questions.q: Is your pain located high on your buttock, right along your belt line?
Does it hurt to lie on that side at night, forcing you to switch positions?
Do you feel pain or a sense of your hip 'giving way' when you stand on one leg to put on pants?
Does walking, standing for a long time, or climbing stairs make the ache worse?
Have you been told you have 'SI joint pain' but treatments for it haven't helped?

tests.name: Single Leg Stance Test
tests.how: Stand in front of a mirror and lift one foot off the ground, balancing on the painful leg for 30 seconds. Watch your hips in the mirror.
tests.positive: If the hip of your lifted leg drops down, or if your familiar pain is reproduced in the standing leg's buttock within 30 seconds, it suggests gluteus medius weakness.

tests.name: Resisted Hip Abduction
tests.how: Lie on your good side with your legs straight. Have a partner gently press down on your top ankle as you try to lift the leg toward the ceiling.
tests.positive: Significant weakness or reproduction of your pain compared to the other side points to gluteus medius involvement.

causes: Sitting for long periods with legs crossed.
Standing with all your weight shifted onto one hip ('hip-sitting').
Running on a banked surface (like the edge of a road) or always running the same direction on a track.
Weakness from inactivity, leading to overuse when activity is resumed.
Sleeping on one side without a pillow between the knees.
redFlags: Numbness or tingling that travels down the leg.
Loss of bowel or bladder control.
Pain that is constant and severe, even at rest.
History of a recent fall or trauma to the hip.

calm.name: Glute Medius Release (Ball)
calm.how: Lie on your side with a lacrosse or tennis ball under the fleshy part of your upper buttock, just below the pelvic bone. Gently roll to find tender spots and hold with steady pressure.

calm.name: Clamshells (Isometric)
calm.how: Lie on your side with knees bent and hips stacked. Without moving your pelvis, gently lift your top knee. Hold at the top without pain, focusing on the muscle contraction.

calm.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
calm.how: Perform this movement slowly and gently to improve hip mobility without stressing the irritated muscle.

restore.name: Standing Clamshell
restore.dose: 2 x 15 reps per side, every other day
restore.how: This exercise activates the gluteus medius in a functional, weight-bearing position. Focus on keeping your pelvis level.

restore.name: Glute Walk
restore.dose: 2 x 10 steps each direction, every other day
restore.how: Place a resistance band around your ankles or knees. Take slow, controlled side steps, keeping your toes pointed forward and your torso upright.

restore.name: Figure-4 Stretch
restore.how: Lie on your back and cross one ankle over the opposite knee. Gently pull the bottom thigh toward your chest until you feel a stretch in the buttock of the crossed leg.

strengthen.name: Standing Hip Abduction/Adduction
strengthen.dose: 3 x 12 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Use a cable or band to add resistance as you move your leg out to the side. Maintain a stable torso and pelvis throughout the movement.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: This variation challenges pelvic stability, forcing the gluteus medius to work harder to prevent the hip from dropping.

strengthen.name: Step Up
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Focus on keeping your knee aligned over your foot and your pelvis level as you step up. This is a key functional strengthener for the glute medius.

habits: Avoid 'hip-sitting'; stand with your weight evenly distributed on both feet.
When sitting, avoid crossing your legs for long periods.
Sleep with a pillow between your knees if you are a side-sleeper.
When carrying a heavy bag or child, switch sides frequently.
glute-med.expect: You should notice less pain at night and with standing within 2-3 weeks. Consistent strengthening for 6-8 weeks is often needed to build the endurance to prevent the pain from returning.
glute-med.seePro: Book an evaluation if you have a 'snapping' sensation in your hip, if pain persists beyond 3-4 weeks, or if you have significant weakness that makes you feel unstable.

glute-min.origin: Outer surface of the ilium (pelvic bone), below the gluteus medius.
glute-min.insertion: Anterior aspect of the greater trochanter of the femur.
glute-min.action: Abducts the hip (moves leg out) and internally rotates the thigh. A key stabilizer of the hip joint.
symptoms: Deep, aching pain in the buttock that is hard to pinpoint.
Pain that refers down the side of the thigh and leg, sometimes all the way to the ankle.
Pain that refers down the back of the thigh and calf, mimicking sciatica.
Intense pain when lying on the affected side, often worse than with gluteus medius.
Pain and a limp when walking, especially after getting up from a chair.

questions.q: Does your pain travel down the outside of your leg, possibly reaching your ankle?
Does your pain sometimes travel down the back of your leg, making you think you have sciatica?
Is it nearly impossible to lie on the painful side at night?
Do you have a noticeable limp, especially for the first few steps after you stand up?
Is the pain a deep, constant ache in your buttock that you can't seem to touch directly?

tests.name: Gluteus Minimus Palpation
tests.how: Lie on your good side. Find the bony point of your hip (greater trochanter). The gluteus minimus trigger points are often found just in front of and above this bone. Press deeply to explore for exquisite tenderness.
tests.positive: Finding a spot of extreme, sharp tenderness that reproduces your familiar buttock and leg pain.

causes: Sitting on a wallet in your back pocket.
A direct fall onto the side of the hip.
Prolonged sitting, especially in a chair that is too high or too hard.
Walking or running with poor pelvic stability (a 'hip drop' gait).
Wearing worn-out shoes that alter your walking mechanics.
mimics: Lumbar radiculopathy (true sciatica from a disc herniation)
redFlags: True weakness (foot drop) or loss of sensation in the leg or foot.
Loss of bowel or bladder control.
Pain that is not relieved by any position and is worsening.
History of cancer, fever, or unexplained weight loss.

calm.name: Glute Minimus Release (Ball)
calm.how: Lie on your side with a lacrosse or tennis ball placed just in front of the bony point of your hip. Lean into it gently, breathing deeply. Avoid rolling directly on the bone.

calm.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
calm.how: This gentle mobility drill helps to improve internal and external rotation of the hip, which can help calm an irritated gluteus minimus.

calm.name: Side-Lying Pillow Squeeze
calm.how: Lie on your side with a pillow between your knees. Gently squeeze the pillow and hold, engaging the inner thigh muscles, which can help the outer hip muscles relax.

restore.name: Standing Clamshell
restore.dose: 2 x 15 reps per side, every other day
restore.how: This exercise helps activate and strengthen the gluteus medius and minimus in a functional standing position.

restore.name: Standing Hip IR Liftoff
restore.dose: 2 x 10 reps per side, every other day
restore.how: This specifically targets the internal rotation function of the gluteus minimus. Focus on slow, controlled movement without leaning your torso.

restore.name: Piriformis Stretch (Seated)
restore.how: While seated, cross one ankle over the opposite knee. Gently lean forward with a flat back until you feel a stretch in the buttock. This can help stretch the deep hip rotators.

strengthen.name: Glute Walk
strengthen.dose: 2 x 10 steps each direction, every other day
strengthen.how: Use a resistance band around your ankles or knees. The side-stepping motion is excellent for building endurance in both the gluteus medius and minimus.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Drive through one heel to lift the hips level, without letting the pelvis drop on the free side. Pause 2 seconds at the top.

strengthen.name: Side Crab Walk
strengthen.dose: 3 x 6 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Stay low with a band around the knees or ankles and step sideways, keeping toes forward and the pelvis level.

habits: Never sit on your wallet. Keep it in your front pocket or jacket.
Get up and walk around at least once every hour.
Ensure your office chair provides good support and is at the correct height.
Invest in supportive footwear and replace running shoes regularly.
glute-min.expect: Due to its common mimicry of sciatica, this muscle can be stubborn. Consistent release and activation can provide relief from the referred leg pain within 2-4 weeks. Building robust strength to correct underlying walking patterns may take 2-3 months.
glute-min.seePro: Book an appointment if you have numbness, tingling, or true weakness in your leg, or if the pain does not begin to improve after 3 weeks of dedicated effort.

piriformis.insertion: Superior aspect of the greater trochanter of the femur.
piriformis.action: Externally rotates the hip (turns the leg outward) when the hip is extended, and abducts the hip when it is flexed.
symptoms: A deep, aching pain in the center of the buttock.
Pain that refers down the back or back-outside of the thigh, often stopping at the knee.
Numbness or tingling down the back of the leg if the muscle is compressing the sciatic nerve.
Pain that is significantly worse with sitting, especially on hard surfaces or while driving.
Difficulty crossing the affected leg over the other one.

questions.q: Is your pain focused in the dead center of one buttock?
Does sitting for more than 15-20 minutes dramatically increase your buttock pain?
Does the pain travel down the back of your thigh, but usually not past your knee?
Do you get relief by standing up and walking around after sitting?
Do you feel pain when you try to pull your knee towards your opposite shoulder?

tests.name: Piriformis Stretch Test (FAIR Test)
tests.how: Lie on your back, cross the ankle of the painful side over the opposite knee. Gently pull the bottom knee toward your chest and slightly toward the opposite shoulder.
tests.positive: Reproduction of your specific buttock and/or posterior thigh pain indicates piriformis involvement.

causes: Prolonged sitting, which compresses and shortens the muscle.
Sitting on a wallet in a back pocket ('wallet neuritis').
Overuse from activities like running or cycling without proper glute strength.
Anatomical variation where the sciatic nerve passes through the piriformis muscle.
Direct trauma or fall onto the buttock.
mimics: Lumbar radiculopathy (true sciatica from a disc herniation)
redFlags: Loss of bowel or bladder control (cauda equina syndrome).
Progressive leg weakness, such as a 'foot drop'.
Numbness in the 'saddle' area (groin and inner thighs).
Pain that is severe, constant, and not relieved by any change in position.

calm.name: Piriformis Release (Ball)
calm.how: Sit on the floor with your knees bent. Place a tennis or lacrosse ball under the center of the painful buttock. Support yourself with your hands and gently roll to find the tender spot, then hold with steady pressure.

calm.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
calm.how: This is an excellent gentle mobilizer for the deep hip rotators. Move slowly and within a pain-free range of motion.

calm.name: Figure-4 Stretch (Gentle)
calm.how: Lie on your back, cross the ankle of the painful side over the opposite knee. Do NOT pull yet. Just hold this position and breathe, allowing the muscle to relax.

restore.name: Figure-4 Stretch (Active)
restore.how: From the gentle Figure-4 position, now reach through and gently pull the bottom thigh toward your chest until you feel a comfortable stretch in the buttock.

restore.name: Hip Neuroglide
restore.how: This is crucial for piriformis issues. It helps the sciatic nerve slide more freely relative to the piriformis muscle, reducing irritation and referred symptoms.

restore.name: Clamshells
restore.dose: 2 x 15 reps per side, every other day
restore.how: Lie on your side with knees bent and hips stacked. Lift your top knee without rocking your pelvis back. This strengthens other hip rotators to take the load off the piriformis.

strengthen.name: Standing Hip ER Liftoff
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: This directly strengthens the piriformis and other external rotators in a functional, standing position. Focus on control, not height.

strengthen.name: Glute Bridge
strengthen.how: Strengthening the main gluteus maximus muscle provides stability to the pelvis and can reduce the over-activity and strain on the smaller piriformis.

strengthen.name: Hip Thrust
strengthen.how: Shoulders on a bench, drive the hips up by squeezing the glutes, ribs down. Lower slowly; add load only when pain-free.

habits: Take your wallet out of your back pocket permanently.
Set a timer to get up and walk every 20-30 minutes when sitting.
When driving, use a seat cushion with a cutout for the tailbone/piriformis area.
Try to sit with your feet flat on the floor rather than with your legs crossed.
piriformis.expect: Relief from sitting-related pain can often be felt within the first 1-2 weeks. Reducing nerve irritation and building enough glute strength to prevent recurrence is a longer process, typically taking 6-12 weeks of consistent work.
piriformis.seePro: Schedule an in-person evaluation if you experience true numbness, tingling, or weakness that doesn't improve with nerve glides, or if your pain is not significantly better after 4 weeks.

glute-max.origin: Ilium (back of the hip bone), sacrum, and coccyx (tailbone).
glute-max.insertion: Gluteal tuberosity of the femur (thigh bone) and the iliotibial (IT) band.
glute-max.action: The main muscle for extending your hip. It powers movements like standing up from a chair, climbing stairs, running, and lifting.
symptoms: A deep, nagging ache in the buttock.
Pain concentrated around the tailbone (coccyx) and the bony part you sit on (ischial tuberosity).
Stiffness and pain after sitting for a long time, especially on hard surfaces.
A feeling of weakness when climbing stairs or getting up from a squat.
Pain that makes it hard to lie on your back or the affected side.
A 'bruised' feeling deep in the buttock.

questions.q: Is your pain mainly in the fleshy part of your buttock, possibly near your tailbone?
Does the ache get worse after sitting for more than 30 minutes, especially on a hard chair?
Do you feel pain or weakness when pushing up stairs, walking up a hill, or rising from a deep chair?
Is the pain a deep ache rather than a sharp, shooting, or tingling pain down your leg?
Does pressing deeply into the main part of your buttock reproduce your specific ache?

tests.name: Active Hip Extension Test
tests.how: Lie on your stomach with your legs straight. Squeeze the buttock muscles on the painful side and lift that entire leg a few inches off the floor, keeping the knee straight.
tests.positive: You feel your specific buttock pain, or the leg feels significantly weaker or heavier than the other side.

tests.name: Glute Bridge Test
tests.how: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Squeeze your buttocks and lift your hips toward the ceiling.
tests.positive: This movement reproduces your buttock or tailbone pain, or you feel your hamstrings cramping because the glutes aren't working well.

causes: Prolonged sitting, which compresses and deactivates the muscle.
Sudden increase in activities like running, hiking, or weightlifting (squats, deadlifts).
Direct trauma, such as a fall onto the buttocks.
Sleeping on a hard mattress or on one side without support.
An inactive lifestyle leading to weak, inhibited gluteal muscles.
Poor form during exercise, leading to overuse or strain.
mimics: Sciatica or lumbar radiculopathy (nerve root irritation).
redFlags: Pain accompanied by numbness or tingling in the 'saddle' area (groin, inner thighs).
Sudden, unexplained loss of bowel or bladder control.
Progressive weakness in the leg, causing you to trip or your foot to 'drop'.
Pain that is constant, severe, and doesn't change with position or movement.

calm.name: Glute Pressure Release
calm.how: Sit on a lacrosse ball or tennis ball, placing it on the most tender spot in your buttock. Gently roll to apply pressure, but avoid sharp, shooting pain.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Lie on your back with feet on a wall or chair, knees and hips at 90 degrees. Focus on deep belly breaths to relax the pelvic floor and hips.

calm.name: Dynamic Childs Pose
calm.how: Gently rock your hips side to side in a child's pose to create space and mobility in the low back and hips.

restore.name: Quadruped Glute Kick
restore.dose: 3 x 15 per side, every other day
restore.how: On all fours, keep your core braced and extend one leg back, squeezing the glute at the top. Avoid arching your lower back.

restore.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
restore.dose: 3 x 10 per side, every other day
restore.how: Lie on your back with one knee bent and the other leg straight. Drive through the heel to lift your hips, focusing the work in your glute.

restore.name: Hip Neuroglide
restore.how: Perform this gentle nerve mobilization to ensure the nerves around the hip are moving freely.

strengthen.name: Hip Thrust
strengthen.how: With your upper back on a bench and a weight across your hips, drive your hips up by squeezing your glutes. Keep your chin tucked.

strengthen.name: Romanian Deadlift
strengthen.how: Holding weights, hinge at your hips with a flat back, feeling a stretch in your hamstrings. Squeeze your glutes to return to standing.

strengthen.name: Constant Glute Engagement
strengthen.how: Practice this cue to gently engage your glutes with each step, improving your mind-muscle connection throughout the day.

habits: Take frequent breaks from sitting. Use our 'Walk Break Protocol Seated' every 30 minutes.
Sit on a cushion or donut pillow to reduce direct pressure on the muscle.
When standing, maintain a neutral pelvis instead of letting your hips sway forward.
Focus on pushing through your heels when climbing stairs or standing up to engage the glutes.
glute-max.expect: With consistent application of this protocol, most people feel a significant reduction in pain within 2-3 weeks. Building full strength and resilience can take 6-8 weeks.
glute-max.seePro: Book an appointment if your pain is severe, doesn't improve after 2 weeks of self-care, or if you experience any of the 'Red Flags'.

tfl.origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) - the bony point at the front of your hip.
tfl.action: Flexes, abducts, and internally rotates the hip. It helps stabilize the pelvis when you're standing on one leg.
symptoms: A sharp or aching pain at the front and/or outer part of the hip.
Pain that refers down the outside of the thigh, often mistaken for IT band syndrome.
Discomfort that worsens when lying on the affected side at night.
Pain when standing up after prolonged sitting.
A feeling of tightness or restriction at the front of the hip pocket area.
Pain that is aggravated by running, especially on a banked surface.

questions.q: Is your pain located at the very front and side of your hip, right where a front pocket would be?
Does the pain travel down the outside of your thigh, but usually stops before reaching your knee?
Is it painful to lie directly on the affected hip at night?
Do you feel a sharp 'catch' when you lift your knee towards your chest or swing your leg out to the side?
Does your pain get worse with prolonged walking or running, but feel better with rest?

tests.name: Ober's Test (Modified)
tests.how: Lie on your pain-free side with the bottom leg bent for stability. Let the top (painful) leg drop down behind you towards the floor. A partner can help stabilize your pelvis.
tests.positive: You feel a sharp pain or strong stretch at the front/side of your hip, or the leg is unable to drop below parallel to the floor.

tests.name: Resisted Hip Flexion/Abduction
tests.how: While seated, try to lift your knee up and out to the side against resistance from your own hand.
tests.positive: This action reproduces the specific pain at the front-side of your hip.

causes: Prolonged sitting with hips flexed, which shortens the muscle.
Running or cycling with poor mechanics, causing the TFL to overwork.
Weak gluteus medius muscles, forcing the TFL to compensate for pelvic stability.
Sleeping in the fetal position, which keeps the muscle in a shortened state.
Wearing worn-out shoes or running on uneven surfaces.
Leg length discrepancy.
mimics: IT band syndrome (though TFL is often the root cause).
Hip labral tear or femoroacetabular impingement (FAI).
redFlags: A 'clicking' or 'locking' sensation deep inside the hip joint.
Inability to bear weight on the leg.
Pain accompanied by fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss.
Pain that is severe and constant, even at rest.

calm.name: TFL Pressure Release
calm.how: Lie on your side with a lacrosse ball or foam roller just below and in front of the bony point of your hip. Gently roll to find the tender spot and hold pressure.

calm.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
calm.how: Sit on the floor and gently rotate your hips from side to side. This mobilizes the hip joint without stressing the TFL.

calm.name: Pillow Belt Reset
calm.how: Use this technique to gently reset the pelvis and reduce compensatory tension in the hip flexors.

restore.name: Couch Stretch
restore.how: Perform this stretch gently, focusing on squeezing the glute of the back leg to open the front of the hip. Do not force it.

restore.name: Standing Clamshell
restore.dose: 3 x 15 per side, every other day
restore.how: This exercise activates the gluteus medius, which helps reduce the workload on the TFL. Focus on rotating the hip, not just lifting the leg.

restore.name: Standing Hip CARs
restore.how: Perform slow, controlled circles with your hip to improve joint mobility and control, reducing strain on the TFL.

strengthen.name: Side Crab Walk
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 steps each way, twice weekly
strengthen.how: Place a band around your knees or ankles. Stay low and take slow, controlled steps sideways, keeping tension on the band to strengthen your gluteus medius.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.how: This strengthens the gluteus maximus, a key stabilizer that prevents the TFL from overworking.

strengthen.name: Step Up
strengthen.how: Focus on driving through the heel of the front foot and keeping your pelvis level to build single-leg stability.

habits: Avoid sitting with your legs crossed.
When sleeping on your side, place a pillow between your knees to keep your hips in a neutral alignment.
Stand up and stretch your hips into extension (like in the Couch Stretch) every 30-60 minutes.
Check your running form; ensure your feet don't cross the midline ('crossover gait').
tfl.expect: You should notice less pain with daily activities within 1-2 weeks. Full resolution, especially for athletes, may take 4-6 weeks as you retrain movement patterns and build glute strength.
tfl.seePro: Schedule a visit if you have a painful clicking in the hip, if the pain doesn't improve with 2 weeks of care, or if it significantly impacts your ability to walk or sleep.

rectus-femoris.origin: Anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) - a bony point on the front of the pelvis, just below the TFL origin.
rectus-femoris.insertion: Tibial tuberosity via the patellar tendon (the bony bump below your kneecap).
rectus-femoris.action: A key part of the quadriceps group. It extends the knee (straightens the leg) and also flexes the hip (lifts the knee towards the chest).
symptoms: A deep, nagging ache felt around or behind the kneecap (patella).
Pain at the front of the hip, near the hip bone, especially when lifting the leg.
Stiffness and pain in the front of the knee after sitting for a long time ('movie-goer's sign').
Pain that is worse when going down stairs or down a hill.
A feeling of weakness or instability in the knee.
Difficulty fully straightening or bending the knee due to pain.

questions.q: Is your main pain a deep ache around or under your kneecap?
Does the pain get worse after you've been sitting for a while with your knees bent?
Do you also sometimes feel a separate pain point at the very front of your hip bone?
Is going DOWN stairs more painful than going up?
Does your knee feel stiff when you first stand up?

tests.name: Ely's Test
tests.how: Lie on your stomach. Have a partner gently bend your knee, bringing your heel towards your buttock.
tests.positive: You feel a sharp pain in the front of your thigh or hip, and the hip on the same side may lift off the table as the muscle pulls on it.

tests.name: Resisted Knee Extension
tests.how: Sit on a chair with your knee bent. Try to straighten your leg against resistance from your own hand placed on your shin.
tests.positive: This action reproduces the ache around your kneecap or pain in the front of your thigh.

causes: Prolonged sitting, which keeps the muscle in a shortened state at the hip and lengthened at the knee.
Overuse from activities like kicking, sprinting, or cycling.
Weak gluteal muscles, causing the rectus femoris to overwork as a hip flexor.
Direct trauma, like a blow to the front of the thigh.
Poor squatting or lunging mechanics.
An imbalance between the different quadriceps muscles.
redFlags: A 'pop' sound at the time of injury, followed by immediate swelling and inability to straighten the leg (possible quad tendon rupture).
A visible deformity or a gap in the muscle on the front of the thigh.
Knee locking, catching, or giving way completely.
Significant, rapid swelling of the knee joint.

calm.name: Quad Foam Rolling
calm.how: Lie face down with a foam roller under your front thigh. Gently roll from the hip to just above the knee, avoiding the kneecap itself. Pause on tender spots.

calm.name: Knee Circles
calm.dose: 2 x 10 circles each way, twice daily
calm.how: Stand and perform slow, controlled circles with your knees to gently mobilize the joint and improve fluid dynamics without load.

calm.name: Heel Slides
calm.how: Lie on your back and gently slide your heel towards your buttock to bend the knee, then slide it back out. Move only within a pain-free range.

restore.name: Couch Stretch
restore.how: This is the key stretch for the rectus femoris as it extends the hip and flexes the knee. Squeeze the glute of the back leg to intensify the stretch.

restore.name: Knee Neuroglide
restore.how: This helps ensure the femoral nerve, which runs through the quads, is moving freely. Perform gently.

restore.name: Quad Sets
restore.how: Sit or lie with your leg straight. Tighten the muscle on the front of your thigh, trying to push the back of your knee down. This re-establishes muscle activation.

strengthen.name: Step Up
strengthen.how: Focus on a slow, controlled lowering (eccentric) phase, as this builds strength and resilience in the quad tendon and muscle.

strengthen.name: Bodyweight Squat
strengthen.how: Practice squatting with perfect form, ensuring your knees track over your feet and you're using your glutes to power the movement up.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.how: Strengthening your glutes helps to offload the rectus femoris from its hip flexion duties, reducing overuse.

habits: When sitting for long periods, try to periodically straighten your leg out under your desk.
Use our 'Walk Break Protocol Seated' to get up and move every 30-60 minutes.
Adjust your bike seat height. A seat that is too low can increase strain on the rectus femoris.
Avoid sitting on your feet or in a deep 'W' sit position.
rectus-femoris.expect: Pain from sitting should decrease within a week or two. Building the strength to handle activities like running and stairs without pain typically takes 4-8 weeks of consistent effort.
rectus-femoris.seePro: Book an evaluation if you experience knee locking or complete giving-way, if you heard a 'pop' during an injury, or if pain is not improving after 3 weeks of following the protocol.

vmo.origin: Medial lip of the linea aspera and intertrochanteric line of the femur (inner back and top of the thigh bone).
vmo.insertion: Medial border of the patella (inner edge of the kneecap) and tibial tuberosity.
vmo.action: Part of the quadriceps group, its primary role is to extend the knee. The lower fibers (often called the VMO) are crucial for the final degrees of extension and for keeping the kneecap tracking correctly in its groove.
symptoms: Aching or sharp pain on the inner side of the knee and kneecap.
A feeling that the knee might 'give way' or buckle, especially on stairs.
Swelling or puffiness on the inside of the knee, just above the kneecap.
A 'crunching' or 'grinding' sound (crepitus) under the kneecap with movement.
Pain that is worse when going up or down stairs, squatting, or running.
Difficulty fully straightening the leg with a 'locking' sensation.

questions.q: Is your pain located specifically on the inner side of your knee or kneecap?
Does your knee ever feel like it's going to buckle or give out, especially on stairs?
Do you see or feel a 'teardrop' shaped muscle on the inside of your thigh just above the knee, and is it tender to press on?
Is the pain worse after activities that involve repeated knee bending, like running or squatting?
Does it hurt to sit for a long time with your knee bent?

tests.name: VMO Contraction Test
tests.how: Sit on the floor with your leg straight out in front of you. Place your fingers on the 'teardrop' muscle on the inside of your thigh, just above the kneecap. Try to tighten only this muscle.
tests.positive: You feel pain under your fingers, or you are unable to contract this muscle without contracting the entire thigh.

tests.name: Terminal Knee Extension Test
tests.how: Stand with a resistance band looped around the back of your painful knee and anchored to something in front of you. Let the band pull your knee into a slight bend, then straighten your leg by squeezing your quad.
tests.positive: This movement reproduces your specific inner knee pain.

causes: An imbalance between the vastus medialis and the vastus lateralis (outer quad), causing the kneecap to pull sideways.
Weakness or poor activation of the VMO, often following a knee injury or surgery.
Flat feet (overpronation), which can cause the lower leg to rotate inward and affect kneecap tracking.
Weak hip and gluteal muscles, leading to poor leg alignment.
A sudden increase in squatting, lunging, or running volume.
redFlags: The knee is locked in a bent position and you cannot straighten it.
A 'pop' sound at the time of injury followed by significant, rapid swelling.
Inability to put any weight on the leg.
Redness, heat, and extreme tenderness in the knee joint (could be infection or gout).

calm.name: VMO Soft Tissue Release
calm.how: Sit with your leg slightly bent. Use your thumbs or a massage ball to apply gentle but firm pressure to the tender muscle fibers on the inside of your thigh, just above the knee.

calm.name: Quad Sets with Medial Focus
calm.how: Sit with your leg straight. Place a small rolled towel under your knee. Squeeze your quad to straighten the leg and lift your heel, focusing on the inner quad muscle.

calm.name: Knee Neuroglide
calm.how: Gently perform this nerve glide to ensure the nerves supplying the quad are not restricted, which can inhibit muscle function.

restore.name: Terminal Knee Extensions (TKEs)
restore.dose: 3 x 15 per side, every other day
restore.how: Loop a resistance band around the back of your knee, anchored in front of you. Step back to create tension. Bend and straighten the last 20-30 degrees of knee extension, focusing on the VMO.

restore.name: Wall Sit with Ball Squeeze
restore.dose: 3 x 30-45 sec holds, every other day
restore.how: Perform a wall sit at a comfortable height. Place a small ball between your knees and maintain a gentle squeeze to increase VMO activation.

restore.name: Single Leg Balance
restore.dose: 3 x 30 sec holds per side, daily
restore.how: This improves proprioception and stability around the knee joint, which is crucial for VMO function.

strengthen.name: Step Up
strengthen.how: Use a low step. Focus on keeping your knee aligned over your second toe and avoid letting it collapse inward. Control the movement on the way down.

strengthen.name: Bodyweight Squat (Heels Elevated)
strengthen.how: Place your heels on a small plate or book. This allows for a more upright torso and can help you focus on quad activation, including the VMO.

strengthen.name: Step Up
