strengthen.how: Step up onto a low box, keeping the knee lined up over the second toe; lower slowly over 3 seconds.

habits: Avoid letting your knee collapse inward during daily activities like climbing stairs or standing up.
Consider footwear or orthotics if you have significantly flat feet.
When sitting, try to avoid positions that twist the knee, like sitting with one foot tucked under you.
Focus on squeezing your quad to fully 'lock out' your knee at the top of each step when walking.
vmo.expect: A reduction in buckling sensations and daily pain can often be felt in 2-4 weeks. Rebuilding the VMO's strength and coordination to prevent recurrence during sports can take 8-12 weeks.
vmo.seePro: Book an appointment if your knee is locking, if it swells up significantly after activity, or if the feeling of instability persists despite 3-4 weeks of consistent exercise.

vastus-lateralis.origin: Greater trochanter and linea aspera of the femur (thigh bone).
vastus-lateralis.insertion: Patella (kneecap) and tibial tuberosity (upper shin bone) via the patellar ligament.
vastus-lateralis.action: Extends (straightens) the knee. It is a primary power muscle for standing up, climbing stairs, squatting, and running.
symptoms: Aching pain along the outside of the thigh.
Pain that refers down to the outer side of the knee.
Sharp pain when lying on the affected side, often disturbing sleep.
A feeling of stiffness or a 'catching' sensation in the knee.
Weakness or a feeling of instability when squatting or going down stairs.

questions.q: Is your pain mainly on the *outer* side of your thigh, sometimes traveling to the outside of your knee?
Does lying directly on that side in bed make the pain noticeably worse?
Do you feel a sharp pain on the outside of your knee when you squat or go down stairs?
Does your knee sometimes feel stiff, as if it's hard to bend or straighten fully?
Have you recently increased your running, cycling, or squatting activities?

tests.name: Single Leg Squat Test
tests.how: Stand on one leg and slowly bend your knee as if sitting in a chair, going only as far as is comfortable. Observe your knee's movement in a mirror.
tests.positive: Pain on the outside of the thigh or knee, or if your knee wobbles or dives inward, can indicate weakness or tightness in this muscle.

causes: Overuse from activities like running, cycling, or leg-heavy gym workouts.
Sitting for long periods with knees bent, especially in a cramped space.
Sleeping on your side without a pillow between your knees, compressing the muscle.
Direct trauma, like a fall or impact to the outer thigh.
Muscle imbalances, such as weak gluteal muscles, causing the quads to overwork.
mimics: Lumbar radiculopathy (nerve pain from the low back)
redFlags: Inability to bear weight on the leg.
Visible, significant swelling or deformity around the knee or thigh.
A 'popping' sound at the time of injury followed by immediate, severe pain.
Numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation spreading down the leg.

calm.name: Foam Roll Outer Thigh
calm.how: Lie on your side with a foam roller under your outer thigh. Roll slowly from your hip to just above your knee, pausing on tender spots for 20-30 seconds.

calm.name: Gentle Knee Bends
calm.how: Holding onto a counter for support, slowly bend and straighten your knees through a pain-free range of motion. Do not push into sharp pain.

restore.name: Standing Quad Stretch
restore.how: Stand on one leg, holding onto something for balance. Grab your other ankle and gently pull your heel towards your buttock, feeling a stretch in the front of your thigh.

restore.name: Couch Stretch
restore.how: Follow the video to perform this deep stretch for the quads and hip flexors. Keep your core engaged to protect your lower back.

strengthen.name: Bodyweight Squat
strengthen.how: Focus on keeping your knees aligned over your second toe; don't let them collapse inward. Control the movement on the way down and up.

strengthen.name: Lunges
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8-12 per leg, every other day
strengthen.how: Take a controlled step forward, lowering your hips until both knees are bent at about a 90-degree angle. Push back to the starting position.

habits: When sleeping on your side, place a pillow between your knees to keep your hips aligned.
Avoid sitting with your legs crossed for long periods.
Take regular breaks from sitting to stand up and stretch your legs.
Ensure your bike seat height is properly adjusted to avoid over-stressing the quads.
vastus-lateralis.expect: With consistent adherence to the protocol, most people feel a significant reduction in pain within 2-4 weeks. Full recovery and return to sport may take 6-8 weeks.
vastus-lateralis.seePro: Book an appointment if pain is severe, doesn't improve after 2 weeks of self-care, or if you suspect a more serious injury like a ligament or meniscus tear.

popliteus.origin: Lateral condyle of the femur (outer thigh bone at the knee).
popliteus.insertion: Posterior surface of the tibia (back of the shin bone).
popliteus.action: Internally rotates the tibia on the femur to 'unlock' the knee from a straight position, allowing it to bend. It also helps stabilize the back of the knee.
symptoms: Sharp pain located directly in the back of the knee.
Pain that is worse when walking or running, especially downhill.
A feeling of instability or that the knee might 'give way' when twisting.
Difficulty fully straightening or 'locking' the knee.
Pain when crouching or squatting down low.

questions.q: Is your pain located precisely in the hollow at the back of your knee?
Is the pain significantly worse when you walk or run downhill?
Do you feel a sharp pain when you try to squat down low?
Does your knee feel unstable, especially when twisting or turning?
Do you have pain when you first 'unlock' your knee from a fully straight position to begin bending it?

tests.name: Resisted Knee Flexion Test
tests.how: Sit on a chair and cross the ankle of your good leg over the front of the painful leg's ankle. Try to bend the painful knee against the resistance of your other leg.
tests.positive: Pain in the back of the knee during this resisted movement points to the popliteus or hamstring tendons.

causes: Overuse in sports that involve a lot of downhill running (e.g., trail running).
A sudden twist of the knee while the foot is planted.
Chronic over-pronation of the foot (foot rolling inward).
Muscle imbalances, particularly weak hamstrings or glutes.
Returning to activity too quickly after a previous knee injury.
mimics: Posterior horn of the meniscus tear
Baker's cyst (a fluid-filled sac behind the knee)
redFlags: A 'pop' at the time of injury with immediate, significant swelling.
Inability to put any weight on the leg.
A feeling of the knee being 'locked' where you cannot bend or straighten it at all.
Visible swelling and redness in the back of the knee.

calm.name: Gentle Knee Rotations
calm.dose: 2 x 10 circles each way, twice daily
calm.how: Sit on a high chair so your feet don't touch the floor. Gently swing your lower leg to make small circles, moving from the knee joint.

calm.name: Pressure Release Behind Knee
calm.how: Sit and place a lacrosse or tennis ball in the crease behind your knee. Gently bend and straighten your leg to apply pressure to the muscle. Avoid pressing on the very center of the knee pit.

restore.name: Knee Neuroglide
restore.how: Follow the video to gently mobilize the nerves around the back of the knee. This is a gentle flossing motion, not an aggressive stretch.

restore.name: Heel Slides
restore.how: Lie on your back and slowly slide the heel of your affected leg towards your buttock, bending the knee. Slide back to the start. Move only within a pain-free range.

strengthen.name: Terminal Knee Extensions (Band)
strengthen.how: Anchor a resistance band to a post. Loop the other end around the back of your knee. Step back to create tension, then straighten your knee against the band's pull.

strengthen.name: Wall Sits
strengthen.dose: 3 x 30-60 sec holds, every other day
strengthen.how: Lean your back against a wall and slide down until your knees are at a comfortable angle. Hold this position, ensuring your knees track over your ankles.

habits: Avoid locking your knees when standing for long periods.
When walking downhill, take shorter steps and try to land with a slightly bent knee.
Ensure your footwear provides adequate support to prevent over-pronation.
Strengthen your glute muscles (e.g., with bridges, clamshells) to improve overall leg stability.
popliteus.expect: Because it's a small stabilizer, popliteus pain can be stubborn. Consistent, gentle exercises should bring noticeable relief in 2-3 weeks, with a return to more demanding activities in 4-6 weeks.
popliteus.seePro: Book an appointment if you suspect a meniscus or ligament injury, if the knee is locking or giving way, or if pain does not improve with 2-3 weeks of conservative care.

gastroc.origin: Two heads from the medial and lateral condyles of the femur (back of the thigh bone just above the knee).
gastroc.insertion: Calcaneus (heel bone) via the Achilles tendon.
gastroc.action: Plantarflexes the foot (points the toes down) and assists in flexing (bending) the knee. It's the primary 'push-off' muscle for walking, running, and jumping.
symptoms: A deep, cramp-like ache in the upper or middle part of the calf.
Pain that can refer up into the back of the knee.
Aching pain in the arch of the foot, especially in the morning or after rest.
Frequent calf cramps, especially at night.
A feeling of tightness or pulling in the calf when walking up stairs or hills.

questions.q: Do you get intense, cramp-like pain in your upper calf, sometimes even at night?
Does your pain also seem to travel into the arch of your foot?
Is the pain worse when you push off your toes, like when running, jumping, or climbing stairs?
Does the back of your knee ache, in addition to your calf pain?
Do you often wear high heels or shoes with a significant heel-to-toe drop?

tests.name: Calf Raise Test
tests.how: Stand on one leg, holding onto something for balance. Perform a single-leg calf raise, pushing up onto the ball of your foot.
tests.positive: Sharp pain in the calf, weakness, or an inability to lift the heel off the ground can indicate a gastrocnemius issue.

causes: Sudden increase in running mileage or intensity.
Activities with a lot of jumping or hill climbing.
Wearing high heels, which keeps the muscle in a shortened position.
Dehydration or electrolyte imbalances (e.g., low magnesium or potassium).
Switching to minimalist or 'zero-drop' shoes too quickly.
mimics: Soleus muscle strain (pain is typically lower in the calf)
Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) - a blood clot (this is a medical emergency)
redFlags: Sudden, severe calf pain with swelling, redness, and warmth (could be a DVT - go to ER).
A 'pop' or feeling of being 'shot' in the back of the leg during activity, with inability to walk properly (possible Achilles tendon rupture or 'tennis leg').
Pain that doesn't change with movement or rest.
Numbness or a 'pins and needles' feeling in the foot.

calm.name: Foam Roll Calf
calm.how: Sit on the floor with a foam roller under your calf. Use your hands to support your weight and roll from below the knee to above the ankle. Cross one leg over the other for more pressure.

calm.name: Straight-Knee Calf Stretch
calm.dose: 2 x 30 sec per side, twice daily
calm.how: Stand facing a wall, step one foot back, keeping the back leg *straight* and the heel on the floor. You should feel this higher up in the calf.

restore.name: Ankle Neuroglide
restore.how: Follow the video to gently mobilize the nerves that run through the calf. This helps differentiate between muscle tightness and nerve tension.

restore.name: Wall Calf Stretch (Straight Knee)
restore.how: Stand facing a wall with hands on the wall for support. Step one foot back, keeping the back leg straight and heel firmly on the floor until you feel a stretch in the upper calf.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Calf Drops
strengthen.dose: 3 x 15 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Stand on a step. Use both feet to rise up onto your toes, then lift the uninjured foot and *slowly* lower the heel of the affected foot below the step level. Use both feet to rise up again.

strengthen.name: Toe Walk
strengthen.how: Walk around on the balls of your feet, keeping your heels off the ground. This builds endurance in the calf muscles.

habits: Stay well-hydrated and ensure adequate electrolyte intake, especially if you are active.
Gradually transition to new footwear over several weeks.
Avoid sitting with your feet tucked under you for long periods.
Incorporate regular calf stretching into your post-workout routine.
gastroc.expect: For mild strains or trigger points, you should feel better within 1-2 weeks. A more significant strain may take 4-6 weeks of consistent rehab to return to full activity.
gastroc.seePro: Seek immediate medical attention for any red flag symptoms. Book an appointment if you suspect an Achilles tendon rupture or if pain is severe and not improving after 2 weeks.

soleus.origin: Posterior (back) surface of the tibia and fibula, underneath the gastrocnemius.
soleus.insertion: Calcaneus (heel bone) via the Achilles tendon.
soleus.action: Plantarflexes the foot (points the toes down). It is a powerful postural muscle, active whenever you are standing to prevent you from falling forward.
symptoms: A deep, aching pain in the lower half of the calf.
Pain that refers directly into the heel and Achilles tendon area.
Pain that feels like 'plantar fasciitis' but is located more in the heel pad.
Stiffness and pain that is worse after long periods of standing or walking.
Pain that is often a constant, low-grade ache rather than a sharp, acute pain.

questions.q: Is your pain a deep ache in your *lower* calf, heel, or Achilles tendon?
Does your pain get significantly worse after prolonged standing or walking, like a day of shopping or sightseeing?
Does the pain feel similar to plantar fasciitis, but more in the back of the heel than the bottom of the foot?
Is the pain more of a constant, nagging ache than a sharp, stabbing pain?
Do you feel pain when you press deeply into the sides of your Achilles tendon, into the fleshy part of your lower calf?

tests.name: Bent-Knee Calf Raise Test
tests.how: Stand on one leg with the knee significantly bent (about 45 degrees), holding a wall for balance. Try to lift your heel off the ground. This isolates the soleus.
tests.positive: Pain in the lower calf or heel, or significant weakness/inability to lift the heel, points to a soleus issue.

causes: Jobs or activities that require prolonged standing on hard surfaces.
Running long distances, as the soleus is a primary endurance muscle.
Wearing unsupportive footwear with poor shock absorption.
Driving for long hours, keeping the foot on the pedals.
A gait pattern with excessive forward lean or a heavy heel strike.
mimics: Heel spur or stress fracture of the calcaneus
Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) - a medical emergency
redFlags: Sudden, severe calf pain with swelling, redness, and warmth (could be a DVT - go to ER).
A 'pop' or tearing sensation in the Achilles area (possible Achilles rupture).
Inability to bear weight or walk.
Pain that is present and severe even at rest, especially at night.

calm.name: Bent-Knee Calf Stretch
calm.dose: 2 x 30 sec per side, twice daily
calm.how: Face a wall and step one foot back. Keeping both heels on the floor, bend both knees until you feel a deep stretch in the lower calf of the back leg.

calm.name: Self-Massage Lower Calf
calm.how: Sit on the floor and use your thumbs or a massage ball to apply firm, sustained pressure to tender spots in the lower, fleshy part of your calf, to the sides of the Achilles tendon.

restore.name: Ankle Neuroglide
restore.how: Follow the video instructions for this gentle nerve mobilization exercise. This helps ensure the nerves in the lower leg are moving freely.

restore.name: Seated Calf Stretch
restore.how: Sit on the floor with one leg extended. Loop a towel or band around the ball of your foot and gently pull back, keeping your knee slightly bent to target the soleus.

strengthen.name: Seated Calf Raises
strengthen.how: Sit on a chair with your feet flat on the floor. Place a weight (e.g., a heavy book or dumbbell) on your knees. Slowly lift your heels as high as possible, then lower them back down.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Calf Drops (Bent Knee)
strengthen.dose: 3 x 15 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Perform as shown in the video, but maintain a bent knee throughout the movement to place more emphasis on the soleus muscle during the lowering phase.

habits: Wear supportive shoes, especially if you stand or walk for long periods.
Use an anti-fatigue mat if you have a standing desk or work on a hard floor.
Avoid standing with your knees locked back.
On long drives, use cruise control when safe to do so and move your ankle around periodically.
soleus.expect: Soleus issues can be persistent due to their constant use in standing and walking. Expect gradual improvement over 3-6 weeks with consistent stretching and strengthening. Full resolution may take longer.
soleus.seePro: Seek immediate medical attention for any red flag symptoms. Book an appointment if pain is preventing you from walking normally or if there is no improvement after 3-4 weeks of dedicated self-care.

tib-post.origin: Posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula, and the membrane between them.
tib-post.insertion: Multiple bones on the underside of the foot, primarily the navicular bone.
tib-post.action: Points the foot down and turns it inward. It is the primary muscle that holds up the main arch of your foot.
symptoms: Aching pain deep in the calf or along the inner shin bone.
Sharp pain on the inside of the ankle or in the arch, especially with activity.
A feeling that your arch is collapsing or your foot is becoming flatter.
Weakness or instability when trying to stand on your tiptoes.
Pain that gets worse after long periods of standing, walking, or running.
Morning stiffness in the inner ankle and arch.

questions.q: Is your pain located along the inside of your ankle bone, running down into your arch?
Do you feel like the arch on the inside of your foot is getting lower or 'falling'?
Is it very difficult or painful to do a single-leg heel raise (go up on your tiptoes) on the affected side?
Does your pain feel deep inside your calf, rather than on the surface?
Does wearing shoes with good arch support seem to help?

tests.name: Single Leg Heel Raise
tests.how: Stand on the affected foot only and try to raise your heel off the ground, going up onto your tiptoes. You can lightly touch a wall for balance.
tests.positive: A positive test is significant pain on the inside of the ankle, inability to lift the heel, or if your heel rolls outward as you try to lift it.

causes: Over-pronation or having 'flat feet'.
A sudden increase in impact activities like running or jumping.
Wearing unsupportive footwear for long periods.
Chronic ankle instability from previous injuries.
Being overweight, which increases the load on the arch.
Age-related changes to the tendon.
redFlags: Inability to bear any weight on the foot after an injury.
Numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in the foot.
Sudden, severe swelling and bruising around the ankle without a clear injury.
Signs of a blood clot in the calf: localized swelling, redness, and warmth.

calm.name: Lacrosse Ball Arch Release
calm.how: While seated, roll a lacrosse or tennis ball under the arch of your foot with firm pressure. Focus on any tender spots to release tension in the muscles supporting the tendon.

calm.name: Ankle Pumps
calm.dose: 3 x 15 reps, several times per day
calm.how: While sitting or lying down, gently point your toes away from you, then pull them back towards your shin. This gentle movement helps reduce swelling and stiffness.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Follow the video to lie in a relaxed position. This helps calm the nervous system and reduce overall muscle guarding and pain perception.

restore.name: Short Foot Exercise
restore.how: With your foot flat on the floor, try to shorten your foot by pulling the ball of your foot towards your heel, creating an arch. Do this without curling your toes.

restore.name: Ankle Neuroglide
restore.how: Follow the video to gently mobilize the nerves around the ankle. This can help reduce irritation and improve tissue health in the area.

restore.name: Towel Curls
restore.how: Sit with your foot flat on a towel. Use your toes to scrunch the towel towards you, which helps strengthen the small muscles in your foot that support the arch.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Calf Drops
strengthen.how: Perform on a step as shown, focusing on a very slow (3-4 second) and controlled lowering of your heel. This builds strength and resilience in the tendon.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Balance
strengthen.how: Stand on one leg, focusing on keeping your arch lifted and your ankle stable. This retrains the muscle's crucial role in stabilizing your foot.

strengthen.name: Toe Walk
strengthen.how: Walk on your tiptoes as shown in the video. This directly strengthens the tibialis posterior and other calf muscles that support the arch.

habits: Wear supportive shoes with good arch support daily. Avoid going barefoot on hard surfaces.
Consider an over-the-counter orthotic insert to provide consistent arch support.
Gradually progress your activity levels. Avoid sudden jumps in running mileage or intensity.
Maintain a healthy weight to reduce the daily stress on your feet and ankles.
tib-post.expect: With consistent daily exercises and supportive footwear, mild symptoms often improve in 2-4 weeks. More significant tendinopathy can take 6-12 weeks or longer to fully resolve.
tib-post.seePro: Book an appointment if you are unable to perform a single-leg heel raise, if pain is severe and not improving after 2 weeks of self-care, or if you suspect a fracture.

tib-ant.name: Tibialis anterior
tib-ant.origin: Upper, outer surface of the shin bone (tibia).
tib-ant.insertion: A bone on the inside of the mid-foot (medial cuneiform) and the base of the big toe bone (first metatarsal).
tib-ant.action: Lifts the foot and toes up toward the shin (dorsiflexion) and helps turn the foot inward (inversion). It prevents your foot from 'slapping' the ground when you walk.
symptoms: Aching or sharp pain on the front of the shin, just to the outside of the shin bone.
Pain at the front of the ankle, where the foot meets the leg.
Pain that sometimes travels down to the top of the big toe.
A feeling of weakness when trying to lift your foot or toes.
Pain that is worse when walking or running, especially downhill or down stairs.
The muscle may feel tight or tender to the touch.

questions.q: Is your pain located in the muscle on the front and outer side of your shin bone?
Does the pain sometimes refer to the front of your ankle or the top of your big toe?
Is the pain worse when you go down stairs or walk/run downhill?
Do you notice the pain after driving for a long time or after activities that involve a lot of foot tapping?
Do your shoes feel too tight across the top of your foot?

tests.name: Resisted Foot Lift
tests.how: While sitting, cross your legs so the affected ankle rests on the other knee. Place your hand on top of your foot and try to lift your foot up against your hand's resistance.
tests.positive: A positive test is pain or noticeable weakness in the muscle on the front of your shin.

tests.name: Heel Walk
tests.how: Try to walk for 10-15 steps on your heels only, keeping the front part of your feet off the ground.
tests.positive: A positive test is a sharp increase in your shin pain or an inability to perform the walk.

causes: Overuse from activities like running (especially downhill), hiking, or kicking sports.
Tight calf muscles, which force the tibialis anterior to work harder to lift the foot.
Switching to minimalist shoes or a different running style too quickly.
Lacing shoes, boots, or skates too tightly across the front of the ankle.
Driving for long periods, keeping the foot constantly lifted.
Weakness in the muscle, leading to fatigue and strain.
redFlags: Severe pain, swelling, and redness on the shin after an injury (possible fracture).
Numbness on the top of the foot or a 'foot drop' (a new inability to lift your foot at all).
Intense, tight, or burning pain in the shin that gets progressively worse during exercise and doesn't resolve with rest.
Signs of a blood clot in the calf: localized swelling, redness, and warmth.

calm.name: Tibialis Anterior Release
calm.how: Sit on a chair or the floor. Use your thumbs or a lacrosse ball to apply firm, sustained pressure to tender spots in the muscle on the front/outside of your shin.

calm.name: Gentle Ankle Circles
calm.dose: 10 circles each direction, 3 times per day
calm.how: Sit or lie down and slowly rotate your ankle in large, gentle circles. This improves mobility and blood flow without straining the muscle.

calm.name: Calf Stretch
calm.dose: 2 x 30 seconds per side, twice daily
calm.how: Stand facing a wall with one foot back. Keep the back leg straight and heel on the floor to stretch the upper calf. Then, bend the back knee to stretch the lower calf.

restore.name: Kneeling Shin Stretch
restore.how: Kneel on a soft surface with the tops of your feet flat on the floor. Gently sit back towards your heels until you feel a stretch on the front of your shins.

restore.name: Ankle Neuroglide
restore.how: Follow the video to gently mobilize the nerves that run along the front of the ankle, which can become irritated with this condition.

restore.name: Isometric Dorsiflexion
restore.how: Sit with your heel on the ground. Use your hand or your other foot to provide resistance on top of your foot as you try to lift it, without allowing any movement.

strengthen.name: Heel Walk
strengthen.how: As shown in the video, walk on your heels while keeping the balls of your feet off the ground. This is the most direct way to strengthen the tibialis anterior.

strengthen.name: Banded Dorsiflexion
strengthen.how: Anchor a resistance band to a sturdy object in front of you. Sit and loop the other end around the top of your foot. Pull your toes toward your shin against the band's resistance.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Calf Drops
strengthen.how: Strengthening the opposing calf muscles helps balance the forces around the ankle. Follow the video, focusing on the slow lowering phase.

habits: Ensure your shoes are not laced too tightly, especially over the front of the ankle.
When running, focus on taking shorter, quicker steps to avoid 'over-striding' and slapping your foot down.
Regularly stretch your calf muscles, as tightness there can overload the shin muscles.
Gradually increase the intensity and duration of your activities, especially on hills.
tib-ant.expect: Mild strains often feel significantly better within 1-3 weeks. More persistent pain from chronic overuse can take 4-8 weeks of consistent rehab to resolve.
tib-ant.seePro: Book an appointment if you experience 'foot drop' (inability to lift your foot), numbness on top of the foot, or pain that is severe and doesn't improve with rest.

peroneals.name: Peroneals (fibularis)
peroneals.origin: The outer surface of the lower leg bone (fibula).
peroneals.insertion: One tendon attaches to the outside of the mid-foot (5th metatarsal), and the other runs under the foot to attach to the inside.
peroneals.action: Turn the sole of the foot outward (eversion) and help point the foot down. They are critical for stabilizing the ankle and preventing it from 'rolling' inward.
symptoms: Aching or sharp pain located behind or below the outer ankle bone.
Pain that runs along the outside edge of the foot toward the little toe.
A feeling of ankle instability, weakness, or that it might 'give way'.
Swelling and tenderness on the outside of the ankle.
A snapping or popping sensation on the outside of the ankle with movement.
Pain that is worse with cutting, pivoting, or walking on uneven ground.

questions.q: Is your pain mainly located behind or just below your outer ankle bone?
Do you have a history of 'rolling' your ankle (ankle sprains) on this side?
Does your ankle feel unstable, like it could easily give out from under you?
Is the pain worse when you walk on uneven surfaces like a grassy field or a trail?
Do you ever feel a 'snapping' sensation on the outside of your ankle when you walk or run?

tests.name: Resisted Eversion
tests.how: Sit in a chair with your foot off the ground. Use your hand to provide resistance on the outside edge of your foot as you try to turn the sole of your foot outward.
tests.positive: A positive test is pain or significant weakness felt behind the outer ankle bone.

tests.name: Single Leg Balance
tests.how: Stand on the affected leg and try to balance for 30 seconds without holding on to anything.
tests.positive: A positive test is significant difficulty balancing, a strong feeling of instability, or pain on the outside of the ankle.

causes: Acute ankle sprains, which stretch or damage the peroneal tendons.
Chronic ankle instability from repeated sprains.
Overuse from running on banked surfaces (like the edge of a road) or uneven trails.
Having high-arched feet, which places more stress on the outside of the foot.
Wearing worn-out or improper footwear that lacks side-to-side support.
Weakness in the hip and gluteal muscles, leading to poor leg control.
mimics: Fracture of the 5th metatarsal (base of the little toe)
redFlags: Inability to walk more than a few steps immediately after an ankle injury.
A loud 'pop' at the time of injury followed by rapid swelling and bruising.
Tenderness directly on the bone at the tip of your outer ankle or on the bony bump on the outside of your mid-foot.
Numbness or tingling on the top or outside of your foot.

calm.name: Peroneal Muscle Release
calm.how: Sit on the floor with your leg crossed. Use your thumbs or a lacrosse ball to apply pressure to tender spots in the muscle on the outside of your lower leg, below your knee.

calm.name: Ankle Alphabet
calm.how: Sit with your foot elevated and gently 'draw' the letters of the alphabet in the air with your big toe. This encourages gentle movement in all directions.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Follow the video to lie in a relaxed position. This helps calm the nervous system, which can be overactive after an injury like an ankle sprain.

restore.name: Banded Eversion
restore.how: Anchor a resistance band to a stable object. Sit and loop it around the outside of your foot. Keeping your heel down, rotate your foot outward against the band's resistance.

restore.name: Ankle Neuroglide
restore.how: Follow the video to gently mobilize the nerves around the ankle, which are often irritated after ankle sprains and can contribute to pain.

restore.name: Calf Stretch with Inversion
restore.how: Perform a standard calf stretch against a wall, but turn your back foot slightly inward (pigeon-toed). This will direct the stretch more to the outside of the calf.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Balance
strengthen.how: This is the most important exercise to retrain the stabilizing function of the peroneals. As you get better, try it with your eyes closed or on an unstable surface like a pillow.

strengthen.name: March Balance
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 reps per side, every other day
strengthen.how: This adds a dynamic challenge to your balance, forcing the peroneals to react and stabilize the ankle as you move.

strengthen.name: Side Crab Walk
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 steps each way, every other day
strengthen.how: Place a band around your knees or ankles. Take side steps as shown to strengthen the hip muscles, which are crucial for controlling leg and ankle alignment.

habits: Wear supportive shoes, especially for sports. High-top shoes can provide extra stability if you have a history of sprains.
Pay close attention when walking on uneven ground, trails, or cobblestones.
Avoid sitting for long periods with your ankle 'tucked' under your body.
Incorporate balance exercises into your daily routine, such as standing on one leg while brushing your teeth.
peroneals.expect: Following an acute injury, it can take 4-8 weeks to regain stability and strength. For chronic tendon pain, consistent rehab for 6-12 weeks is often needed for significant improvement.
peroneals.seePro: Book an evaluation if you have persistent ankle instability, a painful 'snapping' tendon, or if you are unable to return to your activities without pain after 4-6 weeks of self-care.

foot-intrinsics.name: Foot muscles (intrinsics)
foot-intrinsics.origin: Various bones within the foot, primarily the heel bone (calcaneus) and metatarsals.
foot-intrinsics.insertion: The toe bones (phalanges). These muscles start and end entirely within the foot.
foot-intrinsics.action: They support the arches of the foot, control fine movements of the toes, and provide your brain with sensory information about the ground.
foot-intrinsics.nerve: Medial and Lateral Plantar Nerves (S1, S2)
symptoms: Sharp, stabbing pain in the heel or arch, especially with the first few steps in the morning.
Aching, cramping, or burning pain in the sole of the foot.
Pain that feels like you are walking on a pebble or a bruise.
General foot fatigue or aching after standing or walking for a while.
Pain that gets much worse when walking barefoot on hard surfaces.
Difficulty or cramping when trying to spread your toes.

questions.q: Is your pain worst with the very first steps you take after getting out of bed or after a long period of sitting?
Does your pain feel like a deep ache or cramp in the arch of your foot?
Does walking barefoot on tile or hardwood floors make your foot pain significantly worse?
Do you find that your feet just feel tired and achy at the end of a long day of standing?
Does wearing very flat, unsupportive shoes (like flip-flops) seem to trigger your pain?

tests.name: Toe Spreading
tests.how: While sitting with your foot flat on the floor, try to spread your toes apart as wide as possible, then bring them back together.
tests.positive: A positive test is an inability to spread the toes, cramping in the arch, or pain during the movement.

tests.name: Short Foot Exercise
tests.how: With your foot flat on the floor, try to lift your arch by sliding the ball of your foot toward your heel without curling your toes or lifting them off the floor.
tests.positive: A positive test is an inability to create an arch, cramping, or pain.

causes: Weakness in the small muscles of the foot, leading to poor arch support.
Consistently wearing unsupportive footwear like flip-flops, flat sandals, or worn-out shoes.
A sudden increase in weight-bearing activity like running, walking, or standing for a new job.
Tight calf muscles, which increases the strain on the bottom of the foot.
Having either very flat feet or very high, rigid arches.
Gaining weight, which increases the load on the feet.
mimics: Plantar fasciitis (these two conditions are very closely related and often occur together)
Heel pad atrophy (thinning of the fat pad under the heel)
Nerve pain from the lower back (radiculopathy)
redFlags: Numbness, tingling, or burning pain in the sole of the foot that doesn't go away.
Pain at night that is severe enough to wake you from sleep.
Visible swelling, redness, and warmth in the heel or arch area.
Inability to put any weight on the foot.

calm.name: Foot Rolling
calm.how: Roll a frozen water bottle or a lacrosse ball under the entire sole of your foot, from heel to toes. This helps massage the muscles and reduce inflammation.

calm.name: Big Toe and Plantar Fascia Stretch
calm.how: While sitting, gently pull your big toe back towards your shin until you feel a stretch in the arch. This is especially helpful to do before taking your first steps in the morning.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Follow the video to get into a relaxed position. While breathing, consciously focus on relaxing the muscles in your feet and letting go of tension.

restore.name: Short Foot Exercise
restore.how: With your foot flat on the floor, shorten your foot by pulling the ball of your foot toward your heel, creating an arch. Do this without curling your toes.

restore.name: Towel Curls
restore.how: Sit with your foot on a small towel. Use only your toes to scrunch the towel towards you. This is a foundational exercise for foot strength.

restore.name: Toe Yoga
restore.dose: 3 x 5 reps of each movement, daily
restore.how: Sit with your foot flat. First, try to lift just your big toe while keeping the others down. Then, try to lift the four smaller toes while keeping the big toe down.

strengthen.name: Toe Walk
strengthen.how: Walking on your tiptoes as shown in the video strengthens the intrinsic muscles and the entire calf complex, which work together to support your foot.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Balance
strengthen.how: While balancing, focus on actively maintaining your arch and feeling the small muscles in your foot working to keep you stable.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Calf Drops
strengthen.how: Strong calf muscles and a healthy Achilles tendon reduce the load on the bottom of the foot. Follow the video, focusing on the slow lowering phase.

habits: Wear supportive shoes and avoid going barefoot on hard surfaces, especially when your pain is active.
Keep a supportive slipper or shoe by your bed to wear for your first steps in the morning.
Gently stretch your foot by pulling your toes back before you get out of bed.
Maintain a healthy weight to decrease the daily load your feet have to support.
foot-intrinsics.expect: Heel and arch pain can be persistent. With consistent daily exercises and better footwear choices, you should notice a gradual improvement in 4-6 weeks. Full recovery can often take 3-6 months.
foot-intrinsics.seePro: Book an evaluation if your pain is severe, you have constant numbness or tingling, or if you see no improvement after 4 weeks of consistent self-care.

ant-delt.origin: Front edge of the outer third of the collarbone.
ant-delt.insertion: Deltoid tuberosity on the outside of the upper arm bone (humerus).
ant-delt.action: Raises the arm forward (flexion), turns it inward and pulls it across the body; drives pressing and front raises.
symptoms: Ache at the front of the shoulder, right over the muscle, that people often assume is the joint.
Pain lifting the arm forward, pressing overhead or pushing a door open.
Tenderness you can press on just below the front of the collarbone tip.
Pain after bench pressing, push-ups or long periods holding the arms forward (steering, typing).
Usually no numbness or tingling.

questions.q: Is the pain at the very front of the shoulder, just below the bony tip of the collarbone?
Does lifting your straight arm forward to shoulder height bring it on?
Did it start after pressing, push-ups or a lot of reaching forward?
Can you press on a tender spot in the front of the shoulder that recreates your ache?
Does it stay around the shoulder rather than travel past the elbow?

tests.name: Resisted forward raise
tests.how: Stand with your arm straight at your side, thumb up. Raise it forward to shoulder height while your other hand pushes down on the wrist.
tests.positive: The front of the shoulder aches or the arm feels weak compared with the other side.

tests.name: Front-delt press test
tests.how: With the arm relaxed, press firmly into the front of the shoulder just below the collarbone tip for 10 seconds.
tests.positive: It reproduces your familiar ache at the front of the shoulder.

causes: Heavy or frequent pressing (bench, push-ups, overhead press) without enough pulling work.
Rounded shoulders and a forward head posture.
Long periods with the arms held forward: driving, typing, carrying.
Sudden overload such as catching a fall or lifting a heavy box to a high shelf.
Weak rear delts and rotator cuff leaving the front delt to do too much.
redFlags: A pop followed by bruising or a bulge in the arm.
Inability to lift the arm at all after a fall or injury.
Shoulder pain with chest pressure, shortness of breath or sweating.
Fever, redness or a hot, swollen shoulder.

calm.name: Front-delt pressure release
calm.how: Lean the front of your shoulder into a ball against a door frame. Find the tender spot and hold gentle pressure while breathing slowly until it eases.

calm.name: Scapular CARs
calm.dose: 2 x 5 slow circles each way, daily
calm.how: Make slow, controlled circles with the shoulder blade, staying in a pain-free range.

calm.name: Shoulder Drop Hold
calm.how: Let the shoulder settle down and back away from the ear and hold, keeping the neck relaxed.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Open the front of the shoulder and chest gently; stop at a stretch, not pain.

restore.name: Thoracic Open Book
restore.how: Rotate through the upper back so the shoulder can sit back without straining the front delt.

restore.name: Face Pull
restore.how: Light band, elbows high, pull toward your face and squeeze the shoulder blades to balance pressing.

strengthen.name: Wall Push Up
strengthen.how: Slow 3-second lowering, shoulder blades gliding around the ribs, no front-shoulder pinch.

strengthen.name: Strict Press
strengthen.how: Light dumbbells, ribs down, press in the slightly-forward 'scapular plane'. Progress only if pain-free next day.

strengthen.name: Rotator Cuff External Rotation
strengthen.how: Build the cuff that keeps the ball centered so the front delt is not overworked.

habits: Balance every set of pressing with at least one set of pulling.
Bring the keyboard and steering hands lower and closer so the arms are not held forward.
Carry bags close to the body or on alternating sides.
Warm up the shoulder with circles before pressing.
ant-delt.expect: Muscle-driven front-shoulder pain usually eases within 1 to 3 weeks of release and load management; full pressing strength returns over 4 to 6 weeks.
ant-delt.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain persists beyond 3 weeks, you cannot raise the arm, or the shoulder catches, clicks painfully or feels unstable.

lat-delt.origin: Outer edge of the acromion (the bony shelf at the top of the shoulder).
lat-delt.insertion: Deltoid tuberosity on the outside of the upper arm bone.
lat-delt.action: Lifts the arm out to the side (abduction) from about 15 to 90 degrees; holds the arm up for overhead or shoulder-height work.
symptoms: Ache over the outside of the shoulder cap and down the side of the upper arm.
Pain lifting the arm out to the side or holding it at shoulder height.
Soreness lying on that shoulder.
Fatigue and ache after carrying bags or working with the arms raised.
Tender spots in the middle of the shoulder cap.

questions.q: Is the pain on the outside of the shoulder cap, not the front or back?
Does lifting your arm out to the side hurt, especially holding it at shoulder height?
Does it ache after carrying heavy bags or working with your arms up?
Is the tender spot on the muscle itself, a few finger-widths below the top of the shoulder?
Does it hurt to lie on that side at night?

tests.name: Resisted side raise
tests.how: Lift your arm out to the side to 45 degrees, palm down, and hold while your other hand presses down at the elbow for 5 seconds.
tests.positive: Ache on the outside of the shoulder cap or obvious weakness compared with the other side.

causes: Repeated lateral raises or overhead work without rest.
Carrying heavy bags with the arm held away from the body.
Sleeping on one side every night.
A weak supraspinatus forcing the lateral delt to start every lift.
Upper back stiffness that limits how the shoulder blade moves.
redFlags: Sudden inability to lift the arm after a fall.
Numbness over the outside of the shoulder with weakness (possible axillary nerve injury).
A hot, red, swollen shoulder or fever.
Pain that wakes you every night regardless of position.

calm.name: Side-delt pressure release
calm.how: Lean the outside of the shoulder into a ball on a wall and hold gentle pressure on the tender spot while breathing slowly.

calm.name: Scapular CARs
calm.how: Slow shoulder-blade circles to restore smooth motion without load.

calm.name: Shoulder Drop Hold
calm.how: Relax the shoulder down away from the ear to unload the deltoid.

restore.name: Rotator Cuff 90 Band Vibration
restore.how: Wake up the cuff so it centers the ball before the deltoid lifts.

restore.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
restore.how: Improve upper-back extension so the shoulder blade can rotate up as you lift.

strengthen.name: Lateral Raise
strengthen.how: Thumbs slightly up, lift to shoulder height only, lower over 3 seconds.

strengthen.name: Abducted External Rotation
strengthen.how: Arm out to the side at 90 degrees, rotate up slowly to build cuff endurance.

strengthen.name: Farmer Carry
strengthen.how: Walk tall with weights at your sides, shoulders level and slightly back.

habits: Switch carrying sides and use a backpack for heavy loads.
Take breaks every 20 minutes when working with the arms raised.
Sleep on your back or the other side with a pillow hugged in front.
lat-delt.expect: Most people feel easier side-lifting within 1 to 2 weeks; endurance for carrying and overhead work builds over 4 to 6 weeks.
lat-delt.seePro: Book an evaluation if lifting the arm stays painful after 3 weeks, there is a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees, or weakness is getting worse.

post-delt.origin: Lower edge of the spine of the shoulder blade.
post-delt.insertion: Deltoid tuberosity on the outside of the upper arm bone.
post-delt.action: Pulls the arm back (extension) and turns it outward; works in rows, pulling and reaching behind you.
symptoms: Ache at the back of the shoulder and the back of the upper arm.
Pain reaching behind you, such as into a back pocket or the back seat.
Soreness after rowing, pulling or throwing.
Tender spots on the back of the shoulder cap.
Sometimes pain lying on the back of that shoulder.

questions.q: Is the pain at the back of the shoulder, behind the shoulder cap?
Does reaching behind you (back pocket, seat belt, back seat) bring it on?
Did it start after rowing, pulling or throwing?
Can you press on a tender spot at the back of the shoulder cap that matches your pain?
Does the pain stay in the shoulder and upper arm without tingling?

tests.name: Resisted backward reach
tests.how: Stand with the arm straight at your side and push it backward against a wall or your other hand for 5 seconds.
tests.positive: Ache at the back of the shoulder or weakness compared with the other side.

causes: High-volume rowing, pulling or throwing.
Sudden backward reach, such as grabbing something from the back seat.
Weak rotator cuff (infraspinatus, teres minor) leaving the rear delt to stabilize.
Rounded upper back keeping the rear delt on constant stretch.
Sleeping with the arm behind you.
mimics: Infraspinatus or teres minor trigger points
redFlags: Shoulder that feels like it slips out the back.
Sudden weakness after a fall onto the outstretched arm.
Numbness over the outside of the shoulder.
Fever or a hot, swollen joint.

calm.name: Rear-delt ball release
calm.how: Lie on your back with a ball under the back of the shoulder cap; let your weight sink in gently and breathe.

calm.name: Scapular CARs
calm.how: Smooth, pain-free shoulder-blade circles.

calm.name: Thread The Needle
calm.how: Rotate gently through the upper back to ease the back of the shoulder.

restore.name: Cross-body stretch
restore.how: Bring the arm across the chest and hold just above the elbow with the other hand. Keep the shoulder blade down.

restore.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
restore.how: Slide the arms with the shoulder blades drawn back and down to balance the back of the shoulder.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: Light band, elbows high, pull apart at face height and pause.

strengthen.name: Rotator Cuff External Rotation
strengthen.how: Elbow tucked, rotate out slowly against a light band.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Pull the elbow toward the hip, shoulder blade back first, lower slowly.

habits: Turn your body instead of reaching straight back for objects.
Keep pulling volume increases to about 10 percent a week.
Sleep with the arm in front of you, not behind.
post-delt.expect: Back-of-shoulder ache from the rear delt usually settles in 1 to 3 weeks; pulling strength returns over 4 to 6 weeks.
post-delt.seePro: Book an evaluation if reaching behind stays painful past 3 weeks or the shoulder feels unstable or clicks painfully.

teres-major.origin: Lower outer corner of the back of the shoulder blade.
teres-major.insertion: Front of the upper arm bone (medial lip of the bicipital groove), next to the lat.
teres-major.action: Pulls the arm down and back and turns it inward; works with the latissimus dorsi in pulling and climbing.
symptoms: Ache at the back of the shoulder and down the back of the upper arm.
Pain reaching up and forward, such as to a high shelf or swimming.
Sometimes ache in the back of the forearm.
Tender thick band of muscle at the back of the armpit.
Stiffness lifting the arm all the way overhead.

questions.q: Is there a tender band of muscle at the back of your armpit, at the bottom corner of the shoulder blade?
Does reaching high overhead or forward pull and hurt at the back of the shoulder?
Does the ache run down the back of the upper arm?
Did it start after pull-ups, rowing, swimming or climbing?
Is it worse at the end of the overhead reach rather than at the start?

tests.name: Overhead reach on the wall
tests.how: Stand with your back flat on a wall and raise the straight arm overhead, trying to touch the wall with your thumb without arching the low back.
tests.positive: You cannot reach the wall and feel pulling or ache at the back of the armpit and shoulder.

causes: Heavy pulling: pull-ups, rows, lat pulldowns, climbing.
Swimming and throwing.
Prolonged work with the arm raised.
Stiff upper back limiting overhead motion.
Weak lower trapezius so the shoulder blade does not rotate up.
redFlags: A pop in the armpit with bruising after a heavy pull.
Swelling or a lump in the armpit.
Numbness or tingling down the inner arm.
Fever or unexplained weight loss.

calm.name: Armpit ball release
calm.how: Lie on your side with a ball under the back of the armpit, at the corner of the shoulder blade. Breathe and let it soften.

calm.name: Dynamic Childs Pose
calm.how: Sit back with arms reaching forward and breathe into the side ribs.

restore.name: Thread The Needle
restore.how: Rotate and reach to lengthen the back of the shoulder.

restore.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
restore.how: Extend the upper back so the arm can go overhead without the teres major pulling.

restore.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
restore.how: Slide the arms up with the shoulder blades rotating smoothly.

strengthen.name: Lat Pulldown
strengthen.how: Full overhead reach at the top, pull elbows to ribs, lower slowly.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Controlled row with a pause at the top.

habits: Add pulling volume gradually.
Stretch the side of the body after swimming or climbing sessions.
Break up long overhead tasks every 15 minutes.
teres-major.expect: Overhead reach usually improves within 2 weeks; full pulling tolerance in 4 to 6 weeks.
teres-major.seePro: Book an evaluation if you cannot raise the arm fully after 3 weeks or there is armpit swelling or nerve symptoms.

pec-major-clav.origin: Front of the inner half of the collarbone.
pec-major-clav.insertion: Front of the upper arm bone (lateral lip of the bicipital groove).
pec-major-clav.action: Raises the arm forward and pulls it across the body; the 'upper chest' in incline pressing.
symptoms: Ache at the front of the shoulder over the front delt, often blamed on the shoulder joint.
Tight upper chest just below the collarbone.
Pain with incline pressing, push-ups or reaching across the body.
Rounded shoulders that feel hard to pull back.
Tender spots just under the collarbone toward the shoulder.

questions.q: Is the pain at the front of the shoulder, but you can find tender spots in the upper chest just under the collarbone?
Does incline pressing or pushing up and forward bring it on?
Does pulling your shoulders back feel tight across the upper chest?
Do you spend hours with rounded shoulders at a desk or phone?
Does the pain stay above the chest without going to the fingers?

tests.name: Doorway upper-chest test
tests.how: Stand in a doorway with the forearm on the frame and the elbow above shoulder height, then step through gently.
tests.positive: Tight pulling or your familiar front-shoulder ache in the upper chest.

causes: Lots of pressing with little pulling.
Rounded shoulders from desk and phone posture.
Sleeping on the side with the arm across the chest.
Carrying in front of the body for long periods.
Shallow chest breathing that keeps the chest muscles working.
redFlags: Chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea or pain into the jaw or left arm: call 911.
A visible gap or bruising in the front of the armpit after a heavy press (possible tear).
Swelling or a lump in the chest or armpit.

calm.name: Upper-chest ball release
calm.how: Place a ball just below the collarbone toward the shoulder against a wall; hold gentle pressure and breathe.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Breathe low into the belly and ribs so the chest muscles can relax.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Arm above shoulder height to target the upper fibers; stretch, not pain.

restore.name: Thoracic Open Book
restore.how: Rotate open through the upper back while the chest lengthens.

restore.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
restore.how: Draw the shoulder blades back and down as the arms slide.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: Strengthen the back of the shoulder to balance the chest.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Push Up
strengthen.how: Lower over 3–4 seconds with the shoulder blades gliding; no front-shoulder pinch.

habits: Set screens at eye level and shoulders back.
Do two sets of pulling for every set of pressing.
Hug a pillow when side-sleeping so the arm does not fall across the chest.
pec-major-clav.expect: Front-shoulder ache from the upper pec usually improves in 1 to 3 weeks with stretching and posture changes.
pec-major-clav.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain persists past 3 weeks or pressing remains painful. Any chest pain with other symptoms needs urgent medical care first.

pec-major-stern.origin: Front of the breastbone and the cartilages of the upper six ribs.
pec-major-stern.insertion: Front of the upper arm bone (lateral lip of the bicipital groove).
pec-major-stern.action: Pulls the arm down and across the chest and turns it inward; the main chest in pressing, hugging and pushing.
symptoms: Ache across the front of the chest that can feel alarming.
Pain running down the inner arm to the inner elbow and sometimes the ring and little fingers.
Chest tightness that changes when you move the arm or press on the muscle.
Pain with bench pressing, push-ups or hugging motions.
Rounded shoulders and shallow breathing.

questions.q: Does pressing on the chest muscle reproduce the chest pain?
Does the pain change when you move your arm or press, rather than with walking or effort?
Does pain travel down the inner arm toward the ring and little fingers?
Did it start after bench pressing, push-ups or heavy carrying in front of you?
Do you sit with rounded shoulders for long periods?

tests.name: Low doorway stretch
tests.how: Place the forearm on a door frame with the elbow below shoulder height and step gently through.
tests.positive: Pulling or your familiar ache across the chest and inner arm.

causes: Heavy or high-volume pressing.
Rounded posture and long desk hours.
Shallow chest breathing and stress.
Carrying children, groceries or boxes in front of the chest.
Sleeping curled with the arms crossed.
mimics: Heart pain (angina): must be ruled out first
redFlags: Chest pain with exertion, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or pain into the jaw or left arm: call 911.
Chest pain that does not change with arm movement or pressure.
Sudden pop and bruising in the chest or armpit after a heavy press.

calm.name: Chest ball release
calm.how: Place a ball on the chest muscle below the collarbone against a wall or doorway; hold gentle pressure and breathe slowly.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Slow belly and rib breathing to switch off over-active chest muscles.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Arm at or just below shoulder height to target the sternal fibers.

restore.name: Lying Open Book
restore.how: Open the chest by rotating the upper back.

restore.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
restore.how: Extend the upper back so the chest is not held shortened.

strengthen.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
strengthen.how: Build the shoulder blade muscles that hold the chest open.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Push Up
strengthen.how: Slow lowering to rebuild pressing tolerance.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Balance chest work with rowing.

habits: Pause every 30 minutes at the desk to roll the shoulders back and breathe.
Keep pressing and pulling in balance.
Carry loads close to the body and switch arms.
pec-major-stern.expect: Muscle-driven chest pain usually eases within 1 to 2 weeks once the muscle is released and posture improves.
pec-major-stern.seePro: Any chest pain should be checked by a doctor first. Book with Dr. Jared once heart causes are ruled out, or if arm and hand symptoms persist.

subclavius.insertion: Underside of the middle third of the collarbone.
subclavius.action: Pulls the collarbone down and forward and steadies it against the breastbone during arm movement.
symptoms: Ache just under the collarbone.
Pain running down the front of the arm and forearm into the thumb, index and middle fingers.
Arm heaviness or tingling when carrying bags on that shoulder.
Symptoms worse with the arm overhead or shoulders pulled down.
Tenderness pressing up under the collarbone.

questions.q: Is there a tender spot just under the middle of your collarbone?
Does pain or tingling run down the front of the arm into the thumb and first two fingers?
Do heavy shoulder bags or backpack straps make it worse?
Does raising the arm overhead for a while bring on arm heaviness?
Do you breathe mostly into your upper chest?

tests.name: Shoulder brace test
tests.how: Pull the shoulders back and down firmly, as if standing at attention, and hold for 30 seconds.
tests.positive: Pain under the collarbone or tingling down the arm that eases when you relax.

causes: Heavy shoulder bags and backpack straps.
Old collarbone fracture or shoulder injury.
Upper-chest breathing.
Rounded shoulders with the collarbone held down.
Repeated overhead work.
redFlags: Arm swelling, blue or pale color, or a cold hand (possible blood vessel compression).
Progressive hand weakness or muscle wasting.
Chest pain with shortness of breath: call 911.

calm.name: Under-collarbone release
calm.how: Use two fingers to apply gentle pressure just under the middle of the collarbone, moving slightly outward while breathing slowly. Never press hard into the hollow.

calm.name: 90/90 Breathing
calm.how: Breathe low so the first rib and collarbone can relax.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Open the front of the shoulder gently; stop if tingling increases.

restore.name: Thoracic Open Book
restore.how: Rotate open to free the front of the chest.

restore.name: Standing Scalene Stretch
restore.how: Ease the neck muscles that share the space with the subclavius.

strengthen.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
strengthen.how: Hold the shoulder blades back without forcing them down.

strengthen.name: Scap Push Ups
strengthen.how: Build the serratus to support the shoulder girdle.

habits: Use a backpack with both straps or a cross-body bag on alternating sides.
Avoid holding the shoulders forced down and back for long periods.
Practice low belly breathing during the day.
subclavius.expect: Collarbone and arm symptoms often ease in 1 to 3 weeks once loading from bags and posture is reduced.
subclavius.seePro: Book an evaluation if tingling persists more than 2 weeks, or sooner if the hand becomes weak, swollen or discolored.

coracobrachialis.origin: Coracoid process (the bony hook at the front of the shoulder blade).
coracobrachialis.insertion: Inner side of the middle of the upper arm bone.
coracobrachialis.action: Pulls the arm forward and toward the body; helps hold the ball of the shoulder in place.
coracobrachialis.nerve: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7), which passes through the muscle.
symptoms: Deep ache at the front of the shoulder.
Pain on the back of the upper arm and forearm, sometimes to the back of the hand and middle finger.
Pain reaching behind your back or lifting the arm overhead.
Tenderness high on the inner upper arm near the armpit.

questions.q: Is there a tender spot high on the inner upper arm, just below the front of the armpit?
Does pain jump from the front of the shoulder to the back of the arm or hand?
Does reaching behind your back (tucking in a shirt) bring it on?
Did it start after push-ups, dips or bench pressing?
Does the outside of your forearm ever feel numb?

tests.name: Hand-behind-back reach
tests.how: Reach the hand behind your back and slide it up the spine; compare with the other side.
tests.positive: Front-of-shoulder ache and a lower reach than the other side.

causes: Push-ups, dips and pressing with the elbows flared.
Carrying heavy items in front of the body.
Rock climbing and gymnastics.
Prolonged reaching forward and across the body.
redFlags: Numbness over the outside of the forearm with weak elbow bending.
A lump or swelling in the armpit.
Chest pain with shortness of breath: call 911.

calm.name: Inner-arm pressure release
calm.how: Press gently with the thumb high on the inner upper arm just below the armpit, holding until it eases. Stop if you feel tingling.

calm.name: Shoulder Drop Hold
calm.how: Let the shoulder settle down and back.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Arm out and slightly behind the body to lengthen the front of the shoulder.

restore.name: Rotator Cuff Internal Rotation
restore.how: Gentle cuff work to share the load of centering the shoulder.

strengthen.name: Wall Push Up
strengthen.how: Elbows at 45 degrees, not flared.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: Balance pushing with pulling.

habits: Keep elbows tucked to about 45 degrees on push-ups and presses.
Carry loads close to the body.
coracobrachialis.expect: Usually settles within 2 to 3 weeks with reduced pressing and gentle stretching.
coracobrachialis.seePro: Book an evaluation if forearm numbness or elbow weakness appears, or pain persists past 3 weeks.

biceps-long.origin: Top of the shoulder socket (supraglenoid tubercle), running through the groove at the front of the upper arm.
biceps-long.insertion: Radial tuberosity of the forearm, below the elbow.
biceps-long.action: Bends the elbow, turns the palm up and helps hold the ball of the shoulder down in the socket.
symptoms: Ache at the front of the shoulder over the biceps groove.
Pain down the front of the arm toward the elbow crease.
Pain lifting with the palm up, or reaching overhead.
A tender cord you can roll under your fingers at the front of the shoulder.

questions.q: Is there a tender spot in the groove at the front of the shoulder that moves when you rotate the arm?
Does lifting or carrying with the palm up hurt at the front of the shoulder?
Does the pain run down the front of the upper arm?
Does reaching overhead or throwing bring it on?
Do you hear a click or snap at the front of the shoulder?

tests.name: Speed's style palm-up raise
tests.how: Hold the arm straight in front, palm up, and raise it against your other hand's resistance.
tests.positive: Pain at the front of the shoulder over the biceps groove.

causes: Repeated overhead work and throwing.
Heavy curls and carrying with the palms up.
Rotator cuff weakness so the biceps works as a stabilizer.
Rounded shoulders that pinch the tendon.
redFlags: A pop followed by a 'Popeye' bulge in the upper arm (tendon rupture).
Shoulder that catches, locks or feels unstable.
Bruising down the arm after lifting.

calm.name: Biceps groove release
calm.how: Use gentle fingertip pressure on the biceps muscle belly (not on the tendon itself) and slowly bend and straighten the elbow.

calm.name: Shoulder Drop Hold
calm.how: Settle the shoulder down and back to unload the tendon.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Arm straight, thumb pointing down and slightly behind you to lengthen the long head.

restore.name: Rotator Cuff External Rotation
restore.how: Strengthen the cuff so the biceps does not have to stabilize.

strengthen.name: Bicep Curl
strengthen.how: Lower over 3–4 seconds; keep the elbow at your side.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Wrist Pronator
strengthen.how: Control turning the palm down to load the biceps gently.

habits: Carry with palms facing your body rather than up.
Limit long overhead work.
Keep shoulders back when working at a desk.
biceps-long.expect: Tendon-region pain usually eases over 2 to 4 weeks; full overhead and lifting tolerance in 6 to 8 weeks.
biceps-long.seePro: Book an evaluation if there is clicking or catching, a bulge in the arm, or no improvement in 3 weeks.

biceps-short.origin: Tip of the coracoid process at the front of the shoulder blade.
biceps-short.insertion: Radial tuberosity below the elbow (shared tendon with the long head).
biceps-short.action: Bends the elbow, turns the palm up and pulls the arm forward and across the body.
symptoms: Ache at the front of the shoulder, closer to the chest than the groove.
Pain on the inner front of the upper arm.
Pain at the elbow crease when lifting or curling.
Tenderness on the inner half of the biceps belly.

questions.q: Is the tender spot on the inner half of the biceps, toward the body?
Does curling or carrying with the palm up hurt at the elbow crease?
Is the shoulder ache nearer the chest than the outside of the shoulder?
Did it start after curls, pull-ups or heavy carrying?
Does reaching across your body bring it on?

tests.name: Resisted curl and turn
tests.how: With the elbow bent at 90 degrees and the palm down, turn the palm up against resistance from your other hand.
tests.positive: Ache in the inner biceps or elbow crease.

causes: Heavy curls and chin-ups.
Carrying boxes with the palms up.
Climbing and gymnastics.
Sudden lifting with the elbow straight.
redFlags: A pop at the elbow with bruising and a lump moving up the arm (tendon rupture).
Inability to turn the palm up with strength.
Numbness in the forearm.

calm.name: Inner biceps release
calm.how: Gently squeeze the inner half of the biceps between thumb and fingers while slowly straightening the elbow.

calm.name: Eccentric Wrist Pronator
calm.how: Gentle, pain-free control to keep the area moving.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Arm out to the side and slightly back, palm facing back.

strengthen.name: Bicep Curl
strengthen.how: Slow 4-second lowering; increase weight only if pain-free next day.

strengthen.name: Row
strengthen.how: Smooth pulling to rebuild arm and back strength together.

habits: Lift boxes with the elbows bent and close to the body.
Build curl and chin-up volume gradually.
biceps-short.expect: Most cases ease in 2 to 3 weeks; strength returns over 4 to 6 weeks.
biceps-short.seePro: Book an evaluation urgently after a pop at the elbow; otherwise if pain persists beyond 3 weeks.

triceps-long.origin: Just below the shoulder socket (infraglenoid tubercle of the shoulder blade).
triceps-long.action: Straightens the elbow and pulls the arm back and down; the only triceps head that crosses the shoulder.
symptoms: Ache at the back of the shoulder and the back of the upper arm.
Pain sometimes spreading up toward the top of the shoulder and base of the neck.
Ache down the back of the forearm.
Pain straightening the arm overhead, such as reaching up or pressing overhead.

questions.q: Does the pain run along the back of the upper arm from the armpit toward the elbow?
Does reaching overhead with the elbow bent (like scratching your upper back) hurt?
Does straightening your arm against resistance bring it on?
Did it start after push-ups, dips, overhead pressing or tennis?
Does it also ache toward the top of your shoulder or neck?

tests.name: Overhead elbow bend
tests.how: Raise the arm overhead and bend the elbow so the hand drops behind your head. Gently push the elbow back with the other hand.
tests.positive: Pulling or your familiar ache along the back of the upper arm and shoulder.

causes: Dips, push-ups, skull-crushers and overhead pressing.
Repetitive hammering or racquet sports.
Using crutches or a walker.
Long periods leaning on the elbows.
mimics: Teres major or minor trigger points
redFlags: A pop at the back of the elbow with weakness straightening the arm.
Numbness on the back of the hand with wrist drop (radial nerve).
Swelling at the point of the elbow with redness or fever.

calm.name: Triceps squeeze release
calm.how: Grip the back of the upper arm near the armpit with the other hand and hold gentle pressure on tender spots while slowly bending and straightening the elbow.

calm.name: Thread The Needle
calm.how: Rotate gently to ease the back of the shoulder.

restore.name: Overhead triceps stretch
restore.how: Arm overhead, elbow bent, use the other hand to ease the elbow back. Keep the ribs down.

restore.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
restore.how: Improve upper-back extension so overhead reaching is easier.

strengthen.name: Tricep Extension
strengthen.how: Slow lowering, elbows steady.

strengthen.name: Overhead Tricep Extension
strengthen.how: Add only once the simpler extension is pain-free; this loads the long head at its longest.

habits: Avoid leaning on the elbows for long periods.
Build dips and pressing volume gradually.
triceps-long.expect: Usually improves within 2 to 3 weeks; overhead pressing tolerance over 4 to 6 weeks.
triceps-long.seePro: Book an evaluation if hand numbness, wrist weakness or elbow swelling appear, or pain persists past 3 weeks.

triceps-lateral.origin: Back of the upper arm bone, above the radial groove.
triceps-lateral.action: Straightens the elbow with force; the outer 'horseshoe' on the back of the arm.
symptoms: Ache in the back of the upper arm on the outer side.
Pain at the outside of the elbow that can be mistaken for tennis elbow.
Ache down the back of the forearm.
Pain pushing up from a chair or doing push-ups.

questions.q: Is the tender spot on the outer back of the upper arm, a hand-width above the elbow?
Do you have outer-elbow pain but gripping is not the main trigger?
Does pushing up from a chair or a push-up bring it on?
Do hammering or racquet sports aggravate it?
Does it ache down the back of the forearm?

tests.name: Resisted elbow straightening
tests.how: Bend the elbow to 90 degrees and push the hand down against your other hand, trying to straighten the arm.
tests.positive: Ache in the outer back of the arm or the outside of the elbow.

causes: Push-ups, dips and bench pressing.
Hammering and tool work.
Tennis backhand.
Pushing up from chairs with weak legs.
redFlags: Wrist drop or numbness on the back of the hand.
Elbow swelling with redness or fever.
A pop with weakness straightening the arm.

calm.name: Outer triceps release
calm.how: Press gently on the outer back of the upper arm and slowly straighten the elbow.

calm.name: Weighted Wrist Circles
calm.dose: 2 x 10 each way, no weight to start, daily
calm.how: Keep the forearm moving comfortably.

restore.name: Overhead triceps stretch
restore.how: Arm overhead, elbow bent, ease the elbow back gently.

strengthen.name: Tricep Kickback
strengthen.how: Upper arm still, straighten with control, lower slowly.

strengthen.name: Tricep Extension
strengthen.how: Smooth, pain-free reps.

habits: Use the legs, not the arms, to stand up from chairs.
Warm up the elbow before tennis or tool work.
triceps-lateral.expect: Usually eases in 2 to 3 weeks with load management and release.
triceps-lateral.seePro: Book an evaluation if outer-elbow pain persists past 3 weeks or there is any hand weakness or numbness.

triceps-medial.origin: Back of the upper arm bone, below the radial groove (deep to the other two heads).
triceps-medial.insertion: Olecranon and the back of the elbow joint capsule.
triceps-medial.action: Straightens the elbow in every push and keeps the joint capsule from pinching.
triceps-medial.nerve: Radial nerve (C6–C8), with a branch shared near the ulnar nerve.
symptoms: Pain at the point of the elbow.
Ache at the inner elbow that can mimic golfer's elbow.
Sometimes ache into the ring and little fingers.
Pain at the end of straightening the elbow or leaning on it.

questions.q: Is the pain right at the point of the elbow or just above it?
Does fully straightening the elbow against resistance hurt?
Does leaning on the elbow aggravate it?
Do you also feel ache on the inner elbow?
Does it sometimes ache toward the ring and little fingers?

tests.name: End-range extension
tests.how: Straighten the elbow fully and press the hand down against a table for 5 seconds.
tests.positive: Ache at or just above the point of the elbow.

causes: Lockout in presses and push-ups.
Leaning on elbows at a desk.
Throwing and racquet sports.
Using crutches.
redFlags: A swollen, red, hot bump at the point of the elbow (infected bursa).
Numbness and weakness in the ring and little fingers.
Inability to straighten the elbow after a fall.

calm.name: Above-elbow pressure release
calm.how: Press gently on both sides just above the point of the elbow and slowly bend and straighten.

calm.name: Eccentric Wrist Pronator
calm.how: Keep the forearm moving without load on the elbow.

restore.name: Gentle elbow bends
restore.how: Slowly bend and straighten the elbow through a comfortable range, no weight.

strengthen.name: Tricep Extension
strengthen.how: Stop just short of hard lockout for the first two weeks.

strengthen.name: Wall Push Up
strengthen.how: Smooth pushing without slamming into lockout.

habits: Pad or avoid leaning on the elbows.
Avoid snapping into lockout during presses.
triceps-medial.seePro: Book an evaluation if there is swelling at the elbow tip, finger numbness or no improvement in 3 weeks.

middle-trap.origin: Spinous processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae (about T1 to T5).
middle-trap.insertion: Inner edge of the acromion and the spine of the shoulder blade.
middle-trap.action: Pulls the shoulder blades together and holds them back against the ribs.
middle-trap.nerve: Spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) with sensory fibers from C3, C4.
symptoms: Burning or aching between the shoulder blade and the spine.
Ache over the top of the shoulder blade.
Worse after long desk sessions with rounded shoulders.
Feels like the area 'needs cracking'.

questions.q: Is the pain a burning ache between the spine and the inner edge of the shoulder blade?
Does it build up the longer you sit at a desk or on your phone?
Does squeezing the shoulder blades together feel weak or bring it on?
Do your shoulders round forward when you are tired?
Does it feel better when you move rather than rest?

tests.name: Prone T hold
tests.how: Lie face down with arms out to the sides, thumbs up, and lift the arms a few inches for 15 seconds.
tests.positive: Burning or your familiar ache between the shoulder blades, or the arms feel weak and shaky.

causes: Rounded shoulders with tight chest muscles stretching the middle trap.
Long desk and phone sessions.
Carrying a heavy backpack.
Weakness from little pulling exercise.
redFlags: Pain between the shoulder blades with chest pain or shortness of breath: call 911.
Sudden tearing upper-back pain.
Pain with fever or unexplained weight loss.

calm.name: Wall ball release
calm.how: Place a ball between the spine and the shoulder blade against a wall and roll slowly, pausing on tender spots.

calm.name: Thoracic Rotation Seated
calm.how: Rotate gently through the upper back.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Open the chest so the middle trap is not constantly stretched.

restore.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
restore.how: Extend over the chair back to undo rounding.

strengthen.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
strengthen.how: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and slightly down as the arms slide.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: Pull apart at face height with a pause.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Start each rep by drawing the shoulder blade back.

habits: Raise screens to eye level.
Set a reminder every 30 minutes to reset posture.
Use both backpack straps.
middle-trap.expect: Burning between the shoulder blades often eases in 1 to 2 weeks; endurance builds over 4 to 6 weeks.
middle-trap.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain persists past 3 weeks, wakes you at night, or comes with chest symptoms (seek urgent care first).

lower-trap.origin: Spinous processes of the middle and lower thoracic vertebrae (about T6 to T12).
lower-trap.insertion: Inner end of the spine of the shoulder blade.
lower-trap.action: Pulls the shoulder blade down and rotates it upward so the arm can reach overhead.
lower-trap.nerve: Spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) with sensory fibers from C3, C4.
symptoms: Ache up the back of the neck toward the base of the skull and behind the ear.
Ache across the top of the shoulder.
Ache along the inner edge of the shoulder blade.
Neck tension that keeps coming back even after neck stretches.

questions.q: Do you get neck or base-of-skull tension that never fully goes away with neck stretches?
Is there a tender spot low on the inner edge of the shoulder blade?
Do your shoulders creep up toward your ears when you reach overhead?
Do you sit slumped for long periods?
Does reaching overhead feel weak or tiring?

tests.name: Prone Y lift
tests.how: Lie face down with arms overhead in a Y, thumbs up, and lift the arms a few inches for 10 seconds.
tests.positive: The arms feel weak and shaky, or you feel your familiar neck or shoulder-blade ache.

causes: Slumped sitting that stretches and weakens the lower trap.
Shoulders shrugging during overhead work.
Tight chest and lats pulling the shoulder blade forward.
Little or no pulling exercise.
mimics: Upper trapezius or levator trigger points
redFlags: Neck pain with arm weakness, numbness or loss of coordination.
Sudden severe headache.
Pain with fever or unexplained weight loss.

calm.name: Lower shoulder-blade ball release
calm.how: Place a ball against a wall low on the inner edge of the shoulder blade and hold gentle pressure on tender spots.

calm.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
calm.how: Extend the upper back gently to undo slumping.

restore.name: Scapular CARs
restore.how: Emphasize the down-and-back part of each circle.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Free the chest so the shoulder blade can sit back.

strengthen.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
strengthen.how: Slide the arms up while keeping the shoulders away from the ears.

strengthen.name: Face Pull
strengthen.how: Finish each rep with the shoulder blades down and back.

habits: Sit back in the chair with support at mid-back.
Think 'shoulders in back pockets' during overhead tasks.
lower-trap.expect: Neck tension often eases within 2 weeks; lower-trap strength takes 4 to 6 weeks to build.
