lower-trap.seePro: Book an evaluation if neck or shoulder pain persists past 3 weeks or there are arm symptoms.

rhomboid-minor.origin: Spinous processes of C7 and T1.
rhomboid-minor.insertion: Inner edge of the shoulder blade at the level of its spine.
rhomboid-minor.action: Pulls the upper part of the shoulder blade toward the spine and slightly up.
symptoms: Ache along the inner edge of the upper shoulder blade, next to the spine.
A 'knot' high between the shoulder blades near the base of the neck.
Ache with long desk work or carrying a bag on one shoulder.
Feels better briefly after cracking or stretching.

questions.q: Is the pain high, at the level of the base of the neck, right beside the spine?
Is there a knot along the inner edge of the top of the shoulder blade?
Do you carry a bag on one shoulder or sit for hours?
Does pulling the shoulder blades together reproduce it?
Does it ease when you move around?

tests.name: Upper squeeze test
tests.how: Pull the shoulder blades together and slightly up and hold for 10 seconds.
tests.positive: Ache high between the shoulder blades near the spine.

causes: Rounded shoulders stretching the rhomboids all day.
Carrying bags on one shoulder.
Long periods reaching forward (keyboard, steering).
Scalene or neck tension referring into the area.
redFlags: Upper-back pain with chest pain or shortness of breath: call 911.
Arm weakness or numbness.
Night pain that does not change with position.

calm.name: Upper rhomboid ball release
calm.how: Ball against a wall, high between the spine and shoulder blade; hold gently on tender spots.

calm.name: Thread The Needle
calm.how: Rotate to ease the upper back.

restore.name: Thoracic Rotation Seated
restore.how: Smooth rotation through the upper back.

restore.name: Standing Scalene Stretch
restore.how: Scalenes often refer here; ease them too.

strengthen.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
strengthen.how: Draw the shoulder blades back without shrugging.

strengthen.name: Row
strengthen.how: Start the pull with the shoulder blades.

habits: Switch bag sides or use a backpack.
Keep the keyboard close so you are not reaching forward.
rhomboid-minor.seePro: Book an evaluation if the knot keeps returning after 3 weeks or there are arm symptoms.

rhomboid-major.origin: Spinous processes of T2 to T5.
rhomboid-major.insertion: Inner edge of the shoulder blade below its spine, down to the bottom corner.
rhomboid-major.action: Pulls the shoulder blade toward the spine and down; steadies it when you pull.
symptoms: Ache between the shoulder blade and the spine, lower down.
A superficial nagging ache that is hard to reach.
Worse after desk work, driving or rowing.
Often appears alongside tight chest muscles.

questions.q: Is the ache between the spine and the lower half of the shoulder blade?
Is it a nagging, superficial ache rather than sharp?
Are your chest muscles tight and shoulders rounded?
Does it build up with desk work or driving?
Does pressing on the area reproduce it?

tests.name: Shoulder blade squeeze
tests.how: Squeeze the shoulder blades together and down and hold for 10 seconds.
tests.positive: Ache between the lower shoulder blade and the spine.

causes: Tight chest muscles pulling the shoulder blades apart.
Long sitting with the arms forward.
Heavy rowing without good form.
Weak middle and lower traps.
mimics: Gallbladder pain on the right side (rare)
redFlags: Pain with chest symptoms or shortness of breath: call 911.
Right-sided pain after fatty meals with nausea.
Pain with fever or weight loss.

calm.name: Rhomboid ball release
calm.how: Lie on a ball placed between the spine and the lower shoulder blade, arms crossed to spread the blades.

calm.name: Thread The Needle
calm.how: Rotate to ease the area.

restore.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
restore.how: Release the chest that pulls the shoulder blades apart.

restore.name: Thoracic Extension Over Chair
restore.how: Open up the upper back.

strengthen.name: Floor Slide Scapular Retract
strengthen.how: Squeeze back and down with control.

strengthen.name: Dumbbell Row
strengthen.how: Pause at the top with the shoulder blade drawn in.

habits: Stretch the chest daily, not just the upper back.
Take posture breaks every 30 minutes.
rhomboid-major.expect: Usually eases within 1 to 3 weeks once the chest is released and the back strengthened.
rhomboid-major.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain persists past 3 weeks or keeps returning.

wrist-ext.origin: Lateral epicondyle and the ridge above it (outside of the elbow).
wrist-ext.insertion: Bases of the second and third metacarpals on the back of the hand.
wrist-ext.action: Lifts the wrist back and steadies it whenever you grip.
wrist-ext.nerve: Radial nerve and its deep branch (C6, C7).
symptoms: Pain at the outside of the elbow (tennis elbow).
Ache down the back of the forearm to the back of the hand near the thumb side.
Pain gripping, shaking hands, lifting a cup or turning a key.
Weaker grip.

questions.q: Does gripping or lifting a cup with the palm down hurt at the outside of the elbow?
Is there a tender spot just below the bony bump on the outside of the elbow?
Does lifting your wrist back against resistance hurt?
Do you type, use a mouse or use tools a lot?
Does it ache down the back of the forearm toward the thumb side of the hand?

tests.name: Resisted wrist extension
tests.how: With the elbow straight and palm down, lift the hand back against resistance from your other hand.
tests.positive: Pain at the outside of the elbow.

causes: Repetitive gripping, mouse use and typing with the wrist bent back.
Racquet sports and tool use.
Sudden increase in lifting or yard work.
Neck and shoulder tension adding load.
mimics: Triceps lateral head or supinator trigger points
redFlags: Elbow swelling with redness or fever.
Wrist drop or weak finger straightening.
Pain after a fall with inability to straighten the elbow.

calm.name: Forearm extensor release
calm.how: Press with the thumb or a ball on the tender spots of the upper outer forearm while slowly bending the wrist up and down.

calm.name: Weighted Wrist Circles
calm.dose: 2 x 10 each way, no weight to start, daily
calm.how: Gentle circles to keep the wrist moving.

restore.name: Wrist extensor stretch
restore.how: Elbow straight, palm down, gently bend the wrist down with the other hand.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Wrist Drops
strengthen.how: Lift with the other hand, lower slowly over 3–4 seconds. Mild discomfort is acceptable; sharp pain is not.

strengthen.name: Farmer Carry
strengthen.how: Light grip endurance once lowering is comfortable.

habits: Keep the wrist straight on the keyboard and mouse.
Lift with the palm up when you can.
Use a thicker grip on tools and racquets.
wrist-ext.expect: Tendon-driven elbow pain takes 6 to 12 weeks of consistent loading; muscle tenderness eases sooner.
wrist-ext.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain persists past 4 weeks, wakes you at night, or there is any weakness or numbness.

finger-ext.origin: Lateral epicondyle (outside of the elbow) by the common extensor tendon.
finger-ext.insertion: Backs of the fingers (extensor hood of fingers 2 to 5).
finger-ext.action: Straightens the fingers and helps lift the wrist.
finger-ext.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the radial nerve (C7, C8).
symptoms: Ache in the back of the forearm.
Pain on the back of the hand into the middle or ring finger.
Stiff, achy fingers after typing or gaming.
Outer-elbow ache with finger use more than wrist use.

questions.q: Does straightening your middle finger against resistance cause outer-elbow or forearm pain?
Does pain run down the back of the hand toward the middle or ring finger?
Do typing, gaming or playing an instrument bring it on?
Do your fingers feel stiff after heavy use?
Is the tender spot in the upper back of the forearm, not right on the elbow bump?

tests.name: Resisted middle-finger extension
tests.how: With the elbow straight and palm down, press down on the middle finger while trying to straighten it.
tests.positive: Pain in the back of the forearm or outside of the elbow.

causes: Long typing, mouse, phone or gaming sessions.
Playing piano or guitar.
Gripping and releasing tools repeatedly.
Wrist bent back while typing.
mimics: Radial tunnel / posterior interosseous nerve irritation
redFlags: Inability to straighten the fingers (finger drop).
Swollen, hot finger joints.
Numbness on the back of the hand.

calm.name: Back-of-forearm release
calm.how: Roll a ball along the upper back of the forearm while opening and closing the fingers slowly.

calm.name: Weighted Wrist Circles
calm.dose: 2 x 10 each way, no weight, daily
calm.how: Keep the forearm and fingers moving.

restore.name: Finger and wrist flexion stretch
restore.how: Make a gentle fist, then bend the wrist down with the elbow straight until a mild stretch.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Wrist Drops
strengthen.how: Slow lowering to build tendon tolerance.

strengthen.name: Rubber band finger opening
strengthen.how: Place a rubber band around the fingertips and open the fingers against it slowly.

habits: Take a 1-minute break every 30 minutes of typing or gaming.
Keep wrists neutral on the keyboard.
finger-ext.expect: Usually improves in 2 to 6 weeks with load changes.
finger-ext.seePro: Book an evaluation if fingers become weak or numb, or pain persists past 4 weeks.

wrist-flex.origin: Medial epicondyle (inside of the elbow) by the common flexor tendon.
wrist-flex.insertion: Bases of the second metacarpal (FCR) and the pisiform and fifth metacarpal (FCU).
wrist-flex.action: Bends the wrist forward and steadies it in pulling, lifting and throwing.
wrist-flex.nerve: Median nerve (FCR, C6, C7) and ulnar nerve (FCU, C7–T1).
symptoms: Pain at the inside of the elbow (golfer's elbow).
Ache on the palm side of the forearm and wrist.
Pain gripping, lifting or throwing.
Weaker grip.

questions.q: Is the pain at or just below the bony bump on the inside of the elbow?
Does bending the wrist forward against resistance hurt?
Does gripping, golf, throwing or lifting with the palm up bring it on?
Does it ache down the palm side of the forearm?
Do you ever get tingling in the ring and little fingers?

tests.name: Resisted wrist flexion
tests.how: With the elbow straight and palm up, bend the wrist forward against resistance from your other hand.
tests.positive: Pain at the inside of the elbow.

causes: Golf, throwing and racquet sports.
Heavy gripping and lifting with the palms up.
Climbing and pull-ups.
Sudden increase in manual work.
redFlags: Numbness and weakness in the ring and little fingers.
Elbow instability after a throwing injury.
Swelling with redness or fever.

calm.name: Forearm flexor release
calm.how: Roll a ball along the upper palm-side forearm while slowly bending the wrist.

calm.name: Weighted Wrist Circles
calm.dose: 2 x 10 each way, no weight, daily
calm.how: Gentle motion.

restore.name: Wrist flexor stretch
restore.how: Elbow straight, palm up, gently pull the fingers and wrist back.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Wrist Pronator
strengthen.how: Slow, controlled rotation to load the inner-elbow tendons.

strengthen.name: Eccentric wrist curl
strengthen.how: Palm up on a table, lift a light weight with both hands and lower slowly with one.

habits: Check golf and throwing technique.
Use gloves or thicker grips for heavy holding.
wrist-flex.expect: Tendon-related inner-elbow pain usually needs 6 to 12 weeks of consistent loading.
wrist-flex.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain persists past 4 weeks or finger numbness appears.

finger-flex.origin: Medial epicondyle, upper forearm bones and the membrane between them.
finger-flex.insertion: Middle and end segments of the fingers and thumb (palm side).
finger-flex.action: Closes the fingers and thumb into a grip.
finger-flex.nerve: Median nerve and, for the ring and little fingers, the ulnar nerve (C7–T1).
symptoms: Ache in the palm and the front of the fingers.
A catching or locking finger when you open the hand.
Forearm fatigue and ache after gripping.
Stiff fingers in the morning.

questions.q: Do you feel ache in the palm or along the front of the fingers when gripping?
Does a finger catch or click when you open your hand?
Does long gripping (tools, phone, steering wheel, climbing) bring it on?
Is the forearm on the palm side tender when you squeeze it?
Are the fingers stiff first thing in the morning?

tests.name: Grip and release
tests.how: Make a tight fist for 10 seconds, then open the hand fully and spread the fingers.
tests.positive: Ache in the palm or forearm, or a finger that catches as it opens.

causes: Long gripping: tools, phone, steering, climbing.
Heavy carrying with a narrow handle.
Repetitive pinching and clicking.
Diabetes and inflammatory conditions (increase trigger-finger risk).
redFlags: A finger locked closed that will not open.
Red, hot, swollen finger (possible infection).
Numbness in the thumb and first fingers that wakes you at night.

calm.name: Palm and forearm release
calm.how: Roll a ball in the palm and along the palm-side forearm while opening and closing the hand.

calm.name: Tendon glides
calm.how: Move slowly through straight hand, hook fist, full fist, tabletop and straight fist.

restore.name: Finger flexor stretch
restore.how: Elbow straight, palm up, gently pull the fingers back.

restore.name: Weighted Wrist Circles
restore.how: Light, smooth wrist motion.

strengthen.name: Eccentric Wrist Pronator
strengthen.how: Build forearm control.

strengthen.name: Farmer Carry
strengthen.how: Thick handles if available; stop before grip fails.

habits: Use thicker grips and gloves.
Switch hands and take breaks during long gripping.
Open and spread the hands every 30 minutes.
finger-flex.expect: Muscle ache eases within 2 weeks; catching fingers may take 4 to 8 weeks.
finger-flex.seePro: Book an evaluation if a finger locks, numbness appears, or symptoms persist past 4 weeks.

iliocostalis.origin: Back of the pelvis (iliac crest), sacrum and the back of the ribs.
iliocostalis.insertion: Angles of the ribs and the transverse processes of the lower neck vertebrae.
iliocostalis.action: Extends the spine and bends it to the side; the outer column of the back extensors.
iliocostalis.nerve: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves (segmental).
symptoms: Low-back ache that spreads into the buttock (lumbar part).
Ache at the lower shoulder blade, sometimes wrapping toward the belly (thoracic part).
Stiffness getting up after sitting.
Pain bending to the side or standing up from bending.

questions.q: Is the tender spot a few finger-widths out from the spine, not right beside it?
Does the low-back ache spread down into the buttock?
Does side-bending away from the painful side pull and hurt?
Is it worst getting up from a chair or straightening from bending?
Do you sometimes feel ache wrapping toward the belly or under the shoulder blade?

tests.name: Side-bend test
tests.how: Stand tall and slide one hand down the outside of the leg, then the other.
tests.positive: Pulling or your familiar ache on the side opposite the bend, a few inches from the spine.

causes: Long sitting followed by sudden bending or lifting.
Lifting and twisting at the same time.
Weak glutes and core leaving the back to do the work.
Standing in one position for long periods.
redFlags: Loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness in the saddle area: emergency.
Flank pain with fever or painful urination.
Pain after a fall, with osteoporosis, or with weight loss.

calm.name: Back extensor ball release
calm.how: Lie on a ball placed a few inches out from the spine at the sore level and let your weight sink in gently.

calm.name: Cat Cow Desk Variation
calm.how: Smooth, pain-free spinal motion.

restore.name: Sit Turn Lean
restore.how: Side-bend and rotate gently to lengthen the outer back.

restore.name: Dynamic Childs Pose
restore.how: Walk the hands to the side to stretch the opposite side of the back.

strengthen.name: Dowel Hip Hinge
strengthen.how: Hinge from the hips with a neutral spine so the glutes share the load.

strengthen.name: Dead Bug
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Keep the low back gently pressed down as the limbs move.

habits: Stand up every 30 minutes.
Hinge from the hips when lifting.
Avoid lifting and twisting at the same time.
iliocostalis.expect: Muscle-driven low-back pain usually improves in 1 to 3 weeks.
iliocostalis.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain spreads below the knee, there is numbness or weakness, or no improvement in 2 to 3 weeks.

longissimus.origin: Sacrum, back of the pelvis and lower vertebrae (common tendon).
longissimus.insertion: Transverse processes of the vertebrae and the lower ribs, up to the skull.
longissimus.action: Extends the spine and holds upright posture.
longissimus.nerve: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves (segmental).
symptoms: Pain low in the buttock and over the SI joint, often well below the muscle.
Ache beside the spine when standing for long periods.
Stiffness in the morning that eases with movement.
Pain arching back or straightening up.

questions.q: Is your pain low in the buttock or over the SI joint, but tender spots are higher up beside the spine?
Does long standing or walking upright bring it on?
Does arching backward hurt?
Is it stiff in the morning and better once you move?
Does sitting slumped relieve it a little?

tests.name: Standing back-bend
tests.how: Stand with hands on hips and gently arch backward.
tests.positive: Your familiar ache beside the spine or low in the buttock.

causes: Long standing with a sway-back posture.
Weak abs and glutes.
Heavy lifting with an arched back.
Running on hard surfaces.
redFlags: Saddle numbness or loss of bladder or bowel control: emergency.
Leg weakness or foot drop.
Night pain with fever or weight loss.

calm.name: Paraspinal ball release
calm.how: Lie on a ball just beside the spine at the tender level; breathe and let it soften.

calm.name: Cat Cow Desk Variation
calm.how: Gentle spinal motion.

restore.name: Pike Forward Fold
restore.how: Fold gently with soft knees, letting the back lengthen.

restore.name: Dynamic Childs Pose
restore.how: Rock back to stretch the low back.

strengthen.name: Dead Bug
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Build the abs that counter sway-back.

strengthen.name: Hip Thrust
strengthen.how: Drive with the glutes, ribs down, no arching.

habits: Stand with weight even and knees soft.
Shift positions every 20 to 30 minutes when standing.
longissimus.seePro: Book an evaluation if pain spreads down the leg, there are nerve symptoms, or no improvement in 2 to 3 weeks.

adductor-longus.origin: Front of the pubic bone near the midline.
adductor-longus.insertion: Middle third of the back of the thigh bone (linea aspera).
adductor-longus.action: Pulls the thigh inward and helps flex the hip; steadies the pelvis in cutting and kicking.
symptoms: Deep groin pain.
Ache along the inner thigh down to the inner knee and top of the shin.
Pain with kicking, sprinting, cutting or getting out of a car.
Tenderness near the pubic bone.

questions.q: Is the pain deep in the groin near the pubic bone?
Does squeezing your knees together against resistance hurt?
Does kicking, sprinting or changing direction bring it on?
Does the ache run down the inner thigh toward the knee?
Does getting out of a car hurt?

tests.name: Squeeze test
tests.how: Lie on your back with knees bent and squeeze a pillow or ball between the knees for 5 seconds.
tests.positive: Pain in the groin or inner thigh.

causes: Soccer, hockey and sports with cutting and kicking.
Sudden increase in sprinting.
Weak core and hip strength.
Tight hips limiting rotation.
redFlags: A pop in the groin with bruising.
A bulge in the groin that increases with coughing (hernia).
Groin pain with fever or painful urination.
Hip pain that makes you limp or wakes you at night.

calm.name: Inner thigh release
calm.how: Lie face down with the leg out to the side and a ball under the inner thigh; ease weight onto tender spots.

calm.name: Gentle isometric squeeze
calm.dose: 5 x 10 sec at 50% effort, twice daily
calm.how: Squeeze a pillow between the knees gently; pain should stay under 3/10.

restore.name: Standing Hip Abduction/Adduction
restore.how: Slow, controlled sweeps in a pain-free range.

restore.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
restore.how: Restore hip rotation to unload the groin.

strengthen.name: Copenhagen plank (short lever)
strengthen.dose: 3 x 15 sec per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Side plank with the top knee on a bench; lift the hips. Progress to the foot on the bench over weeks.

strengthen.name: Cossack Squat
strengthen.dose: 3 x 6 per side, twice weekly (from week 4)
strengthen.how: Only partial depth at first; keep the heel down.

habits: Warm up the groin before sport.
Build sprinting and cutting gradually.
adductor-longus.expect: Muscle-level groin pain improves in 2 to 4 weeks; return to cutting sports in 4 to 8 weeks.
adductor-longus.seePro: Book an evaluation if the squeeze test stays painful after 3 weeks, or if there is a bulge, limp or night pain.

adductor-magnus.origin: Lower pubic bone and the sitting bone (ischial tuberosity).
adductor-magnus.insertion: Back of the thigh bone along its length and the adductor tubercle above the inner knee.
adductor-magnus.action: Pulls the thigh inward and helps extend the hip like a hamstring.
adductor-magnus.nerve: Obturator nerve (L2–L4) and the tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L4).
symptoms: Deep pain inside the pelvis or groin, hard to pinpoint.
Ache along the inner thigh from the groin toward the knee.
Pain with deep squats, lunges or wide stances.
Pain sitting on the sitting bone.

questions.q: Is the pain deep in the groin or pelvis and hard to pinpoint?
Do deep squats or wide stances bring it on?
Is the inner thigh tender along its length toward the knee?
Does sitting on hard surfaces make it ache near the sitting bone?
Did it start after lunges, sumo lifts or horseback riding?

tests.name: Wide-stance hinge
tests.how: Stand with feet wide and toes out, hinge forward from the hips with a flat back.
tests.positive: Pulling or your familiar ache in the inner thigh or deep groin.

causes: Deep squats, sumo deadlifts and lunges.
Horseback riding and skiing.
Tight hamstrings and adductors from sitting.
Sudden splits or slips.
redFlags: Pelvic pain with fever, urinary or bowel symptoms.
A pop with bruising on the inner thigh.
Numbness on the inner thigh with weakness.

calm.name: Inner thigh release
calm.how: Use a ball or foam roller along the inner thigh, pausing on tender spots.

calm.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
calm.how: Gentle hip rotation.

restore.name: Standing Hip Abduction/Adduction
restore.how: Controlled sweeps in a pain-free range.

restore.name: Dynamic Childs Pose
restore.how: Knees wide to lengthen the adductors gently.

strengthen.name: Romanian Deadlift
strengthen.how: Slow hinge with soft knees; loads the hamstring part of the magnus.

strengthen.name: Cossack Squat
strengthen.dose: 3 x 6 per side, twice weekly (from week 4)
strengthen.how: Partial depth first.

habits: Warm up before deep squats or wide stances.
Use a cushion on hard seats.
adductor-magnus.seePro: Book an evaluation if deep pelvic pain persists, or comes with urinary, bowel or menstrual symptoms.

biceps-femoris.origin: Long head: sitting bone (ischial tuberosity). Short head: back of the thigh bone.
biceps-femoris.insertion: Head of the fibula on the outside of the knee.
biceps-femoris.action: Bends the knee, extends the hip and turns the lower leg outward.
biceps-femoris.nerve: Sciatic nerve: tibial part (long head) and common fibular part (short head), L5–S2.
symptoms: Ache at the back of the knee on the outside.
Pain up the back-outside of the thigh.
Tightness with sprinting or long strides.
Ache sitting for long periods.

questions.q: Is the pain on the outer back of the knee or the outer back of the thigh?
Does sprinting or long striding bring it on?
Is there a tender cord on the outside of the back of the knee?
Does sitting for a long time make it ache?
Does straightening the knee with the hip bent pull on the outside of the thigh?

tests.name: Straight-leg raise with outward turn
tests.how: Lie on your back and raise the straight leg with the foot turned slightly in, compared with the other side.
tests.positive: Pulling or ache along the outer back of the thigh before the other side.

causes: Sprinting and kicking.
Long sitting with knees bent.
Weak glutes making the hamstrings overwork.
Running without warm-up.
redFlags: A sudden pop and bruising at the back of the thigh.
Foot drop or numbness on the top of the foot.
Calf swelling and warmth (possible clot).

calm.name: Outer hamstring release
calm.how: Sit with a ball under the outer back of the thigh and slowly straighten and bend the knee.

calm.name: Hip Neuroglide
calm.how: Keep the sciatic nerve gliding without stretching hard.

restore.name: Pike Forward Fold
restore.how: Gentle fold with soft knees.

restore.name: Dowel Hip Hinge
restore.how: Learn to hinge so the hamstrings lengthen under control.

strengthen.name: Romanian Deadlift
strengthen.how: Slow lowering over 3 seconds.

strengthen.name: Hip Thrust
strengthen.how: Strong glutes take load off the hamstrings.

habits: Warm up before sprinting.
Break up long sitting every 30 minutes.
biceps-femoris.expect: Mild cases improve in 2 to 3 weeks; return to sprinting in 4 to 6 weeks.
biceps-femoris.seePro: Book an evaluation after any pop or bruising, or if pain persists past 3 weeks.

medial-hamstrings.insertion: Inner upper shin (semitendinosus via the pes anserinus; semimembranosus at the back-inner tibia).
medial-hamstrings.action: Bend the knee, extend the hip and turn the lower leg inward.
medial-hamstrings.nerve: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2).
symptoms: Ache at the buttock crease and sitting bone.
Pain down the back of the thigh.
Ache at the inner back of the knee, sometimes into the inner calf.
Pain sitting on hard chairs.

questions.q: Is the pain at the inner back of the knee or the buttock crease?
Does sitting on a hard chair hurt at the sitting bone?
Does bending forward with straight legs pull at the inner back of the thigh?
Did it start after running hills, sprinting or deadlifts?
Does it ache into the inner calf?

tests.name: Straight-leg raise with inward turn
tests.how: Lie on your back and raise the straight leg with the foot turned slightly out, compared with the other side.
tests.positive: Pulling or ache along the inner back of the thigh before the other side.

causes: Long sitting on hard surfaces.
Hill running and sprinting.
Heavy deadlifts without progression.
Weak glutes.
redFlags: A pop and bruising at the buttock crease.
Calf swelling, warmth or redness (possible clot).
Numbness in the sole of the foot with weakness.

calm.name: Inner hamstring release
calm.how: Sit with a ball under the inner back of the thigh and slowly bend and straighten the knee.

calm.name: Hip Neuroglide
calm.how: Gentle nerve gliding.

restore.name: Pike Forward Fold
restore.how: Gentle fold with soft knees.

restore.name: Dowel Hip Hinge
restore.how: Hinge pattern practice.

strengthen.name: Romanian Deadlift
strengthen.how: Slow lowering; progress load gradually.

strengthen.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Heel close to the buttock to load the hamstrings.

habits: Use a cushion and stand up every 30 minutes.
Build hill running gradually.
medial-hamstrings.expect: Usually improves in 2 to 4 weeks; tendon pain at the sitting bone can take 8 to 12 weeks.
medial-hamstrings.seePro: Book an evaluation if sitting pain persists past 3 weeks, or after any pop with bruising.

vastus-intermedius.origin: Front and outer side of the upper two-thirds of the thigh bone.
vastus-intermedius.insertion: Kneecap and, through the patellar tendon, the front of the shin.
vastus-intermedius.action: Straightens the knee; deep under the rectus femoris.
symptoms: Ache in the front of the mid-thigh.
Pain climbing stairs or standing up from a chair.
Weak or tired thigh when straightening the knee.
Tenderness deep in the front of the thigh.

questions.q: Is the ache in the front middle of the thigh rather than at the knee?
Does climbing stairs or standing up from a chair bring it on?
Is it hard to fully straighten the knee with strength?
Is there deep tenderness in the mid-thigh when you press firmly?
Does bending the knee fully feel tight in the thigh?

tests.name: Sit-to-stand
tests.how: Stand up from a chair five times without using your hands.
tests.positive: Ache in the front of the mid-thigh or weakness compared with the other leg.

causes: Sudden increase in stairs, hills or squats.
Thigh bruise (direct blow) that was not rehabbed.
Long periods sitting with the knee bent.
Weak hips placing extra load on the thigh.
redFlags: A hard, very painful lump after a blow to the thigh.
Deep thigh pain that worsens with running and at night (possible stress fracture).
Knee you cannot straighten after an injury.

calm.name: Quad roller release
calm.how: Lie face down with a foam roller under the front of the thigh and roll slowly, pausing on deep tender spots.

calm.name: Knee Circles
calm.how: Gentle knee motion.

restore.name: Couch Stretch
restore.how: Gentle stretch to the front of the thigh, ribs down.

restore.name: Knee Neuroglide
restore.how: Smooth knee and nerve motion.

strengthen.name: Step Up
strengthen.dose: 3 x 10 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Low box, slow lowering over 3 seconds.

strengthen.name: Bodyweight Squat
strengthen.how: Comfortable depth; progress range over weeks.

habits: Increase stairs and hills gradually.
Take breaks from long sitting to straighten the knees.
vastus-intermedius.seePro: Book an evaluation if there is a hard lump, night pain, or no improvement in 3 weeks.

ext-oblique.origin: Outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs.
ext-oblique.insertion: Iliac crest, the abdominal aponeurosis to the midline (linea alba) and the pubic bone.
ext-oblique.action: Rotates the trunk to the opposite side, bends it sideways and compresses the abdomen.
symptoms: Ache or burning in the abdominal wall or the side of the belly.
Pain that can feel like heartburn, a hernia or a side stitch.
Pain into the groin on the same side.
Pain twisting, coughing or getting out of bed.

questions.q: Does twisting your trunk reproduce the pain?
Does tensing your stomach (like a crunch) make a tender spot in the abdominal wall hurt more?
Does it ache into the groin on the same side?
Did it start after rotational sport, heavy lifting or coughing?
Is it unrelated to eating?

tests.name: Head-lift test (Carnett sign)
tests.how: Lie on your back, find the most tender spot, then lift your head and shoulders to tense the abdomen while pressing the spot.
tests.positive: The spot hurts the same or more when the abdomen is tensed, which points to the wall muscle rather than an organ.

causes: Rotational sports: golf, tennis, throwing.
Heavy lifting with twisting.
Chronic coughing.
Stiff upper back forcing the trunk to rotate at the abdomen.
redFlags: Abdominal pain with fever, vomiting, or a rigid belly: seek urgent care.
A bulge in the groin or abdomen.
Pain related to eating, with blood in stool or black stools.

calm.name: Thread The Needle
calm.how: Slow rotation through the upper back so the abdomen can relax.

calm.name: Baseball Cable Stretch
calm.how: Open the front of the trunk gently.

restore.name: Lying Open Book
restore.how: Rotate the upper back while the hips stay still.

restore.name: Quadruped T-Spine Rotation
restore.how: Restore upper-back rotation.

strengthen.name: Dead Bug
strengthen.dose: 3 x 8 per side, every other day
strengthen.how: Anti-rotation core control with the low back gently down.

strengthen.name: Farmer Carry
strengthen.how: Walk tall; one-arm carries train anti-rotation.

habits: Turn the whole body instead of twisting at the waist when lifting.
Treat a lingering cough.
Warm up rotation before sport.
ext-oblique.expect: Abdominal wall pain from the obliques usually eases in 1 to 3 weeks.
ext-oblique.seePro: Abdominal pain needs a doctor first if it comes with fever, vomiting, a bulge or changes with eating. Book with Dr. Jared once organ causes are ruled out.
